title: Astrophysical Fluid Dynamics
text:
Preface
These are the lecture notes for ASTRO 442, an introduction to the fluid dynamics and magnetohydrodynamics of astrophysical systems. They are written to be self-contained: the textbook, Clarke and Carswell’s Principles of Astrophysical Fluid Dynamics (Clarke and Carswell 2007), is optional further reading. Each chapter ends with pointers to the relevant sections of the textbook.

title: Astrophysical Fluid Dynamics
text:
How to use these notes

One chapter per lecture topic. Canvas lists which chapter goes with each lecture.
Everything is numbered by chapter. Equation (9.14) is the fourteenth numbered equation of Chapter 9, and Exercise 8.4 is the fourth exercise of Chapter 8. When you ask a question about the notes, quote these numbers.
In-class worksheets appear near the end of each chapter, followed by the exercises. Homework assignments on Canvas list the exercises to solve, for example “Exercises 2.1, 7.3”.
Optional material is set apart in boxes titled “Going further”; you can skip it on a first reading.

title: 1  Fluids as Continua
text:
1.1 Fluid elements
Astrophysical systems contain very large numbers of elementary particles. However, for most applications, we are only interested in the dynamics of the gas or plasma on scales that are large compared to the typical length scale of interaction between its constituents particles. In this context, it is convenient to treat matter as a continuum. That is, instead of keeping track of the momentum and position of each particle in the system, we describe it using equations for the evolution of macroscopic, average quantities.
We imagine matter as being composed of fluid elements. These are parcels of gas, or plasma, that have a characteristic size that is much smaller than the scales in which we are interested, but that still contain a large enough number of fluid constituents, molecules, or ions, so that it makes sense to talk about their properties, such as temperature. In other words, we require a fluid element \(\mathcal{V}\) to be a parcel of matter that can be considered to be in thermodynamic equilibrium. We will call fluid a system that is composed of fluid elements. As we will see later, the equations of motion for fluids do not explicitly depend on the size or shape of the fluid elements, so we will not attempt to define them more precisely. The only requirement is that fluid elements should exist. We will also discuss later what happens when the concept of fluid element breaks down. For the moment, we will assume that the system we are studying can be decomposed in fluid elements and we will derive equation of motion for these fluid elements.
We define the number density of a fluid element \(\mathcal{V}\) to be \[
n = \frac{\text{``number of particles in $\mathcal{V}$''}}{\text{``volume
$\mathcal{V}$''}} \qquad [\operatorname{cm}^{- 3}] .
\tag{1.1}\] As the system evolves, the number of particles inside the volume element \(\mathcal{V}\) remains constant, but the size of the volume changes, so \(n\) depends on both \(\mathcal{V}\) and the time \(t\).
An associated concept is that of the mass density (or simply density) \[
\rho = \frac{\text{``mass contained in $\mathcal{V}$''}}{\text{``volume of
$\mathcal{V}$''}} \qquad [\mathrm{g} \operatorname{cm}^{- 3}] .
\tag{1.2}\] If the gas is composed of identical particles of mass \(m\), then \(\rho = mn\). For mixtures with many constituents \[
\rho = \sum_{i = 1}^N m_i n_i = \sum_{i = 1}^N m_i Y_i n = \mu n,
\tag{1.3}\] where we have introduced the particle number fractions \(Y_i = n_i / n\) and the mean molecular weight \(\mu\). We can also decompose \(\rho\) in terms of the mass densities of the different species \(\rho_i = m_i n_i\): \[
\rho = \sum_{i = 1}^N \rho_i = \sum_{i = 1}^N X_i \rho .
\tag{1.4}\] The \(X_i = \rho_i / \rho\) are the mass fractions. \(Y_i\) measures the relative contribution of each species to the number density, while \(X_i\) measures the relative contribution to the mass density. In general, \(X_i \neq Y_i\), unless all particle species have the same mass.
We also assume that each element has fixed velocity \[
\mathbf{v}= \text{``velocity of $\mathcal{V}$''} \qquad [\operatorname{cm}
\mathrm{s}^{- 1}]
\tag{1.5}\] and temperature \[
T = \text{``temperature of $\mathcal{V}$''} \qquad [\mathrm{K}] .
\tag{1.6}\] With these definitions in place, we are now ready to state explicitly the assumptions that we are making when we treat a gas or a plasma as a fluid. Consider region \(\mathcal{R}\) filled with matter. We say that this system can be treated as a fluid if the following assumption holds.
This assumption tells us that it makes sense to say that there is a single value of density, temperature, and velocity at each point. This assumption is violated, for example, in systems in which different particle species move independently. Such systems can sometimes be described as multi-fluids, that is systems in which there are different kinds of fluid elements that interact with each other. Plasmas in weakly collisional regimes can sometimes be treated as multi-fluids. A gas of photons in vacuum, instead, cannot be treated as a (multi-)fluid, since at each point in space there are photons traveling in infinitely many different directions.
The assumption also implies that sufficiently small parcels of material are in thermodynamic equilibrium, so that fluid elements have a well defined temperature. This is also called local thermodynamic equilibrium (LTE) condition. This condition is violated in some impulsive phenomena, such as in shock waves. Violations of LTE can sometimes be included in the fluid model. We will see two examples later: the effect of viscosity and heat conduction and the treatment of shocks. In other cases, it is necessary to describe non-LTE effects using a combination of fluid and non-fluid models. For example, to simulate the effect of cosmic rays on the dynamics of clouds in the interstellar medium it is necessary to solve separate equations for the cosmic rays, which cannot be treated as a fluid, and for the rest of the matter, for which the fluid approximation holds very well.
It is important to note that whether or not the fluid assumption holds is not an absolute statement, but also depends on the time and length scale of interest. For example, the dynamics of dark matter in the Bullet cluster (Figure 1.1) cannot be described using the fluid approximation. This is because dark matter does not flow with a single velocity. On the other hand, on cosmological scales, dark matter dynamics can be reasonably well described using a pressure-less fluid model: this is the so-called Zel’dovich approximation.

title: 1  Fluids as Continua
text:
1.2 The continuity equation
We now assume to have a system that can be described as a fluid. We wish to derive equations to predict how \(\rho\), \(\mathbf{v}\), and \(T\) evolve for all fluid elements. To this aim, we will use three fundamental laws in classical physics: 1) the law of conservation of mass; 2) Newton’s second law; and 3) the first law of thermodynamics. The law of conservation of mass gives rise to the continuity equation, which we will now derive.






Figure 1.2: Fluid element stretching in the \(x\)-direction.



Consider the infinitesimal fluid element \(\mathcal{V}\) shown in Figure 1.2. Let \(\mathrm{d} x\) be the size of the fluid element along the \(x\)-direction at some time \(t\). Let \(v_x\) be the \(x\)-component of the velocity. If we take the origin to be the center of the fluid element, the velocity with which the left face is moving is \(v_x \left( - \tfrac{\mathrm{d} x}{2} \right)\), while the velocity of the right face is \(v_x \left( \tfrac{\mathrm{d} x}{2} \right)\). For the moment, we assume \(v_y = v_z = 0\). The initial volume of \(\mathcal{V}\) is \(V = \mathrm{d} x \mathrm{d} y \mathrm{d} z\). At time \(t + \mathrm{d} t\), \(\mathcal{V}\) is deformed and has volume \[
V' = \left( \mathrm{d} x + \left[ v_x \left( \tfrac{\mathrm{d} x}{2} \right) - v_x
\left( - \tfrac{\mathrm{d} x}{2} \right) \right] \mathrm{d} t \right) \mathrm{d} y
\mathrm{d} z = \left( \mathrm{d} x + \frac{\partial v_x}{\partial x} \mathrm{d} x \mathrm{d}
t \right) \mathrm{d} y \mathrm{d} z,
\tag{1.7}\] so the relative rate in the change of volume of \(\mathcal{V}\) is \[
\frac{1}{V}  \frac{\mathrm{d} V}{\mathrm{d} t} = \frac{1}{V}  \frac{V' - V}{\mathrm{d}
t} = \frac{\partial v_x}{\partial x} .
\tag{1.8}\] In an analogous way, we can find the rate of change of an infinitesimal volume \(V\) if \(v_y\) and \(v_z\) are nonzero: \[
\frac{1}{V}  \frac{\mathrm{d} V}{\mathrm{d} t} = \frac{\partial v_x}{\partial x} +
\frac{\partial v_y}{\partial y} + \frac{\partial v_z}{\partial z} = \nabla
\cdot \mathbf{v}.
\tag{1.9}\] We have derived this equation for a cubical fluid element. However, it turns out that this equation holds in general. The extension of this result to finite (as opposed to infinitesimal) fluid elements is known as the Reynolds theorem, which states that
\[
\frac{\mathrm{d} V}{\mathrm{d} t} = \int_{\partial \Omega} \mathbf{v} \cdot
\mathbf{n} \mathrm{d} S = \int_{\Omega} \nabla \cdot \mathbf{v} \mathrm{d} V,
\tag{1.10}\] where \(\Omega\) is some extended region comoving with the flow, \(\partial \Omega\) is the surface enclosing \(\Omega\), and \(\mathbf{n}\) is the outwards pointing normal to it.
A proof of this theorem is outside the scope of this course, but it can be found in any book on continuum mechanics. Its geometrical interpretation is illustrated in Figure 1.3. The first equality means that the rate of change of the volume of \(\Omega\) is equal to the surface integral of the component of the velocity normal to the volume. This makes sense, because the tangent part of the velocity does not alter the shape of the volume, but corresponds locally to a rotation, while the normal components corresponds to an expansion/contraction of \(\Omega\). The second equality follows from the Gauss divergence theorem. Because \(\nabla \cdot \mathbf{v}\) determines the rate of change of the fluid element volumes, it is also called the expansion.






Figure 1.3: The instantaneous rate of change in the volume of a region is equal to the flux of the velocity field through its boundary.



If we denote by \(\mathcal{M}\) the mass of a fluid element \(\mathcal{V}\), and use the fact that \(\mathcal{M}\) is conserved, then we find \[
\rho = \frac{\mathcal{M}}{V} \Longrightarrow \frac{\mathrm{d} \rho}{\mathrm{d} t} =
- \frac{\mathcal{M}}{V^2}  \frac{\mathrm{d} V}{\mathrm{d} t} = -
\frac{\mathcal{M}}{V}  \frac{1}{V}  \frac{\mathrm{d} V}{\mathrm{d} t} = - \rho
\nabla \cdot \mathbf{v} .
\tag{1.11}\] We can rearrange the terms to obtain \[
\boxed{\frac{1}{\rho}  \frac{\mathrm{d} \rho}{\mathrm{d} t} = - \nabla \cdot
\mathbf{v}}
\tag{1.12}\] This is the continuity equation. The first of the fundamental equations of motion for fluids. Note that this equation can also be written in terms of \(n\): \[
\frac{1}{n}  \frac{\mathrm{d} n}{\mathrm{d} t} = - \nabla \cdot \mathbf{v}.
\tag{1.13}\] The continuity equation also holds separately for the \(n_i\) and \(\rho_i\) of each species in the fluid, as long as there are no chemical reactions converting between the species, i.e., \(\dot{X}_i = \dot{Y}_i = 0\).






TipExample



A flow in which all fluid elements have the same velocity has \(\nabla \cdot \mathbf{v}= 0\), since \(\mathbf{v}\) is a constant, so \(\rho = \operatorname{const}\).








TipExample



Consider a planar flow \(\mathbf{v}= (- y, x, 0)\) [arbitrary units]. This is an example of a rotating flow, as shown in the visualization below:






Figure 1.4: Velocity field \(\mathbf{v}= (-y, x, 0)\).



This flow also has \(\rho = \operatorname{const}\): \[
\nabla \cdot \mathbf{v}= \frac{\partial v_x}{\partial x} + \frac{\partial
v_y}{\partial y} = \frac{\partial (- y)}{\partial x} + \frac{\partial
(x)}{\partial y} = 0.
\tag{1.14}\]








TipExample



In cylindrical coordinates \((\varpi, z, \phi)\), a generic rotating flow with rotational axis along \(z\) takes the form \[
\mathbf{v}= v_{\phi}  \hat{\boldsymbol{\phi}} .
\tag{1.15}\] Rotating flows preserve the volume of fluid elements if \[
\nabla \cdot \mathbf{v}= \frac{1}{\varpi}  \frac{\partial (\varpi
v_{\varpi})}{\partial \varpi} + \frac{1}{\varpi}  \frac{\partial
v_{\phi}}{\partial \phi} + \frac{\partial v_z}{\partial z} =
\frac{1}{\varpi}  \frac{\partial v_{\phi}}{\partial \phi} = 0.
\tag{1.16}\] That is, as long as all fluid elements with fixed \((\varpi, z)\) rotate with the same angular frequency.


Flows for which \(\nabla \cdot \mathbf{v}= 0\) everywhere are said to be incompressible. An important property of incompressible flows is that the net flux of the velocity field across any closed surface should vanish: \[
\int_{\partial \Omega} \mathbf{v} \cdot \mathbf{n} \mathrm{d} \Sigma =
\int_{\Omega} \nabla \cdot \mathbf{v} \mathrm{d} \Omega = 0.
\tag{1.17}\] We can interpret this result graphically by introducing the velocity field lines, also called streamlines. These are curves \((x (s), y (s), z (s))\) satisfying \[
\frac{\mathrm{d} x}{\mathrm{d} s} = v_x, \quad \frac{\mathrm{d} y}{\mathrm{d} s} = v_y,
\quad \frac{\mathrm{d} z}{\mathrm{d} s} = v_z .
\tag{1.18}\] In an incompressible flow streamlines cross each closed surface at least twice and there are no sources or sinks for the streamlines (Figure 1.5).






Figure 1.5: Streamlines in an incompressible flow (left) cross each closed surface twice. Expansion or compression flows (right) have streamline sources or sinks. Note the analogy with the solenoidal geometry of magnetic field lines in magnetism.

title: 1  Fluids as Continua
text:
1.3 Radial flows
Most astrophysical transients are the result of explosions that generate approximately radial outflows. As such, an important class of flows are those for which the gas is flowing in the radial direction: \[
\mathbf{v}= v_r  \hat{\mathbf{r}} .
\tag{1.19}\] These are called radial flows. In the previous equation, \(v_r\) could in principle depend on both radial \(r\), but also on the direction \(\theta, \varphi\).
From the continuity equation, we find that radial flows are generically compressible: \[
\begin{alignedat}{2}
\nabla \cdot \mathbf{v} &{}={} && \frac{1}{r^2}  \frac{\partial}{\partial r}
(r^2 v_r) + \frac{1}{r \sin \theta}  \frac{\partial}{\partial \theta} (\sin
\theta v_{\theta}) \\
&&& + \frac{1}{r \sin \theta}  \frac{\partial
v_{\varphi}}{\partial \varphi}  \\
&{}={} && \frac{1}{r^2}  \frac{\partial}{\partial r}  (r^2 v_r) \\
&{}={} && \frac{\partial v_r}{\partial r} + \frac{2}{r} v_r \neq 0.
\end{alignedat}
\tag{1.20}\] Note that, the radial direction, \(\hat{\mathbf{r}}\), is not well defined at the origin, since all directions are radial there. This implies that \(v_r (r = 0) = 0\). This regularity condition also ensures that the fluid element at the origin is not “broken” (transported in different directions), but only stretched.
An important example of radial flow is that of an homologously expanding (or contracting) sphere of gas. Here, “homologous” means that the relative rate of change of the volume of each fluid element, \(\frac{1}{V} \frac{\mathrm{d} V}{\mathrm{d} t}\), is equal for all fluid elements. To see how this works, we consider a sphere of gas that at time \(t = 0\) has a constant density \(\rho_0\). The assumption of constant density is not necessary, as all calculations will remain valid even for variable density, but it will make the results more transparent.
In an homologous flow, the velocity of fluid elements that are at \(r = p\) at \(t = 0\) is given by \[
v_r (r = p, t = 0) = Hp,
\tag{1.21}\] where \(H\) is a constant. At later times, we assume that each fluid elements continues to move with the velocity it had initially. In other words, we are assuming that fluid elements are not subject to any force and they coast at their original velocity. This is Newton’s first law applied to the fluid elements.
To find the change in density in the system, we could be tempted to write \[
\nabla \cdot \mathbf{v}= \frac{1}{r^2}  \frac{\partial}{\partial r}  (r^2
v_r) \overset{!!!}{=} \frac{1}{r^2}  \frac{\partial}{\partial r}  (r^3 H) = 3 H,
\tag{1.22}\] but this is incorrect. The issue is that at any time \(t \neq 0\), the velocity of a fluid element at the location \(r\) is not \(Hr\). Instead, its velocity is \(Hp\), where \(p\) is the position that that fluid element had at time \(t = 0\).
To find it, we consider the equation of motion of the fluid element originally located at \(r = p\): \[
\frac{\mathrm{d} r (t ; p)}{\mathrm{d} t} = Hp, \qquad r (0 ; p) = p.
\tag{1.23}\] This can be integrated to find \[
r (t ; p) = p + Hpt.
\tag{1.24}\] Solving for \(p\) gives \[
p = \frac{r}{1 + Ht} .
\tag{1.25}\] This means that \[
v_r (r, t) = \frac{rH}{1 + Ht} \neq rH.
\tag{1.26}\] The continuity equation gives \[
\frac{1}{\rho}  \frac{\mathrm{d} \rho}{\mathrm{d} t} = - \nabla \cdot \mathbf{v}= -
3 \frac{H}{1 + Ht} .
\tag{1.27}\] Note that the expansion (or compression if \(H < 0\)) rates depend only on \(H\) and \(t\) and not on the initial position of the fluid element \(p\). In other words, all fluid elements are expanding/contracting at the same rate.
To make this result more transparent, we define \(R (t)\) to be the radius of the expanding/contracting gas sphere at time \(t\). Evidently, \(\dot{R} (t) = HR_0\) and \(R (t) = R_0 (1 + Ht)\). So Equation 1.27 can be written as \[
\boxed{\frac{\dot{\rho}}{\rho} = - 3 \frac{\dot{R}}{R}}
\tag{1.28}\] The flows produced by many types of astronomical explosions can be described well as homologously expanding flows at sufficiently late times. Typically, once the gas has expanded to twice its initial radius. This is because as the gas expands, it rearranges to reach pressure equilibrium. Afterwards, the fluid elements are not subject to any net force, so they coast at a fixed velocity. As we will see later, among all possible coasting flows, homologous expansion is the only one that preserves pressure equilibrium, so it is an attractive solution.

title: 2  Thermodynamics Refresher
text:
2.1 Equation of state for ideal gases
In our discussion so far, we have considered a gas to be a set of fluid elements, each with its own macroscopic velocity \(\mathbf{v}\). However, gases are actually composed of particles, each with its own microscopic velocity. How do we reconcile these two pictures? For simplicity, let’s consider a fluid element \(\mathcal{V}\) containing a single species of atoms, each having mass \(m\). Let \(\mathbf{u}_i\) be the velocity of the \(i\)th particle. Then we can decompose \(\mathbf{u}_i\) as \[
\mathbf{u}_i =\mathbf{v}+\mathbf{w}_i,
\tag{2.1}\] where \[
\mathbf{v}= \langle \mathbf{u} \rangle = \frac{1}{N}  \sum_{i = 1}^N
\mathbf{u}_i,
\tag{2.2}\] is the average velocity and \(\mathbf{w}_i\) is the peculiar velocity of each particle. By definition \(\langle \mathbf{w} \rangle = 0\).
Because the random component of the velocity averages to zero, it does not impact the continuity equation. To see this, consider the net mass flux across the grayed surface in Figure 2.1. Over any given \(\mathrm{d} t\), only the particles in the region with volume \(\langle u_x \rangle \mathrm{d} t \mathrm{d} A\) cross the surface, so the mass flux is \[
nm \langle u_x  \rangle \mathrm{d} t \mathrm{d} A = \rho v_x \mathrm{d} t \mathrm{d} A
\tag{2.3}\] However, the random motion of particles contributes to a net momentum flux. This is because each particle contributes a momentum \(mu_x\), so the momentum flux is \[
F \mathrm{d} t = nm \langle u_x^2 \rangle \mathrm{d} t \mathrm{d} A = \rho v_x^2 \mathrm{d}
t \mathrm{d} A + \rho \langle w_x^2 \rangle \mathrm{d} t \mathrm{d} A.
\tag{2.4}\] Note that the momentum flux per unit time has units of \[
[F] = [\rho v_x^2 \mathrm{d} A] =\mathrm{g} \operatorname{cm} \mathrm{s}^{- 2},
\tag{2.5}\] so the quantity \(\rho \langle w_x^2 \rangle\) is a force per unit area. We define as gas pressure the quantity \[
p = \frac{1}{3} \rho \langle | \mathbf{w} |^2 \rangle .
\tag{2.6}\] The factor \(1 / 3\) can be understood to come from the fact that pressure forces are the result of random motion in three directions. In analogy, the quantity \(\rho v_x^2\) is called the ram pressure. If you are swimming in a river the ram pressure is the force that tries to drag you along with the flow, while the pressure is responsible for the buoyancy you experience.
For a monoatomic gas with particles of mass \(m\), the rms velocity can be computed using the equipartition theorem1: \[
m \langle | \mathbf{w} |^2 \rangle = 3 k_B T,
\tag{2.7}\] where \(T\) is the temperature in Kelvin and \(k_B\) is the Boltzmann constant, which in CGS units reads \[
k_B \cong 1.380649 \times 10^{- 16} \operatorname{erg} \mathrm{K}^{- 1} .
\tag{2.8}\] Combining this with Equation 2.6 we find the equation of state for an ideal gas: \[
\boxed{p = nk_B T.}
\tag{2.9}\] Often, the equation of state for ideal gases is written in terms of the ideal gas constant \(\mathcal{R}\) as \[
p = \frac{\mathcal{R}}{N_A m} \rho T,
\tag{2.10}\] where \(N_A\) is Avogadro’s number. Since \(n = \frac{\rho}{m}\), we see that \(\mathcal{R}\) is just an alias for \(N_A k_B\). For mixtures of monoatomic gases, Equation 2.9 remains unchanged, but \(n\) is now the number density of particles of any species, but Equation 2.10 becomes \[
p = \frac{\mathcal{R}}{N_A \mu} \rho T,
\tag{2.11}\] where \(\mu\) is the mean molecular weight: \[
\mu = \frac{\rho}{n} .
\tag{2.12}\] Thermal motion is not only a source of pressure, but also a reservoir of energy for the gas. In other words, because of their motion, the particles in the gas have average kinetic energy per unit mass \[
\varepsilon = \frac{1}{2} \langle | \mathbf{w} |^2 \rangle = \frac{3}{2 m}
k_B T \Longrightarrow k_B T = \frac{2}{3} m \varepsilon .
\tag{2.13}\] Using this definition we can eliminate the temperature from the ideal-gas equation of state: \[
p = \frac{2}{3} \rho \varepsilon,
\tag{2.14}\] where we have used the definition \(\rho = nm\).
The last equation is a particular case of a \(\Gamma\)-law equation of state: \[
\boxed{p = (\Gamma - 1) \rho \varepsilon,}
\tag{2.15}\] where \(\Gamma = \frac{5}{3}\) for a monoatomic gas. The \(\Gamma\)-law equation of state is a good approximation also for non monoatomic gases or mixture of gases, for which Equation 2.14 does not hold. For example, air can be described with a \(\Gamma\)-law equation of state with \(\Gamma = 1.4\). Another example is given by radiation-dominated gases, which we discuss below. Note that it is possible to rewrite Equation 2.15 as \[
p = (\Gamma - 1) e,
\tag{2.16}\] where \(e = \rho \varepsilon\) is the gas energy density, measured in \(\mathrm{erg} / \mathrm{cm}^3\).

title: 2  Thermodynamics Refresher
text:
2.2 The first law of thermodynamics
The first law of thermodynamics applied to a fluid element of volume \(V\) and mass \(\mathcal{M}\) reads \[
\mathrm{d} E = \delta Q - \delta W.
\tag{2.17}\] It states that the amount of energy in the fluid element increases by the amount of heat absorbed by the fluid element, \(\delta Q\), and decreases by the amount of mechanical work done, \(\delta W\).
For a perfect fluid, the change in the mechanical work is given by \[
\delta W = p \mathrm{d} V,
\tag{2.18}\] where \(V\) is the volume of the fluid element. In the case of nonperfect fluids, there are corrections that arise from the anisotropic components of the stress tensor.
For an ideal gas, the amount of absorbed heat is given by \[
\delta Q = T \mathrm{d} S.
\tag{2.19}\] In many cases, it is convenient to work with the first law of thermodynamics using specific (per unit mass) quantities: \[
\varepsilon = \frac{E}{\mathcal{M}}, \qquad w = \frac{W}{\mathcal{M}},
\qquad q = \frac{Q}{\mathcal{M}}, \qquad s = \frac{S}{\mathcal{M}}, \qquad v
= \frac{V}{\mathcal{M}} = \frac{1}{\rho} .
\tag{2.20}\] In terms of the specific quantities, the first law reads \[
\mathrm{d} \varepsilon = \delta q - \delta w = T \mathrm{d} s - p \mathrm{d} v = T
\mathrm{d} s + \frac{p}{\rho^2} \mathrm{d} \rho .
\tag{2.21}\] In the case of adiabatic flows \(\delta q = 0\), the first law simplifies to \[
\mathrm{d} \varepsilon = \frac{p}{\rho^2} \mathrm{d} \rho .
\tag{2.22}\] For a \(\Gamma\)-law equation of state \(\varepsilon = \frac{p}{(\Gamma - 1) \rho}\), so we find \[
\frac{1}{\rho} \mathrm{d} p - \frac{p}{\rho^2} \mathrm{d} \rho = (\Gamma - 1)
\frac{p}{\rho^2} \mathrm{d} \rho \Longrightarrow \frac{\mathrm{d} p}{p} = \Gamma
\frac{\mathrm{d} \rho}{\rho} .
\tag{2.23}\] This can be integrated to yield \[
\boxed{p = K \rho^{\Gamma},}
\tag{2.24}\] where \(K\) is an integration constant. Equation 2.24 represents a so-called polytropic equation of state. Note that for an adiabatic flow, \(K\) is constant with time in each fluid element, but \(K\) does not have to be the same in each fluid element. A comparison between Equation 2.24 and Equation 2.15 shows that \[
K = (\Gamma - 1) \rho^{1 - \Gamma} \varepsilon .
\tag{2.25}\] Note that, since Equation 2.24 is barotropic, this equation of state, together with the continuity and velocity equations, form a closed system of equations, using which it is, in principle, possible to compute all quantities in the flow. However, the polytropic equation of state cannot be applied if \(\delta q \neq 0\), due to the presence of heating or cooling of the gas. Even if the flow is adiabatic (\(\delta q = 0\)), there are irreversible thermodynamic processes that operate in shocks. When this happens, the steps we took to get  Equation 2.24 from Equation 2.21 are no longer valid, because \(\delta Q\) and \(\delta W\) are not exact differentials. In all these situations, it is necessary to derive a new equation, in addition to the equation of state and the velocity and continuity equations, to close the system. This will be accomplished with the energy equation, discussed below.

title: 2  Thermodynamics Refresher
text:
2.3 Radiation pressure
Gas-pressure is not the only relevant source of pressure in astrophysical flows. Radiation pressure is another important component. While gas pressure arises due to the random (or thermal) component of the velocity of particles, radiation pressure arises as a result of momentum deposition by photons in optically thick conditions, in which radiation can be considered to be isotropic and in thermal equilibrium with the gas. It is not possible to derive radiation pressure in the same way as we derived the gas pressure, because photons are not classical particles and a rigorous derivation would require us to use quantum mechanics. However, we can find an expression for the radiation pressure up to a constant factor using classical thermodynamics.
Consider a region filled with radiation and let \(e\) be the energy density in radiation. We assume that the radiation field is isotropic, meaning that there is an equal probability to find a photon traveling in each direction. In other words, the energy density of photons per unit solid angle of direction is \(J = \frac{e}{4 \pi}\). Let’s compute the flux of momentum crossing an area \(\mathrm{d} A\) with normal \(\hat{\mathbf{n}}\) (shown in Figure 2.2).






Figure 2.2: Area element for the calculation of the radiation pressure.



Each photon with energy \(\varepsilon\) carries a momentum \(\varepsilon / c\). Over the time interval \(\mathrm{d} t\) photons in the volume \(\mathrm{d} V = c \mathrm{d} t \mathrm{d} A \cos \theta\) will cross \(\mathrm{d} A\), each carrying a normal component of the momentum equal to \(\varepsilon / c \cos \theta\), so the overall flux of momentum is \[
\int J (\cos \theta)^2 \mathrm{d} t \mathrm{d} A \mathrm{d} \Omega = \frac{e \mathrm{d} t
\mathrm{d} A}{4 \pi} \int_0^{2 \pi} \mathrm{d} \varphi \int_0^{\pi} \mathrm{d} \theta \sin \theta
(\cos \theta)^2 = \frac{1}{3} e \mathrm{d} t \mathrm{d} A \Longrightarrow
\boxed{p = \frac{1}{3} e.}
\tag{2.26}\] So we have found that the radiation pressure can be described with a \(\Gamma\)-law equation of state with \(\Gamma = 4 / 3\). However, to be able to actually compute the pressure, we need to find a relation between \(e, p\) and the temperature \(T\). Consider the following thought experimental setup (Figure 2.3):






Figure 2.3: Blackbody enclosure.



The first and second law of thermodynamics read \[
\delta Q = \mathrm{d} E + p \mathrm{d} V, \quad T \mathrm{d} S = \delta Q.
\tag{2.27}\] The energy can be written in terms of the energy density as \(E = eV\), so \[
\mathrm{d} E = \mathrm{d} eV + e \mathrm{d} V = V \frac{\mathrm{d} e}{\mathrm{d} T} \mathrm{d} T + e
\mathrm{d} V
\tag{2.28}\] Solving Equation 2.27 for \(\mathrm{d} S\) and using Equation 2.26 to eliminate \(p\), we find \[
\mathrm{d} S = \frac{V}{T}  \frac{\mathrm{d} e}{\mathrm{d} T} \mathrm{d} T + \frac{4}{3}
\frac{e}{T} \mathrm{d} V.
\tag{2.29}\] We can rewrite the previous equation as: \[
\left( \frac{\partial S}{\partial T} \right)_V = \frac{V}{T}  \frac{\mathrm{d}
e}{\mathrm{d} T}, \qquad \left( \frac{\partial S}{\partial V} \right)_T =
\frac{4}{3}  \frac{e}{T} .
\tag{2.30}\] Since \(\mathrm{d} S\) is an exact differential: \[
\frac{\partial^2 S}{\partial V \partial T} = \frac{1}{T}  \frac{\mathrm{d}
e}{\mathrm{d} T} = \frac{4}{3}  \frac{1}{T}  \frac{\mathrm{d} e}{\mathrm{d} T} -
\frac{4}{3}  \frac{e}{T^2} = \frac{\partial^2 S}{\partial T \partial V} .
\tag{2.31}\] Combining the terms we find \[
\frac{\mathrm{d} e}{\mathrm{d} T} = 4 \frac{e}{T} \Longrightarrow \boxed{e =
aT^4 .}
\tag{2.32}\] The constant of integration, is the radiation constant. It can be derived using quantum mechanics: \[
a \cong 7.5646 \times 10^{- 15} \operatorname{erg} \operatorname{cm}^{- 3} \mathrm{K}^{- 4}
.
\tag{2.33}\] The radiation constant is related to the Stefan–Boltzmann constant \(\sigma\) by \[
a = \frac{4 \sigma}{c},
\tag{2.34}\] where \(c\) is the speed of light.
In general, both radiation and gas pressure can be present. For example, for ionized stellar matter the pressure and energy densities can be computed as \[
p = \frac{\rho}{\mu} k_B T + \frac{1}{3} aT^4, \qquad e = \rho \varepsilon =
\frac{3}{2}  \frac{\rho}{\mu} k_B T + aT^4 .
\tag{2.35}\]

title: 2  Thermodynamics Refresher
text:
2.4 Energy equation
The first law of thermodynamics can be used to derive the energy equation for a perfect fluid. We start from the first law written for the energy per unit volume \[
\mathrm{d} \varepsilon = \delta q + \frac{p}{\rho}  \frac{\mathrm{d} \rho}{\rho} .
\tag{2.36}\] Dividing both terms by \(\mathrm{d} t\) and multiplying by \(\rho\) gives \[
\boxed{\rho \frac{\mathrm{d} \varepsilon}{\mathrm{d} t} = \rho \dot{q} - p
\nabla \cdot \mathbf{v}.}
\tag{2.37}\] The first term on the RHS is the net heating rate \(\dot{q} = \dot{q}_{\operatorname{heat}} - \dot{q}_{\operatorname{cool}}\). For example,  \(\dot{q}_{\operatorname{heat}}\) might represents the energy generation due to nuclear burning in the gas, while \(\dot{q}_{\operatorname{cool}}\) might be the energy lost by emitting radiation. The second term is the so-called pdV term. It represents the energy spent by doing work on the environment, or on other fluid elements. A list of common heating and cooling processes in astrophysics is given in Clarke and Carswell (2007), Section 4.4.

title: 2  Thermodynamics Refresher
text:
2.5 In-class worksheet
The first law of thermodynamics for an ideal-gas reads \[
\mathrm{d} E = T \mathrm{d} S - p \mathrm{d} V.
\tag{2.38}\] Define the specific (per unit mass) quantities: \[
\varepsilon = \frac{E}{\mathcal{M}}, \qquad w = \frac{W}{\mathcal{M}},
\qquad q = \frac{Q}{\mathcal{M}}, \qquad s = \frac{S}{\mathcal{M}},
\qquad v = \frac{V}{\mathcal{M}} = \frac{1}{\rho} .
\tag{2.39}\]

Find an expression for \(\mathrm{d} \varepsilon\) in terms of \(T, s, p, \rho\).
Consider an ideal-gas with \(p = (\Gamma - 1) \rho \varepsilon\) undergoing an adiabatic process (\(\delta q = 0\)).

Show that \[
p = K \rho^{\Gamma} .
\tag{2.40}\]
What is the relation between \(K\) and \(\varepsilon\)?

Consider an adiabatically expanding radiation-pressure dominated gas sphere. Let \(T\) and \(V\) be the temperature and volume of the gas at a given time \(t.\)

Find an expression for the entropy of the gas \(S\).
Show that \(pV^{4 / 3} = \operatorname{const}\) as the gas expands.

title: 2  Thermodynamics Refresher
text:
2.6 Exercises

Exercise 2.1 (Equation of state of an H/He plasma) Consider a mixture of ionized hydrogen and helium with \(X_{\mathrm{H}} = 70\%\) and \(X_{\mathrm{He}} = 30\%\). The pressure is given by \[
p = p_{\mathrm{ions}} + p_e + p_{\mathrm{rad}},
\tag{2.41}\] where \(p_{\mathrm{ions}}\) is the partial pressure of the ions, \(p_e\) is the partial pressure of the electrons, and \(p_{\mathrm{rad}}\) is the radiation pressure. Treat ions and electrons as ideal monoatomic gasses (with the appropriate mean molecular weights).

Write a code to compute \(p_{\mathrm{ions}}\), \(p_e\), and \(p_{\mathrm{rad}}\) for any given density \(\rho\) and temperature \(T\).
Plot \(p_{\mathrm{ions}}\), \(p_e\), and \(p_{\mathrm{rad}}\) as a function of temperature for \(\rho = 150\,\mathrm{g\,cm^{-3}}\) (central density of the Sun) and for \(\rho = 10^{-24}\,\mathrm{g\,cm^{-3}}\) (ISM density). At what temperature does radiation become dominant in each case?

title: 3  Core-Collapse Supernovae
text:
3.1 Observational facts
Supernovae are among the most energetic and luminous transients in the sky. They are the result of the explosion of massive stars, or of accreting white dwarfs at the end of their lives. Here, we use the tools of fluid mechanics we have developed so far to construct a simple model for these and similar explosive transients, such as novae and kilonovae. Our goal is to understand the basic physics, not to develop precise models, or to discuss all the nuisance of the problem, for which we refer to the specialized literature.
Observationally, supernovae are characterized by a fast rise in the luminosity, on a timescale of a few days. They peak on a timescale of days to weeks and then decline over a timescale of months. A famous example of a core-collapse supernova light curve is given by the SN1987a light curve in Figure 3.1. At peak magnitude, supernovae have luminosity \(L \sim 10^{10} L_{\odot}\), where \(L_{\odot}\) is the luminosity of the Sun. They remain bright for weeks to months, before beginning to fade. At peak, their typical effective temperature is \(T_{\operatorname{eff}} \sim 2 T_{\odot} \approx 12{,}000\,\mathrm{K}\), \(T_{\odot}\) being the effective temperature of the Sun. For a black body, the Stefan–Boltzmann law gives a relation between temperature and luminosity: \[
L = 4 \pi R^2 \sigma T^4,
\tag{3.1}\] where \(\sigma\) is the Stefan–Boltzmann constant \[
\sigma = \frac{ac}{4} = 5.6704 \cdot 10^{-5} \operatorname{erg} \operatorname{cm}^{- 2}
\mathrm{s}^{- 1} \mathrm{K}^{- 4} .
\tag{3.2}\] Assuming in first approximation supernovae to be black body emitters, this implies that the characteristic radius of a supernova at peak magnitude is \[
R_p \sim 2.5 \cdot 10^4 R_{\odot} \approx 10^{15} \operatorname{cm} .
\tag{3.3}\] This is about twenty times larger than the radius of the largest stars. The duration of the peak is of a few weeks, say \(\sim 2 \cdot 10^6 \mathrm{s}\), so the total energy release in photons is \[
\mathcal{E}_r \sim 2 \cdot 10^6 \cdot 10^{10} L_{\odot} \approx 8 \cdot
10^{49} \operatorname{erg} .
\tag{3.4}\] From the observation of Doppler shifted emission and absorption lines, we know that the typical velocities are in the range of \(2{,}000 \operatorname{km} \mathrm{s}^{- 1}\) to \(10{,}000 \operatorname{km} \mathrm{s}^{- 1}\). These velocities are consistent with the estimated length and temporal scales of the supernova phenomenon: \[
v \sim \frac{10^{15} \operatorname{cm}}{10^6 s} = 10^9 \operatorname{cm} \mathrm{s}^{- 1} =
10^4 \operatorname{km} \mathrm{s}^{- 1} .
\tag{3.5}\] The associated kinetic energy is \[
K \sim \frac{1}{2} Mv^2 \approx 10^{51}  \left( \frac{M}{M_{\odot}} \right)
\operatorname{erg} \gg \mathcal{E}_r
\tag{3.6}\]
From these basic observational facts, we know that supernovae must be powered by objects with large surface areas and require large energies. All these numbers already suggest that supernovae could be powered by the explosion of stars. This is most dramatically confirmed by the disappearance of stars previously observed at the location of supernovae.

title: 3  Core-Collapse Supernovae
text:
3.2 Shock breakout
Our supernova model begins with a star of radius \(R_0\) in which a large amount of energy \(\mathcal{E}\), much larger than the gravitational binding energy of the star, is injected. The source of this energy might be gravitational, in the case of core-collapse supernovae, or thermonuclear, but the outcome is similar: the progenitor is disrupted and matter starts expanding with large velocities. To fix our ideas, we will consider the explosion of a red supergiant with \(R_0 \sim 10^{14} \operatorname{cm}\), however all our results can be rescaled for other radii.
Immediately after the energy has been injected on the star, kinetic and internal energy are expected to be in equipartition \(K \sim E \sim \mathcal{E} \sim 10^{51} \operatorname{erg}\), so we can estimate the temperature, assuming the gas to be radiation dominated: \[
E = \frac{4}{3} \pi R^3_0 aT^4 .
\tag{3.7}\] This estimate gives a temperature of \[
T \approx 4.2 \cdot 10^5 \mathrm{K} \left( \frac{R_0}{10^{14} \operatorname{cm}}
\right)^{- 3 / 4}  \left( \frac{E}{10^{51} \operatorname{erg}} \right)^{1 / 4},
\tag{3.8}\] The first light emanating from the supernova is the so-called shock breakout. Because of the high temperature, the radiation spectrum at breakout peaks in the UV and X-ray bands.
We can check if the assumption of radiation dominated gas is consistent by computing the ratio of radiation pressure to gas pressure: \[
\beta = \frac{\frac{1}{3} aT^4}{nk_B T} = \frac{a}{3 k_B}  \frac{T^3}{n}
\approx \frac{a}{3 k_B}  \frac{4 \pi R^3_0}{3}  \frac{\mu}{M} T^3,
\tag{3.9}\] where we have approximated \(n\) with the average density, and \(M\) is the mass of the progenitor. We find \(\beta\): \[
\beta \approx 4.8 \cdot 10^3  \left( \frac{\mu}{m_p} \right)  \left( \frac{1
M_{\odot}}{M} \right)  \left( \frac{R}{10^{14} \operatorname{cm}} \right)^{3 / 4}
\left( \frac{E}{10^{51} \operatorname{erg}} \right)^{3 / 4},
\tag{3.10}\] confirming that radiation dominates at early times. As we will see later, for homologous expansion, \(E \sim R^{- 1}\), so \(\beta\) is independent of the radius to which the ejecta has expanded, and matter remains radiation dominated.

title: 3  Core-Collapse Supernovae
text:
3.3 Radiation diffusion
After the breakout, the star is full of radiation, but the photons need to make their way out of the explosion debris, before they can reach our telescopes. The dominant source of opacity is Thomson scattering on free electrons, but photons can also be absorbed and then re-emitted through various free-free, bound-free, and bound-bound processes. Their path out of the ejecta can be described as a random walk, such as the one illustrated in Figure 3.2.






Figure 3.2: Random walk of a photon in the supernova ejecta.



Consider a photon emitted at some location \(S\) deep inside the supernova ejecta. The photon is not able to escape immediately. Instead, it propagates over a distance \(\lambda_1\) before interacting with matter, either because it is scattered, or because it is absorbed and subsequently re-emitted in a different direction. The photon then moves in a new straight line over another distance \(\lambda_2\) and interacts again. This process is repeated \(N\) times (7 in the figure). We want to estimate how many steps are necessary for the photon to escape.
Let \(\mathbf{r}_1\), \(\mathbf{r}_2\), etc., be the displacement vectors between emission and absorption locations. We want to compute the total displacement \[
\mathbf{R}=\mathbf{r}_1 +\mathbf{r}_2 +\mathbf{r}_3 + \cdots,
\tag{3.11}\] and compare \(| \mathbf{R} |\) with the size of the expanding ejecta cloud \(R\). Since the direction of each step is random \[
\langle \mathbf{R} \rangle = \langle \mathbf{r}_1 +\mathbf{r}_2
+\mathbf{r}_3 + \cdots \rangle = \langle \mathbf{r}_1 \rangle + \langle
\mathbf{r}_2 \rangle + \langle \mathbf{r}_3 \rangle + \cdots = 0.
\tag{3.12}\] However, the root mean square of the displacement does not vanish: \[
\begin{alignedat}{2}
\langle \mathbf{R}^2 \rangle &{}={} && \langle (\mathbf{r}_1 +\mathbf{r}_2
+\mathbf{r}_3 + \cdots) \\
&&& \quad \cdot (\mathbf{r}_1 +\mathbf{r}_2 +\mathbf{r}_3 +
\cdots) \rangle \\
&{}={} && \langle \mathbf{r}_1^2 \rangle + \langle \mathbf{r}_2^2 \rangle +
\langle \mathbf{r}_3^2 \rangle + \cdots \\
&&& + 2 \langle \mathbf{r}_1 \cdot
\mathbf{r}_2 \rangle + 2 \langle \mathbf{r}_1 \cdot \mathbf{r}_3 \rangle +
\cdots
\end{alignedat}
\tag{3.13}\] The mixed products disappear, since the orientation of the displacement vectors is random, but \[
\langle \mathbf{r}_i^2 \rangle = \lambda^2 > 0,
\tag{3.14}\] the photon mean free path. We conclude that \[
\langle \mathbf{R}^2 \rangle = N \lambda^2 .
\tag{3.15}\] Equating this to the size \(R\) of the supernova, we find that the number of interactions experienced by the photon before escaping is \[
N = \left( \frac{R}{\lambda} \right)^2 .
\tag{3.16}\] Neglecting the time between absorption and re-emission, the time required for the photon to escape, the so-called radiative diffusion time, is given by \[
\tau_d = N \frac{\lambda}{c} = \frac{R^2}{\lambda c} .
\tag{3.17}\] The mean free path can be expressed as \(\lambda = 1 / \kappa \rho\) and \(\rho = \frac{3 M}{4 \pi R^3}\), where \(\kappa\) is the opacity, so \[
\tau_d = \frac{\kappa \rho}{c} R^2 = \frac{3}{4 \pi}  \frac{\kappa M}{Rc} .
\tag{3.18}\] Our calculation did not account for geometrical effects, but captured the essence of the problem. A more careful numerical calculation reveals that the characteristic radiation diffusion time scale is \[
\boxed{\tau_d = \frac{\kappa M}{\beta Rc}},
\tag{3.19}\] where \(\beta\) is a geometrical factor, not to be confused with the ratio of radiation to gas pressure. For spherical geometry, \(\beta \approx 13.8\).
Note that, since \(R = R_0 + vt \approx vt\), the diffusion time scale decays with time. On the other hand, the hydrodynamic time scale \(\tau_h = R / \dot{R} \approx t\) increases with time. Most of the radiation will escape at the time at which \(t_p = \tau_d (t_p)\), which is also the time at which diffusion and hydrodynamic time scales become equal: \[
\boxed{t_p = \left( \frac{\kappa M}{\beta cv} \right)^{1 / 2} .}
\tag{3.20}\] This is the peak time of the bolometric luminosity. For Thomson scattering in an hydrogen rich, ionized gas \(\kappa = 0.4 \operatorname{cm}^2 \mathrm{g}^{- 1}\), so \[
t_p = 1.4 \cdot 10^6 \mathrm{s} \left( \frac{M}{M_{\odot}} \right)^{1 / 2}
\left( \frac{\kappa}{0.4 \operatorname{cm}^2 \mathrm{g}^{- 1}} \right)^{1 / 2}
\left( \frac{v}{10^9 \operatorname{cm} \mathrm{s}^{- 1}} \right)^{- 1 / 2} .
\tag{3.21}\] The characteristic radius of the supernova at this time is \[
R_p = R_0 + t_p v \approx t_p v \sim 10^{15} \operatorname{cm} .
\tag{3.22}\] This time scale and characteristic radius are in good agreement with observations. These formulae also show that the typical duration of the rise time of the supernova is proportional to the mass and the opacity and inversely proportional to the velocity. This implies that the explosion of less massive stars produces faster transients, while more massive stars produce light curves that evolve over longer timescales. These relations are key to interpret not only supernovae, but also other explosive transients, such as kilonovae. For SN1987a the inferred velocity from spectroscopy is \(v \sim 0.3 \cdot 10^9 \operatorname{cm} \mathrm{s}^{- 1}\) and the peak time is \(t_p \approx 100 \operatorname{days}\) (see the SN1987a light curve below), so we can estimate \(M \approx 10 M_{\odot}\). This gives an explosion energy of \(\mathcal{E}= \frac{1}{2} Mv^2 \sim 10^{51} \operatorname{erg}\). These estimates are only correct to within an order of magnitude, since they neglect important effects, such as recombination, which we discuss below.

title: 3  Core-Collapse Supernovae
text:
3.4 Ejecta expansion
We describe the supernova outflow as a single fluid element undergoing homologous expansion, the so-called “one-zone approximation”. Accordingly, the equation for energy balance in the ejecta is \[
\rho \frac{\mathrm{d} \varepsilon}{\mathrm{d} t} + p \nabla \cdot \mathbf{v}= \rho
\dot{q} .
\tag{3.23}\] For the moment, we neglect radioactive heating, so \(\dot{q}\) only accounts for the loss of energy due to the escape of photons. Using the fact that \(\rho = M / V\) and \(M\) is constant, we can rewrite this as \[
\frac{\mathrm{d} (\varepsilon M)}{\mathrm{d} t} + pV \nabla \cdot \mathbf{v}= - V
\dot{Q} .
\tag{3.24}\] The first term is just the time derivative of the total internal energy in the ejecta \(E = \varepsilon M\), while the term on the RHS is the total luminosity \(L = - V \dot{Q}\). Using the fact that \(\nabla \cdot \mathbf{v}= \frac{1}{V} \frac{\mathrm{d} V}{\mathrm{d} t}\), the second term in the LHS can be rewritten as \[
pV \nabla \cdot \mathbf{v}= p \frac{\mathrm{d} V}{\mathrm{d} t},
\tag{3.25}\] so the energy equation becomes \[
\dot{E} + p \dot{V} = - L.
\tag{3.26}\] This is, of course, just the first law of thermodynamics applied to the entire supernova.
Using dimensional arguments, we can estimate the luminosity as \[
\boxed{L \approx \frac{E}{\tau_d}},
\tag{3.27}\] where \(E\) is the total thermal energy in the ejecta and \(\tau_d\) is the radiative diffusion time. This formula is valid when \(t \gtrsim \tau_d\), that is after the peak of the light curve, because photons are trapped for \(t \ll \tau_d\). We should be careful with the interpretation of the results we will find using Equation 3.27. For example, we will find that the light curve decays for all times, but, as previously discussed, we actually expect the supernova light curve to rise and then decline. However, Equation 3.27 is only valid after the peak.
It is useful to rewrite the pdV term as \[
p \dot{V} = pV \frac{\dot{V}}{V} = 3 pV \left( \frac{\dot{R}}{R} \right) = 3
pV \frac{1}{\tau_h},
\tag{3.28}\] where we have used the hydrodynamical timescale \(\tau_h = R / \dot{R} = R / v\), and the fact that \[
\frac{\dot{V}}{V} = 3 \frac{\dot{R}}{R} .
\tag{3.29}\] For a radiation dominated gas: \[
p = \frac{1}{3} \rho \varepsilon \Longrightarrow 3 pV = M \varepsilon = E.
\tag{3.30}\] Combining the last two equations with Equation 3.27, we obtain \[
\dot{E} + \frac{E}{\tau_h} = - \frac{E}{\tau_d} \Longrightarrow
\boxed{\frac{\dot{E}}{E} = - \left( \frac{1}{\tau_h} + \frac{1}{\tau_d}
\right) .}
\tag{3.31}\] We remind that this expression is only valid for \(t \gtrsim \tau_d\). Also note that both \(\tau_h\) and \(\tau_d\) depend on time.
At the time of break out, the hydrodynamical time scale is \[
\tau_{h, 0} = \frac{R}{v} = 10^5 \mathrm{s} \left( \frac{R_0}{10^{14}
\operatorname{cm}} \right)  \left( \frac{v}{10^9 \operatorname{cm} \mathrm{s}^{- 1}}
\right)^{- 1} .
\tag{3.32}\] The radiation diffusion time scale can be estimated using \(\kappa \approx 0.4 \operatorname{cm}^2 \mathrm{g}^{- 1}\) to be \[
\tau_{d, 0} = 2 \cdot 10^7 \mathrm{s} \left( \frac{M}{M_{\odot}} \right)
\left( \frac{R_0}{10^{14} \operatorname{cm}} \right)^{- 1} \gg \tau_h .
\tag{3.33}\] So at early times radiation is trapped in the expanding ejecta, however most of the thermal energy is “lost” to pdV work (it is converted to kinetic energy) on a time scale \(t \sim \tau_h\), before it has a chance to escape as radiation. Indeed, at early times we can neglect the radiative losses to find \[
\frac{\dot{E}}{E} + \frac{\dot{R}}{R} = 0 \Longrightarrow ER \sim
\operatorname{const} \Longrightarrow E \sim \frac{1}{R} .
\tag{3.34}\] So after matter has expanded by a factor \(10\), the thermal energy is reduced to a tenth of the initial value. This explains why \(\mathcal{E}_r \ll \mathcal{E}\) in supernovae.
To calculate the bolometric light curve, we write the energy as \[
\frac{\dot{E}}{E} + \frac{\dot{R}}{R} = - \frac{1}{\tau_d (t)}
\Longrightarrow \frac{\mathrm{d} \ln (ER)}{\mathrm{d} t} = - \frac{1}{\tau_d (t)} .
\tag{3.35}\] and expand \(\tau_d (t)\) as: \[
\tau_d (t) = \tau_{d, p}  \frac{R_p}{R_p + vt} = \tau_{d, p}  \frac{R_p /
v}{R_p / v + t} = \frac{\tau_{d, p} \tau_{h, p}}{\tau_{h, p} + t},
\tag{3.36}\] where \(\tau_{d, p}\) and \(\tau_{h, p}\) are the diffusion and hydrodynamic time scale at the peak of the light curve, respectively.
In this way we find \[
\frac{\mathrm{d} \ln (ER)}{\mathrm{d} t} = - \frac{t + \tau_{h, p}}{\tau_{d, p}
\tau_{h, p}} \Rightarrow ER = (E_p R_p) \exp \left( - \frac{\tau_{h, p} t +
t^2 / 2}{\tau_{d, p} \tau_{h, p}} \right) .
\tag{3.37}\] The last expression gives the expression for the luminosity, because \[
L = \frac{E}{\tau_d} = \left( \frac{\beta c}{\kappa M} \right) ER,
\tag{3.38}\] so \[
\boxed{\begin{aligned} L = {} & \left( \frac{\beta cE_p R_p}{\kappa M} \right) \exp \left( -
\frac{\tau_{h, p} t + t^2 / 2}{\tau_{d, p} \tau_{h, p}} \right) \\
& \operatorname{for} t \gtrsim \tau_d .\end{aligned}}
\tag{3.39}\] The luminosity at peak can be estimated as \[
\begin{aligned}
L_0 &= \frac{\beta cE_p R_p}{\kappa M} = \frac{\mathcal{E}_r}{\tau_{d, p}} \\
&\approx 5.2 \cdot 10^{43} \operatorname{erg} \mathrm{s}^{- 1}  \left(
\frac{\mathcal{E}_r}{10^{50} \operatorname{erg}} \right) \left( \frac{R_p}{10^{15}
\operatorname{cm}} \right) \\
&\qquad \times \left( \frac{M_{\odot}}{M} \right)  \left( \frac{0.4
\operatorname{cm}^2 \mathrm{g}^{- 1}}{\kappa} \right)
\end{aligned}
\tag{3.40}\] For SN1987a, we have already estimated \(M \sim 10 M_{\odot}\), so this formula predicts the correct peak luminosity \(L_0 \sim 10^{42} \operatorname{erg} \mathrm{s}^{- 1}\).
This shows that, in absence of radioactive heating, or when radioactive heating is subdominant, the luminosity declines exponentially (after having peaked at \(t = t_p\)). The characteristic decay time for the light curve is given by \[
\begin{aligned}
\tau_{\operatorname{lc}} &= \sqrt{2 \tau_{d, p} \tau_{h, p}} \\
&\approx 2 \cdot 10^6 \mathrm{s} \left( \frac{\kappa}{0.4 \operatorname{cm}^2 \mathrm{g}^{- 1}} \right)^{1/ 2}  \left( \frac{M}{M_{\odot}} \right)^{1 / 2} \\
&\qquad \times \left( \frac{v}{10^9
\operatorname{cm} \mathrm{s}^{- 1}} \right)^{- 1 / 2} .
\end{aligned}
\tag{3.41}\] Note that \(\tau_{\operatorname{lc}}\) does not depend on the expansion radius, but remains constant.
This simple model with no radioactive heating already predicts several key properties of supernovae and other explosive transients. It shows that the luminosity is proportional to the explosion energy per unit mass and inversely proportional to the opacity. It also shows that the typical duration of the transient is proportional to mass and opacity and inversely proportional to the velocity. For example, we have found that the explosion of less massive stars produces faster transients, while more massive stars produce light curves that evolve over longer timescales.

title: 3  Core-Collapse Supernovae
text:
3.5 Radioactive heating
The radioactive decay of \(^{56} \operatorname{Ni}\) to \(^{56} \operatorname{Co}\) and of \(^{56} \operatorname{Co}\) to \(^{56} \operatorname{Fe}\) powers the light curve of supernovae. These decays produce \(\gamma\)-rays and positrons. Some of these particles escape from the ejecta, so their energy does not contribute to the optical light curve. However, especially in the first weeks, the majority of the decay products are reprocessed into thermal radiation. After having included this new heating source, the first law of thermodynamics is: \[
\dot{E} + p \dot{V} = \dot{Q}_{\operatorname{heat}} - L,
\tag{3.42}\] where \(\dot{Q}_{\operatorname{heat}}\) is the energy deposited by the radioactive decays in \(\operatorname{erg} \mathrm{s}^{- 1}\).
Proceeding as before, we can introduce a heating time scale \[
\tau_{\operatorname{heat}} = \frac{E}{\dot{Q}_{\operatorname{heat}}},
\tag{3.43}\] and obtain the energy equation \[
\frac{\dot{E}}{E} + \frac{\dot{R}}{R} = \frac{1}{\tau_{\operatorname{heat}}} -
\frac{1}{\tau_d} \Longrightarrow \boxed{\frac{\mathrm{d} \ln (E R)}{\mathrm{d}
t} = \frac{1}{\tau_{\operatorname{heat}}} - \frac{1}{\tau_d} .}
\tag{3.44}\] With the inclusion of radioactive heating, the light curve changes qualitatively. In particular, the luminosity can continue to grow even after \(t \gtrsim \tau_d\) and reach a higher maximum. To see this, we use the fact that \(E R \sim cL\), which implies that the peak is reached when the RHS of Equation 3.44 vanishes: \[
\frac{1}{\tau_{\operatorname{heat}}} = \frac{1}{\tau_d} \Longrightarrow
\frac{\dot{Q}_{\operatorname{heat}}}{E} = \frac{1}{\tau_d} \Longrightarrow
\boxed{\dot{Q}_{\operatorname{heat}} = \frac{E}{\tau_d} = L.}
\tag{3.45}\] This shows that the luminosity at peak equals the heating rate. This is a key result in supernova theory called “Arnett’s law1”. Since the energy released by each nuclear decay is known from laboratory experiments, Arnett’s law provides a way to estimate the amount of radioactive material produced by the supernova. Type Ia supernovae (Figure 3.3), which are the result of the thermonuclear explosion of white dwarfs, are an example of supernovae in which radioactivity plays the dominant role in the light curve over all times and for which Arnett’s law can be applied.






Figure 3.3: Sample of Type Ia thermonuclear supernova light curves: data and theoretical models. From Arnett (1996); © Princeton University Press, reproduced for non-commercial educational use and not covered by the license of these notes.

title: 3  Core-Collapse Supernovae
text:
3.6 Recombination and nebular phase
After the peak of the light curve, as the explosion debris expand and cool, other physical effects start to become important. First, a larger fraction of gamma rays and positrons escape and/or are not thermalized. Secondly, ions begin to recombine. This removes the free electrons that were responsible for the Thomson opacity from the gas which then becomes transparent in the infrared/optical bands. Thus, as matter recombines, radiation quickly escapes rapidly cooling down the material. This process launches a recombination wave into the supernova debris. The photons we see at this stage are no longer coming from the outer edge of the ejecta, but instead are emitted at a photosphere that is very close to the recombination front.
Recombination of hydrogen and helium is important for many classes of supernovae, including for SN1987a, but their impact is particularly spectacular in hydrogen rich, Type II-P supernovae. Because recombination of hydrogen happens at a fixed temperature2, the luminosity can be estimated as \[
L = 4 \pi R_r^2 (t) \sigma T^4_r,
\tag{3.46}\] where \(T_r\) is the recombination temperature (a constant), and \(R_r (t)\) is the position of the recombination front (which nearly coincides with the photosphere). In Type II-P supernovae, \(R_r (t) \sim \operatorname{const}\) for \(\sim 100\) days and the bolometric luminosity plateaus to a nearly constant value (P stands for plateau). A prototypical example is SN1999em, shown in Figure 3.4.
After the recombination wave has swept through the ejecta, the supernova enters the so called nebular phase. In this stage there is no longer a photosphere, because the material is transparent. The black body approximation fails, because radiation is produced by various decays and matter is no longer in thermodynamic equilibrium. Often, the luminosity decays exponentially, with characteristic time scale equal to the half life of \(^{56} \operatorname{Co}\), so it is possible to fit the decay tail to estimates of the amount of radioactive material. This has to be done carefully, accounting for the thermalization efficiency of positrons and gamma-rays.






Figure 3.4: Bolometric light curve for SN1999em, a classical example of a Type II-P supernova. Data from Elmhamdi et al. (2003); figure courtesy of Viktoriya Morozova, used with permission and not covered by the license of these notes.

title: 3  Core-Collapse Supernovae
text:
3.8 Exercises

Exercise 3.1 (The Katz integral) Consider an homologously expanding radioactive cloud of debris launched by an explosion of some kind, e.g., a supernova.

Assume that the gas is described by the gamma-law equation of state \[
p = (\Gamma - 1) \rho \varepsilon .
\tag{3.48}\] Show that the first law of thermodynamics becomes \[
\frac{\mathrm{d} E}{\mathrm{d} t} = - L + \dot{Q} - 3 (\Gamma - 1)
\frac{E}{t},
\tag{3.49}\] where \(L\) is the luminosity (energy radiated away in erg/s), and \(\dot{Q}\) is the radioactive heating rate in erg/s.
Show that the following exact relation holds under suitable assumptions: \[
\int_0^t L (t') t' \mathrm{d} t' = \int_0^t \dot{Q} (t') t' \mathrm{d} t' .
\tag{3.50}\] The quantity on the LHS is called the Katz integral and can be determined observationally. Discuss the validity of the approximations made to derive this result.
The radioactive heating can be written as \[
\dot{Q} = M (t)  \frac{q}{\tau},
\tag{3.51}\] where \(q\) is the radioactive energy release in erg/g, \(\tau\) is the radioactive decay timescale, and \(M (t) = M_0 e^{- t / \tau}\) is the mass of the radioactive material at time \(t\). Show how \(M_0\) can be estimated from the Katz integral, assuming \(q\) and \(\tau\) to be known from nuclear physics experiments.

title: 4  The Euler Equation
text:
4.1 Internal stresses
Up to this point we have described the motion of fluids in which the velocity field is prescribed, or known. Now we derive the equation of motion for fluids. The acceleration of a fluid element \(\mathcal{V}\) with mass \(\mathcal{M}\) is given by Newton’s law: \[
\mathcal{M} \frac{\mathrm{d} \mathbf{v}}{\mathrm{d} t} =\mathbf{F},
\tag{4.1}\] where \(\mathbf{F}\) is the sum of all forces (the net force) acting on \(\mathcal{V}\). To derive an equation that does not explicitly make reference to the fluid elements, we can divide Equation 4.1 by the volume of \(\mathcal{V}\) to find \[
\rho \frac{\mathrm{d} \mathbf{v}}{\mathrm{d} t} =\mathbf{f},
\tag{4.2}\] where \(\mathbf{f}\) is the force per unit volume acting on the fluid: \[
[\mathbf{f}] = \operatorname{dyn} \operatorname{cm}^{- 3} =\mathrm{g} \operatorname{cm}^{- 2}
\mathrm{s}^{- 2},
\tag{4.3}\] where “\(\operatorname{dyn}\)” (dyne) is the unit of force in CGS units: \[
1 \operatorname{dyn} = 1\mathrm{g} \operatorname{cm} \mathrm{s}^{- 2} .
\tag{4.4}\] There are two type of forces that can act on a fluid element: external and internal forces. In astrophysical applications, gravity is the most common external force. The force per unit volume (body force) due to gravity is \[
\mathbf{f}_g = \rho \mathbf{g}= - \rho \nabla \Psi,
\tag{4.5}\] where \(\mathbf{g}\) is the gravitational acceleration and \(\Psi\) is the gravitational potential. The internal forces are due to the interaction of \(\mathcal{V}\) with other fluid elements.
Consider a container with water at rest on the surface of the Earth. The container has been left undisturbed for sufficiently long time that the velocity of all fluid elements is zero. Let \(\mathcal{V}\) be a fluid element of water somewhere away from the edge of the container. Clearly, \(\mathcal{V}\) is subject to the force of gravity. Since \(\mathcal{V}\) is not in contact with the container, the gravitational force cannot be balanced by a contact force with the walls of the container. Instead, the force on \(\mathcal{V}\) must be balanced by a force exchanged by \(\mathcal{V}\) with the neighboring fluid elements. This show that the equation of motion of a fluid must include the acceleration due to its internal forces. What is their nature?
We consider an infinitesimal fluid element \(\mathcal{V}\) in a fluid at rest, as illustrated in Figure 4.1. We can take the origin of the coordinate system to be the center of \(\mathcal{V}\) and its extent in the three directions to be \(\mathrm{d} x\), \(\mathrm{d} y\), and \(\mathrm{d} z\). We also take the gravitational acceleration \(\mathbf{g}\) to be in the \(z\)-direction.
The fluid element is subject to forces applied by the rest of the fluid to its six square faces and to the force of gravity, which we can take to be applied to its center of mass, as shown in Figure 4.1. Our goal is to determine these forces. Even for a fluid at rest, in principle, these surface forces can have many possible magnitudes and directions, as long as the net force and torque acting on \(\mathcal{V}\) vanish. We cannot make much progress without knowing more about the nature of the fluid.
However, there is a class of fluids, known as perfect fluids, for which the internal forces are particularly simple. In a perfect fluid the surface forces are assumed to be always directed along the perpendicular to each face (as is the case in Figure 4.1). The problem of finding the internal forces thus reduces to that of finding a scalar quantity, called the pressure, that gives the magnitude of the force per unit area across each face of the fluid element: \[
p = \text{``force per unit area''} \qquad [\operatorname{dyn} \operatorname{cm}^{- 2}] .
\tag{4.6}\] In particular, for a perfect fluid the force exerted by the fluid on an infinitesimal surface with outward-directed area element \(\mathrm{d} \mathbf{A}\) is \[
\mathrm{d} \mathbf{F}= - p \mathrm{d} \mathbf{A}.
\tag{4.7}\] In most cases the pressure is positive \(p > 0\), so a fluid element, or equivalently an object immersed in a fluid, is subject to compression.
The concept of perfect fluid is an idealization of reality, but, in practice, liquids and gases can be considered as perfect fluids to very good approximation in most situations. More in general, because the force needs to transform under basis change in the same way as a vector, it can be shown internal forces can be written as \[
\mathrm{d} \mathbf{F}=\mathbf{T} \mathrm{d} \mathbf{A},
\tag{4.8}\] where \(\mathbf{T}\) is a matrix that depends on the properties of the fluid, the so-called stress tensor of the fluid. The perfect fluid is the special case of this general theory in which \[
\mathbf{T}= - p\mathbf{I},
\tag{4.9}\] where \(\mathbf{I}\) is the identity matrix. We will encounter examples of non-perfect fluids later in the course.

title: 4  The Euler Equation
text: Figure 4.1: Force diagram for a fluid element in a static water container.

title: 4  The Euler Equation
text:
4.2 Euler’s equation
We can now consider the net acceleration of the fluid element in the vertical direction. There are three forces to consider: the force of gravity, and the forces at the bottom and at the top of \(\mathcal{V}\). The forces from the side do not contribute, since they are orthogonal to the \(z\)-direction. Putting everything together we find: \[
\mathcal{M} \frac{\mathrm{d} v_z}{\mathrm{d} t} = - \left[ p \left( z =
\tfrac{\mathrm{d} z}{2} \right) - p \left( z = - \tfrac{\mathrm{d} z}{2} \right)
\right] \mathrm{d} A +\mathcal{M}g_z,
\tag{4.10}\] where \(\mathrm{d} A = \mathrm{d} x \mathrm{d} y\), and \(\mathcal{M}= \rho V = \rho \mathrm{d} x \mathrm{d} y \mathrm{d} z\). Dividing both terms by \(V\) gives \[
\rho \frac{\mathrm{d} v_z}{\mathrm{d} t} = - \frac{1}{\mathrm{d} z}  \left[ p \left( z =
\tfrac{\mathrm{d} z}{2} \right) - p \left( z = - \tfrac{\mathrm{d} z}{2} \right)
\right] + \rho g_z = - \partial_z p + \rho g_z .
\tag{4.11}\] A similar derivation can be done for the momentum balance in the \(x\)- and \(y\)-directions to find \[
\rho \frac{\mathrm{d} \mathbf{v}}{\mathrm{d} t} = - \nabla p + \rho \mathbf{g}.
\tag{4.12}\] In the more general case, in which we consider an arbitrary volume force applied onto the fluid, we obtain the so-called Euler, or momentum equation for a perfect fluid: \[
\boxed{\rho \frac{\mathrm{d} \mathbf{v}}{\mathrm{d} t} = - \nabla p
+\mathbf{f}.}
\tag{4.13}\] Note: it is the gradient of the pressure, and not the pressure directly that determines the mechanical response of the fluid. We will see that this has important implications in a number of situations.
In the case of non perfect fluids, Equation 4.13 becomes \[
\rho \frac{\mathrm{d} \mathbf{v}}{\mathrm{d} t} = \nabla \cdot
\mathbf{T}+\mathbf{f},
\tag{4.14}\] where we have introduced the divergence of a tensor, defined to be a vector with components \[
\nabla \cdot \mathbf{T}  = \left(\begin{array}{c}
\partial_x T_{x x} + \partial_y T_{x y} + \partial_z T_{x z}\\
\partial_x T_{y x} + \partial_y T_{y y} + \partial_z T_{y z}\\
\partial_x T_{z x} + \partial_y T_{z y} + \partial_z T_{z z}
\end{array}\right) .
\tag{4.15}\] The momentum Equation 4.14 holds even for solids, which can rarely be described as perfect fluids, but for which the stress tensor can also be defined.






TipExample



Consider a liquid at rest (\(\mathbf{v}= 0\)) in a tank and subject to gravity. The tank is not pressurized, so the surface of the liquid is at the atmospheric pressure \(p_0\), in order to be in mechanical equilibrium with the air. Assume that the tank is sufficiently shallow, so that \(\rho = \operatorname{const}\). What is the pressure at the bottom of the tank?
We can take \(z\) to be the vertical coordinate, \(z = 0\) being the surface of the surface of the liquid and \(z = d > 0\) being the bottom. The force balance in the \(z\)-direction is \[
\partial_z p = \rho g,
\tag{4.16}\] where \(g > 0\) is the acceleration constant1. Integrating this equation, we find \[
p (z) = p_0 + \int_0^z \rho g \mathrm{d} z = p_0 + \rho gz.
\tag{4.17}\] The pressure at the bottom of the tank is \(p_0 + \rho gd\).


Let’s recap our situation. We have started with the continuity equation (Equation 1.12), which describes the evolution of the density \(\rho\) given the velocity \(\mathbf{v}\). To find the velocity we have derived an equation of motion for it, Euler’s equation, which however involves yet another quantity: the pressure. We are still not able to predict the evolution of a fluid, unless we have a way to compute its pressure. This should not be surprising, because so far we have not introduced any equation that tells us which fluid is being considered: water and interstellar gas behave very differently, even though they satisfy the same equations. Their different dynamics is results of the fact that they have different pressures. In general, the pressure for a fluid depends on its density, temperature or entropy, and composition \[
p = p (\rho, T, \{ Y_i \}) .
\tag{4.18}\] This is the so-called equation of state for the matter. As such, to close the system we will need a new equation for temperature, in addition to the equation of state. There are some special cases, however, in which the pressure can be taken to be a function of only the density: \[
p = p (\rho) .
\tag{4.19}\] In this case we say that the equation of state is barotropic. Some important cases that we will encounter in our course are

pressureless fluids, in which \(p = 0\);
isothermal gases, in which \(p = c_s^2 \rho\), where \(c_s > 0\) is a constant, which we will see is equal to the speed of sound in the gas;
polytropic gases, in which \(p = K \rho^{\Gamma}\), where \(K\) and \(\Gamma\) are some known positive constants.

The pressureless approximation can sometimes be employed for highly supersonic flows, or in cases in which the gas is not collisional: dark matter, or dust can be approximated as pressureless fluids in certain cases. The isothermal and polytropic equations of state hold when temperature or entropy are constant in the gas, so the equation of state becomes barotropic. We will discuss this in more detail later.

title: 5  Eulerian and Lagrangian Descriptions
text:
5.1 Motivation
Up to this point, we have considered the equation of motion for individual fluid elements. This is the so-called Lagrangian description of fluid mechanics. However, there are many problems in which it is more convenient to work with equations that describe the density, velocity, and temperature of the fluid at a specific point in space, and not for individual fluid elements. In other words, we want to solve for \(\rho (t, \mathbf{x})\) and \(\mathbf{v} (t, \mathbf{x})\), as opposed to \(\rho (t ; \mathcal{V})\) and \(\mathbf{v} (t ; \mathcal{V})\). This is the so-called Eulerian approach.
As motivation, we consider a celestial body of mass \(M\), for example a planet or a star, that is accreting matter at a constant rate \(\dot{M}\). \(M\) and \(\dot{M}\) are unknown, but we know density and velocity of the fluid at a given radius \(r_0\) from space resolved detection of an emission line. How can we estimate \(M\) and \(\dot{M}\)? We assume the in-falling matter to have no angular momentum, so that the flow is radial. We also neglect radiation pressure and fluid pressure (\(p = 0\)). We will consider the more general case in which pressure forces are included later in the course. However, we remark that the pressureless approximation provides an accurate description of the flow when it is highly supersonic (close to the surface of the accretor).
The equations of motion for the gas (assuming spherical symmetry) are \[
\frac{1}{\rho}  \frac{\mathrm{d} \rho}{\mathrm{d} t} = - \frac{1}{r^2} \partial_r
(r^2 v), \qquad \frac{\mathrm{d} v}{\mathrm{d} t} = - \frac{GM}{r^2} .
\tag{5.1}\] In the new language we have just introduced, these are the Lagrangian equations of motion. That is, they describe the density and velocity of each fluid element. Note that, even though the problem describes a steady state system, we cannot drop the time derivatives, because each individual fluid element is not stationary, but it is in free fall.
Consider a fluid element that starts at rest at large distance from the accretor. Since the fluid elements are not subject to any force beside gravity, they are in free fall \[
v = - \sqrt{\frac{2 GM}{r}} .
\tag{5.2}\] Inserting this into the continuity equation yields: \[
\frac{1}{\rho}  \frac{\mathrm{d} \rho}{\mathrm{d} t} = \frac{3 \sqrt{2 GM}}{2 r^{3 /
2}} .
\tag{5.3}\] Here, we need to be careful, because in the Lagrangian framework \(r = r (t)\), since we are traveling with each fluid element. So, before we can solve the continuity equation, we need to find \(r\) as solution of \[
\frac{\mathrm{d} r}{\mathrm{d} t} = - \sqrt{\frac{2 GM}{r}} .
\tag{5.4}\] This equation can be solved analytically assuming the initial radius to be \(r (0) = r_0\), but its solution is rather complex: \[
r (t) = \left( - \frac{3 \sqrt{2 GM} t}{2} + r_0^{3 / 2} \right)^{2 / 3} .
\tag{5.5}\] Plugging this back into the continuity equation, we find \[
\frac{1}{\rho}  \frac{\mathrm{d} \rho}{\mathrm{d} t} = - \frac{3 \sqrt{2 GM}}{3
\sqrt{2 GM} t - 2 r_0^{3 / 2}} .
\tag{5.6}\] This can be solved with initial conditions \(\rho (0) = \rho_0\) to yield \[
\rho (t) = \frac{2 r_0^{3 / 2} \rho_0}{2 r_0^{3 / 2} - 3 \sqrt{2 GM} t} .
\tag{5.7}\] After all of this work, we still do not have \(\rho\) as a function of radius: for that we need to solve \(t\) from Equation 5.5 and plug the result back into Equation 5.7. We also need to relate \(\rho_0\) to \(\dot{M}\)... Wouldn’t our lives have been much simpler if we could have solved directly for \(\rho (t, r)\)? Yes! As we will see shortly, this problem becomes trivial using the Eulerian formulation of fluid mechanics.

title: 5  Eulerian and Lagrangian Descriptions
text:
5.2 Advective derivative
We leave for a moment the problem of the spherical accretion, to develop the general theory of the Eulerian formulation of fluid mechanics. Let \(A (t ; \mathcal{V})\) be some quantity that is specific to a fluid element \(\mathcal{V}\). For example, \(A\) could be the density or the velocity of the fluid element \(\mathcal{V}\). The same quantity, can also be thought of being a function of position: \[
A (t, \mathbf{x}) := A \left( t ; \text{``fluid element at location
$\mathbf{x}$ at time $t$''} \right) .
\tag{5.8}\] If the law of motion of each fluid elements are known, then it is possible to compute \(A (t, \mathbf{x})\) from \(A (t ; \mathcal{V})\). We have done this in the case of the homologously expanding flow (Section 1.3), when we needed to compute \(v (t, r)\) given \(v (t, p)\), where \(p\) was the “label” we used to identify the fluid elements.
Consider a fluid element \(\mathcal{V}\) with world line \(\mathbf{x} (t)\). Then, at time \(t\) \[
A (t ; \mathcal{V}) = A (t, \mathbf{x} (t)) .
\tag{5.9}\] We can differentiate both sides with respect to \(t\) to find \[
\begin{aligned}
& \frac{\mathrm{d} A (t ; \mathcal{V})}{\mathrm{d} t} =  \frac{\mathrm{d} A (t,
\mathbf{x} (t))}{\mathrm{d} t}  \\
& \quad = \frac{\partial A (t, \mathbf{x} (t))}{\partial t} + \biggl(
\frac{\mathrm{d} x}{\mathrm{d} t} \partial_x + \frac{\mathrm{d} y}{\mathrm{d} t}
\partial_y \\
& \qquad\qquad + \frac{\mathrm{d} z}{\mathrm{d} t} \partial_z \biggr) A (t, \mathbf{x}
(t))  \\
& \quad = \frac{\partial A (t, \mathbf{x} (t))}{\partial t} + \left(
\frac{\mathrm{d} \mathbf{x}}{\mathrm{d} t} \cdot \nabla \right) A (t, \mathbf{x}
(t)) \\
& \quad = \frac{\partial A (t, \mathbf{x} (t))}{\partial t} + (\mathbf{v} \cdot
\nabla) A (t, \mathbf{x} (t)),
\end{aligned}
\tag{5.10}\] where we used the chain rule for differentiation and the definition of velocity. Equation 5.10 gives us a way to relate the time derivative of a quantity defined with respect to fluid elements to the same quantity taken to be a function of spatial position and time. The reason why \[
\frac{\mathrm{d} A (t ; \mathcal{V})}{\mathrm{d} t} \neq \frac{\partial A (t,
\mathbf{x} (t))}{\partial t}
\tag{5.11}\] is that the partial derivative with respect to time considers the rate of change of \(A\) at a fixed location, but there are different fluid elements crossing that location as a function of time. The operator \(\frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d} t}\) that we have used so far is called the advective derivative, because it represents the rate of change of a quantity measured when riding along a fluid element. Equation 5.10 can be written more succinctly as \[
\boxed{\frac{\mathrm{d} A}{\mathrm{d} t} = \frac{\partial A}{\partial t}
+\mathbf{v} \cdot \nabla A.}
\tag{5.12}\] To be mathematically precise, we should keep in mind that this relation represents the equivalence between two different mathematical operations performed on different objects. The \(A\) on the LHS is a function of only time for a fixed fluid element \(\mathcal{V}\), while the \(A\) on the RHS is a function of position and time and is not specific to any single fluid element.

title: 5  Eulerian and Lagrangian Descriptions
text:
5.3 Eulerian formulation of fluid mechanics
The Eulerian equations can be obtained from the Lagrangian equations by replacing all advective derivatives: \[
\frac{\mathrm{d} \rho}{\mathrm{d} t} \rightarrow \frac{\partial \rho}{\partial t} +
(\mathbf{v} \cdot \nabla) \rho, \qquad \frac{\mathrm{d} \mathbf{v}}{\mathrm{d} t}
\rightarrow \frac{\partial \mathbf{v}}{\partial t} + (\mathbf{v} \cdot
\nabla) \mathbf{v}.
\tag{5.13}\]
The continuity equation becomes \[
\frac{\partial \rho}{\partial t} + (\mathbf{v} \cdot \nabla) \rho + \rho
\nabla \cdot \mathbf{v}= 0.
\tag{5.14}\] In Cartesian coordinates, we can expand all derivatives as \[
\begin{aligned}
& (\mathbf{v} \cdot \nabla) \rho + \rho \nabla \cdot \mathbf{v} \\
& \quad = v_x
\partial_x \rho + v_y \partial_y \rho + v_z \partial_z \rho \\
& \qquad\qquad + \rho
\partial_x v_x + \rho \partial_y v_y + \rho \partial_z v_z  \\
& \quad = \partial_x (\rho v_x) + \partial_y  (\rho v_y) + \partial_z  (\rho
v_z) \\
& \quad = \nabla \cdot (\rho \mathbf{v}) .
\end{aligned}
\tag{5.15}\] So the continuity equation can be written as \[
\boxed{\frac{\partial \rho}{\partial t} + \nabla \cdot (\rho \mathbf{v})
= 0.}
\tag{5.16}\]
The velocity equation can be written as \[
\boxed{\rho \frac{\partial \mathbf{v}}{\partial t} + \rho (\mathbf{v}
\cdot \nabla) \mathbf{v}=\mathbf{f}- \nabla p.}
\tag{5.17}\]

title: 5  Eulerian and Lagrangian Descriptions
text:
5.4 Pressure-less spherical accretion
We are now ready to solve the problem of the spherical accretion of a pressure-less fluid that we have attempted to attack at the beginning of this chapter. Because the Eulerian equations deal with quantities as a function of position and time, all time derivatives vanish for a steady flow and we find: \[
\partial_r  (r^2 \rho v) = 0, \qquad v \partial_r v = - \frac{GM}{r^2} .
\tag{5.18}\] The second equation can be written as \[
\frac{1}{2} \partial_r  (v^2 ) = - \frac{GM}{r^2},
\tag{5.19}\] which can be integrated to give (for an in falling flow) \[
v (r) = - \sqrt{\frac{2 GM}{r}} .
\tag{5.20}\] The continuity equation shows that \[
r^2 \rho v = \operatorname{const} .
\tag{5.21}\] Apart from a \(4 \pi\) factor, this is the accretion rate, because the inflow of mass across a surface of radius \(r\) is (assuming spherical symmetry): \[
\dot{M} = - \oint r^2 \rho v \mathrm{d} \Omega = - 4 \pi r^2 \rho v.
\tag{5.22}\] So \[
\rho (r) = - \frac{\dot{M}}{4 \pi r^2 v} = \frac{\dot{M}}{4 \pi \sqrt{2 GM}
r^{3 / 2}} .
\tag{5.23}\] We can now solve for \(M\) using Equation 5.20 and for \(\dot{M}\) using Equation 5.23. We leave this last step as an exercise for the reader.

\begin{alignedat}{2}

\\
x_2 &{}={} && \frac{1}{2}  (p_1 + p_2) e^t - \frac{1}{2}  (p_1 - p_2) e^{- t}, \\
