title: 21  Turbulence
text:
21.2 Kolmogorov’s Theory
Fluid motion is driven by external forces, such as gravity, which have a characteristic scale \(\ell_0\) comparable to the size of the system of interest. For example, for a star \(\ell_0 \sim R\) the star radius. Kolmogorov’s theory starting point is to decompose the flow velocity in some patch of the fluid \(\mathbf{v}\) into a mean flow \(\langle \mathbf{v} \rangle\) and a fluctuating component \(\mathbf{v}'\), not necessarily assumed to be small. The theory then assumes that, if the size \(\ell\) of the region under consideration is sufficiently small, \(\ell \ll \ell_0\), \(\mathbf{v}'\) is universal, at least in a statistical sense, meaning that it does not depend on the particular system, but that is set by the equations of motion.
To keep our notation simple, we set \(\langle \mathbf{v} \rangle = 0\), meaning that \(\mathbf{v}' =\mathbf{v}\). Note that we can always set \(\langle \mathbf{v} \rangle = 0\) by working in the appropriate reference frame, so this is not a restriction on the theory we are developing. We are also going to assume that the flow is incompressible, which is typically a good assumption away from shocks and over a sufficiently small region. The flow is then described by the Navier-Stokes equations \[
\partial_t \mathbf{v}+ (\mathbf{v} \cdot \nabla) \mathbf{v}=\mathbf{g}-
\frac{\nabla p}{\rho} + \nu \nabla^2 \mathbf{v}, \qquad \nabla \cdot
\mathbf{v}= 0,
\tag{21.1}\] where \(\mathbf{g}\) is some external acceleration field, typically gravity in astrophysical applications.
The equation for the evolution of the kinetic energy is obtained by multiplying Equation 21.1 by \(\mathbf{v}\): \[
\frac{1}{2}  [\partial_t v^2 + (\mathbf{v} \cdot \nabla) v^2] =\mathbf{g}
\cdot \mathbf{v}- \frac{1}{\rho} \nabla p \cdot \mathbf{v}+ \nu \nabla^2
\mathbf{v} \cdot \mathbf{v}.
\tag{21.2}\] Consider, the first term on the RHS, representing the work done by the external force on the flow. If \(\ell \ll \ell_0\), then we can take \(\mathbf{g} \sim \operatorname{const}\) over this region and \[
\langle \mathbf{g} \cdot \mathbf{v} \rangle \sim \mathbf{g} \cdot \langle
\mathbf{v} \rangle = 0.
\tag{21.3}\] This suggests that the evolution of \(v\) for \(\ell \ll \ell_0\) is independent on the details of the external force \(\mathbf{g}\), so \(v\) can be universal. Of course, if \(\ell \sim \ell_0\), then \(\langle \mathbf{g} \cdot \mathbf{v} \rangle > 0\) in general, meaning that kinetic energy is injected at the scale \(\ell_0\) by gravity and then evolves according to Equation 21.2.
Let’s now consider the role of pressure (note that \(\rho = \operatorname{const}\)): \[
\langle \nabla p \cdot \mathbf{v} \rangle = \frac{1}{V} \int_V \nabla p
\cdot \mathbf{v} \mathrm{d} V = \frac{1}{V} \int_V [\nabla \cdot (p
\mathbf{v}) - p \nabla \cdot \mathbf{v}] \mathrm{d} V = \frac{1}{V} \oint_S
p\mathbf{v} \cdot \mathbf{n} \mathrm{d} S = 0.
\tag{21.4}\] In the last equation we have assumed that \(\mathbf{v}\) is isotropic (no preferred direction), so \(\mathbf{v} \cdot \mathbf{n}\) is zero on average.
In a similar way, we can rewrite the average of the last term in the RHS of Equation 21.2 as \[
\int_V \nabla^2 \mathbf{v} \cdot \mathbf{v} \mathrm{d} V = \oint_S \mathbf{n}
\cdot (\nabla \mathbf{v}\mathbf{v}) \mathrm{d} S - \int_V \nabla \mathbf{v}:
\nabla \mathbf{v} \mathrm{d} V = - \int_V | \nabla \mathbf{v} |^2 \mathrm{d} V .
\tag{21.5}\] This means that we can simplify the kinetic energy equation to read \[
\partial_t v^2 = 2\mathbf{g} \cdot \mathbf{v}- (\mathbf{v} \cdot \nabla) v^2
- 2 \nu | \nabla \mathbf{v} |^2 .
\tag{21.6}\] As already mentioned, the first term on the RHS is responsible for energy injection. The last term describes kinetic energy dissipation. We can estimate this term as \[
\nu | \nabla \mathbf{v} |^2 \sim \nu \left( \frac{v (\ell)}{\ell} \right)^2,
\tag{21.7}\] where \(v (\ell)\) is the characteristic velocity fluctuation on a length scale \(\ell\): \[
v (\ell) = \langle | \mathbf{v} (\mathbf{x}+\mathbf{l}) -\mathbf{v}
(\mathbf{x}) | \rangle = \frac{1}{V} \int_V | \mathbf{v}
(\mathbf{x}+\mathbf{l}) -\mathbf{v} (\mathbf{x}) | \mathrm{d}^3 \mathbf{x}.
\tag{21.8}\] We use the notation \(A \sim B\) to signify that two quantities, \(A\) and \(B\), are equal up to factors of order unity.
The quantity on the RHS of Equation 21.7 has units of power per unit mass, as expected since it represents the decay rate of energy of the specific (per unit mass) kinetic energy. Equation 21.7 suggests that the energy is dissipated at a scale \(\ell_d\) (the dissipation or Kolmogorov scale) at which the dissipation rate is equal to the mean power of the global flow: \[
\nu \left( \frac{v (\ell_d)}{\ell_d} \right)^2 \sim \frac{v^3
(\ell_0)}{\ell_0} \Longrightarrow \ell_d \sim \ell_0  \left[
\frac{\nu}{\ell_0 v (\ell_0)} \right]^{1 / 2}  \left[ \frac{v (\ell_d)}{v
(\ell_0)} \right] = \frac{\ell_0}{\operatorname{Re}^{1 / 2}}  \left[ \frac{v
(\ell_d)}{v (\ell_0)} \right] .
\tag{21.9}\] In the previous equation, we have introduced the Reynolds number \[
\operatorname{Re} = \frac{\ell_0 v (\ell_0)}{\nu} .
\tag{21.10}\] Experimental observations of fluids in pipes suggest that turbulence sets in when \(\operatorname{Re} \gtrsim 10^3\). In astrophysical situations, \(\operatorname{Re}\) can be much larger. For example, in the interstellar medium \(\operatorname{Re} \sim 10^8\). In neutron star mergers we contend with flows having \(\operatorname{Re} \sim 10^{15}\). Consequently, Equation 21.9 implies that \(\ell_d \ll \ell_0\) for turbulent flows.
Summarizing, in our analysis of Equation 21.6 we have found that kinetic energy is injected at large scale \(\ell_0\) (first term on the RHS) and dissipated at the dissipation scale \(\ell_d \ll \ell\) (last term on the RHS). This means that there is range of scales \(\ell_d \ll \ell \ll \ell_0\), the so-called inertial range, in which the dynamics is dominated by the nonlinear term \((\mathbf{v} \cdot \nabla) v^2\). We can estimate it as \[
(\mathbf{v} \cdot \nabla) v^2 \sim \frac{v^3 (\ell)}{\ell} .
\tag{21.11}\] Note that the non-linear term is different from the other two in that there are no scales linked to it, so we assume that it is independent on the scale \(\ell\), as long as \(\ell_d \ll \ell \ll \ell_0\): \[
\frac{v^3 (\ell)}{\ell} \sim \operatorname{const} \Longrightarrow \boxed{v
(\ell) \sim v (\ell_0)  \left( \frac{\ell}{\ell_0} \right)^{1 / 3}} .
\tag{21.12}\] This assumption is key to the theory of turbulence and is called Kolmogorov’s second similarity hypothesis1. This is an assumption that has been verified many times through direct numerical simulations and experiments. Often this hypothesis is formulated in terms of the Fourier transform of \(v^2 (\ell) :\) \[
E (k) = \int e^{\mathrm{i} k \ell} v^2 (\ell) \mathrm{d} \ell .
\tag{21.13}\] If \(v (\ell) \sim \ell^{1 / 3}\), dimensional analysis shows \(E (k) \sim k^{- 5 / 3}\). A comparison between data and theory over more than 10 orders of magnitude in scale is shown in Figure 21.2, which collects data on turbulence in the local ISM recorded by the Voyager 1 mission. Deviations from the Kolmogorov scaling only appear at very small scales, when plasma kinetic effects become important.






Figure 21.2: Turbulence spectrum measured by Voyager 1 (points) and Kolmogorov spectrum (dashed). From Lee and Lee (2019); © Springer Nature, reproduced for non-commercial educational use and not covered by the license of these notes.



A physical interpretation of the K41 model is given by the Richardson cascade (which actually predates K41). In this model, energy is injected at large scale by \(\mathbf{g}\) and dissipated at small scales by the viscosity. The nonlinear term \((\mathbf{v} \cdot \nabla) v^2\) couples different scales and is responsible for the transport of energy from large scale to small scale, as illustrated in Figure 21.3.






Figure 21.3: The Richardson cascade. Redrawn after Frisch (1995).



The main mechanisms for the transport of energy are vortex stretching and shear (Kelvin-Helmholtz) instabilities. It is possible to show that \(v^3 (\ell) / \ell \sim \operatorname{const}\) implies that, in steady state, the flux of energy across scales is constant.
We can interpret \(v^3 (\ell) / \ell\) as a term that controls the kinetic energy dissipation: \[
\frac{v^3 (\ell)}{\ell} = \frac{v^2 (\ell)}{\tau}, \qquad \tau =
\frac{\ell}{v (\ell)},
\tag{21.14}\] where \(\tau\) is the eddy turnover time, the time over which the specific kinetic energy \(v^2 (\ell)\) is dissipated. To see this, notice that for \(\ell_d \ll \ell \ll \ell_0\), Equation 21.6 reduces to \[
\boxed{\frac{\mathrm{d} v^2 (\ell)}{\mathrm{d} t} \sim - \frac{v^2 (\ell)}{\tau}
.}
\tag{21.15}\] The constancy of \(v^3 (\ell) / \ell\) implies that the rate at which turbulence dissipates kinetic energy is independent on \(\nu\) or on the detailed form of the physical processes responsible for dissipation! Instead, it is set by the dynamics at large scale. In other words, when kinetic energy is injected by mechanical work at large scale in a turbulent flow, turbulence efficiently transports this energy to small scales (generating large velocity gradients) at which point it is dissipated. This is the reason why turbulence theory applies equally well to the flow of water around the propeller of a ship and to the motion of rarefied gas in the intergalactic medium. This finding also justifies turbulence modeling approaches used in simulations.
With Kolmogorov’s second similarity law, we can provide a better estimate for \(\ell_d\). Using Equation 21.12 into Equation 21.9, we can eliminate \(v (\ell_d)\) to find \[
\boxed{\ell_d \sim \left( \frac{\nu}{\ell_0 v (\ell_0)} \right)^{3 / 4}
\ell_0} \sim \ell_d = \operatorname{Re}^{- 3 / 4} \ell_0 .
\tag{21.16}\] This shows that the scale separation in developed turbulence can be enormous. The cost of a direct numerical simulation scales as \[
\operatorname{cost} \sim \left( \frac{\ell_0}{\ell_d} \right)^4 \sim \operatorname{Re}^3,
\tag{21.17}\] which makes it impossible to directly simulate very turbulent flows. Direct numerical simulations cannot probe regimes with \(\operatorname{Re} \gtrsim 10^4\). To study flows with higher Reynolds numbers, it is necessary to give up the idea of simulating all scales in the flow and instead resort to modeling the dynamics below the numerical grid scale using turbulence theory.
Before we discuss some applications of Kolmogorov’s theory, it is worth mentioning its limitations. Astrophysical flows are often supersonic and highly magnetized. Compressibility and magnetic fields can have a profound role on the turbulent cascade. Shocks can directly dissipate energy from large scale to small scales. Magnetic fields can give rise to inverse cascade whereby small magnetic field structure self-organize into large scale ordered fields (turbulent dynamo process). The study of compressible, magnetized turbulence is still an active area of research and beyond the scope of this course. However, even for compressible, magnetized flows, Kolmogorov’s theory provides a good starting point and can often be applied directly.

title: 21  Turbulence
section: 21.3 Shredding of Clouds in a Turbulent Flow
text:
21.3 Shredding of Clouds in a Turbulent Flow
Consider a spherical supernova remnant of radius \(R\) immersed in the turbulent interstellar medium. We want to compute the evolution of \(R\) with time. We will consider three cases, illustrated in Figure 21.4.






Figure 21.4: Distortion of a cloud in a turbulent medium. The three different cases are \(R \sim \ell_d\) (case A), \(\ell_d \ll R \ll \ell_0\) (case B), and \(R \sim \ell_0\) (case C).



If \(R \sim \ell_d\) the particles in the cloud will undergo Brownian random motion, so, as in the case of the random diffusion of photons, we have \(R \sim t^{1 / 2}\). If \(R \sim \ell_0\), then the cloud is primarily advected by the mean flow. The edges of the cloud will still experience random diffusion, so \(R \sim t^{1 / 2}\).
The more interesting case is when \(\ell_d \ll R \ll \ell_0\). In this case, the cloud undergoes rapid distortion: \[
\frac{\mathrm{d} R}{\mathrm{d} t} \sim v \sim R^{1 / 3} \Longrightarrow \frac{\mathrm{d}
R^2}{\mathrm{d} t} \sim Rv \sim R^{4 / 3} .
\tag{21.18}\] This is Richardson’s 4/3-law. We can use the second Kolmogorov similarity hypothesis to find the time dependence for \(R\): \[
v (R) \sim v (\ell_0)  \left( \frac{R}{\ell_0} \right)^{1 / 3}
\Longrightarrow R^{- 2 / 3} \sim \frac{v (R)}{R}  \frac{\ell_0^{1 / 3}}{v
(\ell_0)} \Longrightarrow R \sim \left( \frac{R}{v (R)} \right)^{3 / 2} \sim
t^{3 / 2} .
\tag{21.19}\] Turbulence significantly accelerates the mixing of new elements produced in supernovae with the interstellar medium, where they can subsequently form new stars, planets, and people. Turbulence is essential for life to develop in the Universe.

title: 21  Turbulence
text:
21.4 Turbulence Modeling: Reynolds Stress
Directly simulating turbulent flows is impossible, so one of the goals of turbulence theory is to develop effective strategies to deal with unresolved turbulence in simulations. Commonly used models are the Reynolds averaged Navier-Stokes (RANS) and Large-Eddy Simulations (LES) frameworks. Without going into the details, both approaches are based on the general idea of coarse graining the fluid equations. That is we replace \(\mathbf{v}\) with a suitable average \(\bar{\mathbf{v}}\) and try to come up with equations for it. If we coarse grain the Navier-Stokes equations, we find: \[
\partial_t \mathbf{v}+ \nabla \cdot (\mathbf{v} \otimes \mathbf{v}+ p)
=\mathbf{g}+ \nu \nabla^2 \mathbf{v} \longrightarrow \partial_t
\overline{\mathbf{v}} + \nabla \cdot \overline{(\mathbf{v} \otimes
\mathbf{v}+ p)} = \overline{\mathbf{g}} + \nu \nabla^2 \overline{\mathbf{v}}
.
\tag{21.20}\] These equations are exact, but unfortunately not closed, because we do not have a way to compute \(\overline{\mathbf{v} \otimes \mathbf{v}}\) from \(\bar{\mathbf{v}}\). This is the so-called turbulence closure problem. To work around this, we define the Reynolds stress tensor \[
\mathbf{R}= \overline{\mathbf{v} \otimes \mathbf{v}} - \overline{\mathbf{v}}
\otimes \overline{\mathbf{v}}
\tag{21.21}\] and the momentum equation becomes: \[
\partial_t  \overline{\mathbf{v}} + \nabla \cdot (\overline{\mathbf{v}}
\otimes \overline{\mathbf{v}} +\mathbf{R}+ \overline{p}) =
\overline{\mathbf{g}} + \nu \nabla^2 \overline{\mathbf{v}} .
\tag{21.22}\] Equation 21.22 is the momentum equation for a fluid that has velocity equal to \(\overline{\mathbf{v}}\), pressure \(\overline{p}\), and a new component of the stress tensor \(\mathbf{R}\). Because, \(\overline{\mathbf{v}}\) is some average of the true velocity, Equation 21.22 can be solved on a coarse computational mesh. The problem of modeling turbulence is now reduced to that of finding a good model for \(\mathbf{R}\). There are many such models in the literature.
The simplest model, which is also the most commonly used for astrophysical applications, is the turbulent viscosity or Smagorinsky model. Accordingly, one takes \[
\mathbf{R}= - \frac{1}{2} \nu_T  (\nabla \mathbf{v}+ \nabla^T \mathbf{v}) .
\tag{21.23}\] With this choice, Equation 21.22 becomes \[
\partial_t  \overline{\mathbf{v}} + \nabla \cdot (\overline{\mathbf{v}}
\otimes \overline{\mathbf{v}} + \overline{p}) = \overline{\mathbf{g}} + (\nu
+ \nu_T) \nabla^2 \overline{\mathbf{v}} .
\tag{21.24}\] That is turbulence is described simply as a dissipative process and \(\nu_T\) is an effective turbulent viscosity. The turbulent viscosity, in turn, is often obtained using dimensional analysis arguments: \[
\nu_T = \ell_{\operatorname{mix}} V,
\tag{21.25}\] where \(\ell_{\operatorname{mix}}\) is a characteristic length, also called the mixing length, and \(V\) is a characteristic velocity. For example, in accretion disk theory, \(V = c_s\) and \(\ell_{\operatorname{mix}}\) is taken to be proportional to the scale-height of the disk \(H\): \[
\ell_{\operatorname{mix}} = \alpha H = \alpha \frac{c_s}{\Omega} \Longrightarrow
\nu_T = \alpha \frac{c_s^2}{\Omega},
\tag{21.26}\] where \(\Omega\) is the angular velocity of the flow. This is the so-called \(\alpha\)-viscosity model.
For shear flows along \(x\) with shear in the \(y\)-direction, one can use the velocity gradient instead of \(V\): \[
\nu_T = \ell_{\operatorname{mix}}^2  \left( \frac{\partial \overline{v_x}}{\partial
y} \right) .
\tag{21.27}\] For industrial applications, a popular strategy is to solve additional equations for \(\partial_t \mathbf{R}\), with coefficients calibrated to experimental (wind tunnel) results. More sophisticated “subgrid” models have also been proposed for astrophysical applications, but their detailed description is beyond the scope of this course. See Brandenburg and Nordlund (2011) for more information.
Another popular approach is the Implicit Large-Eddy Simulations (ILES) method, in which \(\mathbf{R}\) is not included explicitly in the equations. Instead, a numerical scheme is chosen that has a numerical viscosity \(\nu_{\operatorname{num}} \approx \nu_T\). This approach is often effective, but ILES simulations need to be accompanied by careful resolution studies to assess their reliability, because accurate results can only be obtained if a sufficient portion of the inertial range is resolved by the simulations.






Figure 21.5: Density in a high-resolution simulation of compressible turbulence in the interstellar medium (Federrath et al. 2021), as shown on the cover of Nature Astronomy, April 2021. © Springer Nature, reproduced for non-commercial educational use and not covered by the license of these notes.

title: 21  Turbulence
text:
21.5 In-class worksheet
Turbulence in Core-Collapse Supernovae. We construct here a simplified model showing the role of turbulence in aiding shock revival in core-collapse supernovae.

Consider a steady accretion shock near the protoneutron star. Assume that the in-falling material is cold and that the velocity downstream of the shock is small. Show that the Rankine–Hugoniot conditions simplifies to \[
p_2 \approx \rho_1 v_1^2, \qquad \frac{\rho_2}{\rho_1} = \frac{\Gamma +
1}{\Gamma - 1},
\tag{21.28}\] where all quantities have their usual meaning.
Find the equilibrium pressure \(p_2\) needed to support the accretion shock at a fixed radius \(r_s\), given the mass of the protoneutron star \(M\), and the accretion rate \(\dot{M}\).
Consider angular averages of the flow, e.g., \[
\langle \mathbf{v} \rangle = \frac{1}{4 \pi} \oint \mathbf{v} \mathrm{d}
\Omega .
\tag{21.29}\] Decompose the velocity downstream of the shock as the sum of an average (laminar) component \(\langle \mathbf{v} \rangle\) and a turbulent fluctuating component \(\delta \mathbf{v}\), \(\mathbf{v}= \langle \mathbf{v} \rangle + \delta \mathbf{v}\). Assume that \(\rho\) depends only on radius, so that \(\langle \rho \mathbf{v} \rangle = \rho \langle \mathbf{v} \rangle\). Define the Reynolds stress as \[
\mathbf{R}= \langle \delta \mathbf{v} \otimes \delta \mathbf{v} \rangle
.
\tag{21.30}\] Show that the conservation of momentum across the shock can be written as \[
\rho_2  \langle v_2 \rangle^2 + \rho_2 R_{r r} + p_2 = \rho_1 v_1^2 .
\tag{21.31}\]
Define the specific turbulent kinetic energy as \[
\varepsilon_{\operatorname{turb}} = \frac{1}{2}  | \delta \mathbf{v} |^2 =
\frac{1}{2}  (R_{\operatorname{rr}} + R_{\theta \theta} + R_{\phi \phi}) .
\tag{21.32}\] Assume that \(R_{\operatorname{rr}} = R_{\theta \theta} + R_{\phi \phi}\) and show that with this definition Equation 21.31 can be written as \[
\begin{aligned}
& \rho_2  \langle v_2 \rangle^2 \\
& \quad + \rho_2  [(\Gamma_{\operatorname{turb}} - 1)
\varepsilon_{\operatorname{turb}} + (\Gamma - 1) \varepsilon_2] \\
& \quad = \rho_1 u_1^2 .
\end{aligned}
\tag{21.33}\] What is the effective adiabatic index of turbulence \(\Gamma_{\operatorname{turb}}\)?
At early times, before the turbulence develop, the accretion shock is stalled at a radius \(r_s\). What happens to the shock, once turbulence develops?

title: 21  Turbulence
text:
21.6 Exercises

Exercise 21.1 (Brownian and Lévy random walks) Consider the random walk of a particle. At each step \(i\) a particle at position \(\mathbf{x}_i\) jumps to position \[
\mathbf{x}_{i + 1} =\mathbf{x}_i + R_i \mathbf{d}_i,
\tag{21.34}\] where \(\mathbf{d}_i\) is a random direction on the sphere (uniform in \(\phi\) and \(\cos \theta\)) and \(R_i\) is either

a fixed constant (Brownian random walk); or
it has a Pareto distribution \(p (R) \sim R^{- 1 - \beta}\), for a given \(\beta\) (Lévy random walk).

The Brownian random walk can be used to model ordinary diffusion process, while Lévy random walks can be used to model effective diffusion and mixing in a turbulent flow (superdiffusion).
Write a code to simulate random Brownian and Lévy random walks with \(\beta = 2 / 3\), then construct averages of the traveled distance \(D_N = | \mathbf{x}_N -\mathbf{x}_0 |\) as a function of \(N\) for the two.
Show that \(D_N \sim N^{\gamma}\) and estimate \(\gamma\) in the two cases. Compare the results with the predictions from Kolmogorov theory for diffusion in a turbulent flow (\(R \sim t^{3 / 2}\)).
[You can use numpy.random.uniform and numpy.random.pareto to generate \(R_i\) and \(\mathbf{d}_i\).]

title: 21  Turbulence
text: The first Kolmogorov similarity hypothesis concerns the universality of the flow at the dissipation scale. This is not relevant to astrophysical applications, because astrophysical plasmas become collisionless at small scale, i.e., they do not behave like a fluid anymore. However, as we will see later, Kolmogorov’s theory still applies for \(\ell \gg \ell_d\).↩︎

title: 22  Introduction to Plasma
text:
22.1.1 Lorentz Force and Maxwell Equations
Most of the baryonic matter in the Universe is in the form of plasma, a state of matter characterized by large electrical conductivity and charge mobility. Not surprisingly, plasma physics plays an important role in many astrophysical systems. Before we are ready to discuss plasmas, or even before we can precisely state what plasma is, it is a good idea to refresh some key concepts from electromagnetism. In the process, we will also introduce CGS units, which are ubiquitous in astronomy.
The starting point for electromagnetism is the observation that some particles, electrons and protons, are endowed with electric charge, which as an intrinsic property, like mass. When two lumps of matter with net charge \(Q_1\) and \(Q_2\) are placed at a distance \(r\), the two experience a force, which we write in CGS units as \[
F = \frac{Q_1 Q_2}{r^2} .
\tag{22.1}\] The force is repulsive if \(Q_1 Q_2 > 0\) and attractive if \(Q_1 Q_2 < 0\). Note that there is no Coulomb constant in the previous equation. This is not a typo, but a feature of CGS units. In these units, charge, which is measured in Statcoulomb, is not a fundamental unit, but can be defined in terms of \(\mathrm{g}\), \(\mathrm{cm}\), and \(\mathrm{s}\) using Equation 22.1: \[
[Q]^2 = [F] L^2 = [M]  [L]  [T]^{- 2}  [L]^2 \Longrightarrow [Q]
=\mathrm{g}^{1 / 2} \mathrm{cm}^{3 / 2} \mathrm{s}^{- 1} = : \mathrm{statC} .
\tag{22.2}\] The charge of the electron is \[
e = 4.8032047 \times 10^{- 10} \mathrm{statC} .
\tag{22.3}\] The Coulomb force on particle 2 can also be thought as the effect on particle 2 of an electrostatic field produced by particle 1. In a system of coordinates centered on particle 1, the lines of force of the electrostatic field produced by particle 1 are \[
\mathbf{E}= \frac{Q_1}{r^2}  \hat{\mathbf{r}}
\tag{22.4}\] and the force on particle 2 is given by \[
\mathbf{F}= \frac{Q_1 Q_2}{r^2}  \hat{\mathbf{r}} = Q_2 \mathbf{E}.
\tag{22.5}\] In general, a charged particle with charge \(Q\) moving in an electromagnetic field experiences the so-called Lorentz force: \[
\mathbf{F}= Q \left( \mathbf{E}+ \frac{\mathbf{v} \times \mathbf{B}}{c}
\right),
\tag{22.6}\] where \(c\) is the speed of light. In CGS units, the electric \(\mathbf{E}\) and magnetic \(\mathbf{B}\) fields are defined by Equation 22.6. They also have the same units, as can be easily checked: \[
[\mathbf{E}] = [\mathbf{B}] = \mathrm{cm}^{- 1 / 2} \mathrm{g}^{1 / 2}
\mathrm{s}^{- 1} .
\tag{22.7}\] The fact that \(\mathbf{E}\) and \(\mathbf{B}\) have the same units in CGS is the main reason why these units are still widely used. Indeed, electric and magnetic fields are different manifestations of a single field: the electromagnetic field, as is revealed by special relativity. The electromagnetic field can be found as solution of the Maxwell’s field equations \[
\begin{array}{lll}
\nabla \cdot \mathbf{E}= 4 \pi q, &  & \nabla \cdot \mathbf{B}= 0,\\
\nabla \times \mathbf{E}= - \frac{1}{c}  \frac{\partial
\mathbf{B}}{\partial t}, &  & \nabla \times \mathbf{B}= \frac{4 \pi}{c}
\mathbf{j}+ \frac{1}{c}  \frac{\partial \mathbf{E}}{\partial t} .
\end{array}
\tag{22.8}\] In the previous equation, \(q\) is the charge density and \(\mathbf{j}\) the current density. The equations in the first row are called the Gauss law for electric and magnetic fields. The second two equations are the Faraday, or induction, equation (left column), and the Ampere-Maxwell law (right column).


22.1.2 Electrostatics
If \(\frac{\partial \mathbf{E}}{\partial t} =\mathbf{B}= 0\), Maxwell equations simplify to \[
\nabla \cdot \mathbf{E}= 4 \pi q,  \nabla \times \mathbf{E}= 0,
\tag{22.9}\] The second equation tells us that \(\mathbf{E}= - \nabla \Phi\), where \(\Phi\) is the electrostatic potential. The latter satisfies the Poisson equation \[
\nabla^2 \Phi = - 4 \pi q.
\tag{22.10}\] Apart from a minus sign, this is the same equation satisfied by the gravitational potential.
The force experienced by a charge \(Q\) in an electrostatic field is \[
\mathbf{F}= Q\mathbf{E}= - Q \nabla \Phi .
\tag{22.11}\]






TipExample



Consider the electrostatic potential generated by a spherical distribution of charge density \(q\) and the force experienced by an electron \(e\) outside the sphere, as illustrated in Figure 22.1.






Figure 22.1: Spherical distribution of charge.



The radial component of the force experienced by a particle of charge \(e\) at a distance \(r\) from a charged sphere, with charge density \(q\) is given by: \[
F_r = - e \partial_r \Phi .
\tag{22.12}\] From the Poisson equation \[
\nabla \cdot \nabla \Phi = - 4 \pi q.
\tag{22.13}\] Integrating both sides over a sphere of radius \(r\), we find \[
- 4 \pi \int_V q \mathrm{d} V = - 4 \pi Q = \int_V \nabla \cdot \nabla \Phi
\mathrm{d} V,
\tag{22.14}\] The RHS gives (using Gauss’ law) \[
\int_V \nabla \cdot \nabla \Phi \mathrm{d} V = \int_S \nabla \Phi \cdot
\hat{\mathbf{r}} \mathrm{d} S = 4 \pi r^2 \partial_r \Phi \Longrightarrow
\partial_r \Phi = - \frac{Q}{r^2} \Longrightarrow F_r = \frac{Qe}{r^2} .
\tag{22.15}\]


Even though electrostatic and gravitational forces have a similar mathematical structure, these forces are very different for two reasons. First, gravity is always attractive, because no forms of matter are known to possess negative mass, while electric charge can be positive or negative and objects of similar charge repel each other. Second, gravity is a very weak force, as we explore with the next example.






TipExample



Consider a proton on the surface of the Sun. It is subject to an attractive gravitational force: \[
F_g = - \frac{GM_{\odot} m_p}{R_{\odot }^2} .
\tag{22.16}\] The proton is also subject to an electrostatic: \[
F_e = \frac{Q_{\odot} e}{R_{\odot}^2},
\tag{22.17}\] where \(Q_{\odot} \approx \frac{M_{\odot}}{m_p} \varepsilon\) is the net charge of the Sun, where \(\varepsilon = (N_p - N_e) / N_p\) is the fractional charge imbalance. Gravity and electrostatic forces balance each other when \[
\varepsilon = \frac{Gm_p^2}{e^2} \sim 10^{- 36} .
\tag{22.18}\] The Sun must be very close to neutral, because even a small charge imbalance would cause particles of the same charge as the Sun to be evaporated from the surface.


The argument we have just made for the Sun apply to most astrophysical systems. This implies that the charge imbalance in astronomical objects must be very small. In other words, they are quasi-neutral. As we will see shortly, quasi-neutrality is one of the key characteristics an ionized gas must have to be considered to be plasma. At this point, it is important to remark that, while we will be concerned only with systems that have zero net charge, these systems can still contain electric currents, which give rise to magnetic fields and internal stresses via the Lorentz force.






NoteGoing further: Conservation Laws in Electrodynamics



If we take the divergence of Ampere’s law we find \[
\frac{\partial \nabla \cdot \mathbf{E}}{\partial t} + 4 \pi
\nabla \cdot \mathbf{j}= 0.
\tag{22.19}\] Using Gauss’ law \[
\frac{\partial q}{\partial t} + \nabla \cdot \mathbf{j}= 0.
\tag{22.20}\] So the charge density satisfies a continuity equation, just like the mass density for a fluid. In other words, the Maxwell equations imply charge conservation.
It is also possible to show that the Maxwell equation imply conservation of the energy in the electromagnetic field. To see this, consider the work done by the electromagnetic field on a fluid with charge density \(q\) and velocity \(\mathbf{v}\). The Lorentz force per unit volume is \[
\mathbf{f}= q \left( \mathbf{E}+ \frac{\mathbf{v} \times \mathbf{B}}{c}
\right) .
\tag{22.21}\] So the work per unit volume is (using \(\mathbf{j}= q\mathbf{v}\) and Ampere’s law) \[
w =\mathbf{f} \cdot \mathbf{v}= q\mathbf{E} \cdot \mathbf{v}=\mathbf{E}
\cdot \mathbf{j}= \frac{1}{4 \pi}  \left[ c (\nabla \times \mathbf{B}) \cdot
\mathbf{E}-\mathbf{E} \cdot \frac{\partial \mathbf{E}}{\partial t} \right] .
\tag{22.22}\] Using the vector identity \[
\mathbf{E} \cdot (\nabla \times \mathbf{B}) =\mathbf{B} \cdot (\nabla \times
\mathbf{E}) - \nabla \cdot (\mathbf{E} \times \mathbf{B})
\tag{22.23}\] and \[
\mathbf{E} \cdot \frac{\partial \mathbf{E}}{\partial t} = \frac{1}{2}
\dfrac{\partial E^2}{\partial t},
\tag{22.24}\] we can write \[
\mathbf{E} \cdot \mathbf{j}= \frac{1}{4 \pi}  \left\{ c [\mathbf{B} \cdot
(\nabla \times \mathbf{E}) - \nabla \cdot (\mathbf{E} \times \mathbf{B})] -
\frac{1}{2}  \frac{\partial E^2}{\partial t} \right\},
\tag{22.25}\] we can use Faraday’s law to get rid of \(c \nabla \times \mathbf{E}\) to rewrite the last equation as \[
\frac{1}{8 \pi}  \frac{\partial (E^2 + B^2)}{\partial t} + \nabla \cdot
\left( \frac{c}{4 \pi} \mathbf{E} \times \mathbf{B} \right) = -\mathbf{E}
\cdot \mathbf{j}.
\tag{22.26}\] We can recognize that this is a conservation law in the form \[
\frac{\partial u_{\operatorname{EM}}}{\partial t} + \nabla \cdot \mathbf{S}=
-\mathbf{E} \cdot \mathbf{j}.
\tag{22.27}\] The last term is the work done by the electric field, so we can interpret \(u_{\operatorname{EM}} = \tfrac{E^2 + B^2}{8 \pi}\) as the energy in the electromagnetic field and the vector \(\mathbf{S}= \frac{c}{4 \pi} \mathbf{E} \times \mathbf{B}\), called the Poynting flux, as the flux of electromagnetic energy. Equation 22.26 is also called the Poynting theorem. As we will see later, the equation for energy conservation for a plasma is just the sum of the energy conservation equations for the matter, which we already know as the energy equation, and the energy conservation equation for the electromagnetic field.




22.1.3 Electromagnetic Waves
The propagation of electromagnetic waves in vacuum can be studied with a similar formalism as that used to study sound waves. Actually, since Maxwell equations are linear, the derivation of the dispersion relation for electromagnetic waves is simpler than that for sound waves. The starting point are the Maxwell equations in vacuum: \[
\begin{array}{lll}
\nabla \cdot \mathbf{E}= 0, &  & \nabla \cdot \mathbf{B}= 0,\\
\nabla \times \mathbf{E}= - \frac{1}{c}  \frac{\partial
\mathbf{B}}{\partial t}, &  & \nabla \times \mathbf{B}= \frac{1}{c}
\frac{\partial \mathbf{E}}{\partial t} .
\end{array}
\tag{22.28}\] We look for solutions in the form \[
\mathbf{E} (t, \mathbf{x}) = \hat{\mathbf{E}}_0 e^{\mathrm{i} (\mathbf{k}
\cdot \mathbf{x}- \omega t)}, \qquad \mathbf{B} (t, \mathbf{x}) =
\hat{\mathbf{B}}_0 e^{\mathrm{i} (\mathbf{k} \cdot \mathbf{x}- \omega t)} .
\tag{22.29}\] Inserting this ansatz into the first row of Equation 22.28, we obtain \[
\nabla \cdot \mathbf{E}= 0 \Longrightarrow \mathrm{i} \mathbf{k} \cdot
\hat{\mathbf{E}}_0 e^{\mathrm{i} (\mathbf{k} \cdot \mathbf{x}- \omega t)} = 0
\Longrightarrow \mathbf{k} \perp \hat{\mathbf{E}}_0
\tag{22.30}\] and, similarly, \(\mathbf{k} \perp \hat{\mathbf{B}}_0\). This means that, differently from sound waves, electromagnetic waves in vacuum are transverse, meaning that \(\mathbf{E}\) and \(\mathbf{B}\) are perpendicular to the direction of propagation of the wave.
From Faraday’s law, we obtain that \[
\frac{\mathrm{i} \omega}{c}  \hat{\mathbf{B}}_0 e^{\mathrm{i} (\mathbf{k} \cdot
\mathbf{x}- \omega t)} = \mathrm{i} \mathbf{k} \times \hat{\mathbf{E}}_0
e^{\mathrm{i} (\mathbf{k} \cdot \mathbf{x}- \omega t)} \Longrightarrow
\frac{\omega}{c}  \hat{\mathbf{B}}_0 =\mathbf{k} \times \hat{\mathbf{E}}_0 .
\tag{22.31}\] This implies that \(\hat{\mathbf{E}}_0 \perp \hat{\mathbf{B}}_0\). From Ampere’s law, we obtain \[
\mathbf{k} \times \hat{\mathbf{B}}_0 = - \frac{\omega}{c}
\hat{\mathbf{E}}_0 .
\tag{22.32}\] Substituting Equation 22.32 into Equation 22.31, we obtain (using the properties of the double vector product) \[
\frac{\omega}{c}  \hat{\mathbf{B}}_0 = - \frac{c}{\omega} \mathbf{k} \times
(\mathbf{k} \times \hat{\mathbf{B}}_0) = \cancel{- \frac{c}{\omega} \mathbf{k}
(\mathbf{k} \cdot \hat{\mathbf{B}}_0)} + \frac{c}{\omega} k^2
\hat{\mathbf{B}}_0 = \frac{c}{\omega} k^2  \hat{\mathbf{B}}_0
\Longrightarrow \boxed{\omega^2 = c^2 k^2} .
\tag{22.33}\] So electromagnetic waves satisfy the same dispersion relation as sound waves, but with \(c\), the speed of light, instead of the sound speed \(c_s\).

title: 22  Introduction to Plasma
text:
22.2 Plasma

22.2.1 What is a Plasma?
Consider a quasi-neutral gas made of electrons and ions. Assume that, due to a thermal fluctuation, a small over density of electrons \(\delta n\) is created in a region with characteristic size \(L\). How large can this fluctuation be?






Figure 22.2: Schematic representation of an over density of electrons.



The electrostatic potential created by this over-density is of order \[
\delta \Phi \sim 4 \pi L^2 e \delta n.
\tag{22.34}\] The potential energy of each electron is \[
U \sim e \delta \Phi .
\tag{22.35}\] Their kinetic is \(K \sim k_B T\) (in thermodynamic equilibrium). Thermal fluctuations should have \(U \sim K\), so \[
4 \pi L^2 e^2 \delta n \sim k_B T \Longrightarrow \frac{\delta n}{n} \sim
\frac{1}{L^2}  \left( \frac{k_B T}{4 \pi ne^2} \right) =: \left(
\frac{\lambda_D}{L} \right)^2,
\tag{22.36}\] where \(n\) is the density of free electrons and we have introduced the Debye length \[
\boxed{\lambda_D = \sqrt{\frac{k_B T}{4 \pi ne^2}} .}
\tag{22.37}\] The Debye length is a characteristic length scale for charge fluctuations in the gas. Over scales \(L \gg \lambda_D\), one can assume that the medium is neutral, if the density of the gas is sufficiently high.
To see this, consider again a uniform gas of electrons and ions. The ion masses are of order \(Am_p \sim (2 \times 10^3) Am_e\), so if ions and electrons have on average the same kinetic energy, as would be expected in equilibrium \(v_{\operatorname{ions}} \ll v_e\). To first approximations, we can consider the ions to be static and immersed in a sea of electrons. If electrons are abundant, each ion will then be surrounded by a sea of electrons, which effectively shield its charge hiding it from the other ions, as shown in Figure 22.3.






Figure 22.3: Electron cloud around an ion of charge \(q\).



It turns out that, in this situation, the electrostatic potential near the ion is \[
\Phi (r) = \frac{q}{r} e^{- r / \lambda_D},
\tag{22.38}\] where \(\lambda_D\) is the Debye length. In other words, the Debye length is also the characteristic screening length. However, screening can only take place if electrons are sufficiently mobile to screen each ion. To quantify this, we define the plasma parameter: \[
\Lambda = \frac{4}{3} \pi n \lambda_D^3 = \frac{1}{6 \sqrt[]{\pi} e^3}  (k_B
T)^{3 / 2} n^{- 1 / 2} .
\tag{22.39}\] The plasma parameter is just the number of electrons in each Debye sphere. We say that a ionized gas for which \(\lambda_D \ll L\) and \(\Lambda \gg 1\) is a plasma. Typical plasma parameters for astrophysical systems are given in Table 22.1. As we can see, astrophysical plasmas span tremendous range in scales.

22.2.2 Cold Plasma Approximation
The cold plasma approximation is used to study the propagation of electromagnetic waves, particularly radio waves, in the interstellar medium. As the name suggests, in the cold plasma approximation we ignore the thermal motion of the electrons. We also take the ions to be stationary. Let’s consider the propagation of an electromagnetic wave through such medium, as illustrated in Figure 22.4.






Figure 22.4: Lorentz force experienced by an electron due to a passing electromagnetic wave.



The Lorentz force experienced by an electron is (assuming \(v \ll c\)): \[
\mathbf{F}= - e \left( \mathbf{E}+ \frac{\mathbf{v} \times \mathbf{B}}{c}
\right) \approx - e\mathbf{E}.
\tag{22.40}\] So, if we take \(\mathbf{E}= \hat{\mathbf{E}}_0 e^{\mathrm{i} (\mathbf{k} \cdot \mathbf{x}- \omega t)}\) and \(\mathbf{v}= \hat{\mathbf{v}}_0 e^{\mathrm{i} (\mathbf{k} \cdot \mathbf{x}- \omega t)}\), we have \[
\quad  \hat{\mathbf{v}}_0 = \frac{e \hat{\mathbf{E}}_0}{\mathrm{i} \omega m_e} .
\tag{22.41}\] The induced current density in the plasma is \[
\hat{\mathbf{j}} = - ne \hat{\mathbf{v}}_0 = \left( \frac{\mathrm{i}
ne^2}{\omega m_e} \right)  \hat{\mathbf{E}}_0 = : \sigma \hat{\mathbf{E}}_0,
\tag{22.42}\] where we have introduced the conductivity \(\sigma\). Charge conservation is \[
\frac{\partial q}{\partial t} + \nabla \cdot \mathbf{j}= 0 \Longrightarrow -
\mathrm{i} \omega \hat{q}_0 + \mathrm{i} \mathbf{k} \cdot \hat{\mathbf{j}}_0 = 0
\Longrightarrow \hat{q}_0 = \frac{\mathbf{k} \cdot
\hat{\mathbf{j}}_0}{\omega} = \frac{\sigma}{\omega} \mathbf{k} \cdot
\hat{\mathbf{E}}_0 .
\tag{22.43}\] Gauss’ law reads \[
\mathrm{i} \mathbf{k} \cdot \hat{\mathbf{E}}_0 = 4 \pi \hat{q}_0 \Longrightarrow
\mathrm{i} \mathbf{k} \cdot \left( 1 - \frac{4 \pi \sigma}{\mathrm{i} \omega}
\right) \hat{\mathbf{E}}_0 = 0.
\tag{22.44}\] Introducing the dielectric constant \[
\begin{gathered}
\epsilon = 1 - \frac{4 \pi \sigma}{\mathrm{i} \omega} = 1 - \left(
\frac{\omega_p}{\omega} \right)^2, \\
\omega_p = \sqrt{\frac{4 \pi
ne^2}{m}} = 56.3 \mathrm{kHz} \left( \frac{n}{1 \mathrm{cm}^{- 3}} \right)^{1 /
2} .
\end{gathered}
\tag{22.45}\] we find that the Maxwell equations reduce to \[
\begin{array}{lll}
\mathrm{i} \mathbf{k} \cdot \epsilon \hat{\mathbf{E}}_0 = 0, &  & \mathrm{i}
\mathbf{k} \cdot \hat{\mathbf{B}}_0 = 0,\\
\mathrm{i} \mathbf{k} \times \hat{\mathbf{E}}_0 = \mathrm{i} \frac{\omega}{c}
\hat{\mathbf{B}}, &  & \mathrm{i} \mathbf{k} \times \hat{\mathbf{B}}_0 = -
\mathrm{i} \frac{\omega}{c} \epsilon \hat{\mathbf{E}}_0 .
\end{array}
\tag{22.46}\] These can be solved in the same way as the vacuum Maxwell equations to find the dispersion relation for electromagnetic waves in a cold plasma \[
c^2 k^2 = \epsilon \omega^2 \Longrightarrow k = \frac{\omega}{c}  \sqrt{1 -
\left( \frac{\omega_p}{\omega } \right)^2} \Longrightarrow \boxed{k =
\frac{1}{c}  \sqrt{\omega^2 - \omega_p^2} .}
\tag{22.47}\] For example, if the wave is propagating in the \(z\)-direction, \(\mathbf{k}= \left(\begin{array}{ccc} 0 & 0 & k \end{array}\right)^T\). Then

If \(\omega < \omega_p\), then \(k\) is imaginary: the wave is damped: \[
\mathbf{E}= \hat{\mathbf{E}}_0 e^{\mathrm{i} \omega t} e^{- \frac{z}{c}
\sqrt{\omega_p^2 - \omega^2}} .
\tag{22.48}\] This is a remarkable property of plasma. Even though the motion of particles and fields in the plasma are described by equations that do not have dissipation, we find that some waves are damped.
If \(\omega > \omega_p\) the wave can propagate, but different frequencies propagate at different speeds: \[
v_g = \frac{\partial \omega}{\partial k} = c \sqrt{1 -
\frac{\omega_p^2}{\omega^2}} .
\tag{22.49}\] This leads to the phenomenon of dispersion, which can be used to estimate the column distance to sources of radio pulses, such as pulsars and fast radio-bursts, as illustrated in Figure 22.5.






Figure 22.5: Different arrival time of a fast radio burst at different frequencies as a result of dispersion in the ISM: the first fast radio burst, FRB 010724. From Lorimer (2018) (figure by E. Keane); © Springer Nature, reproduced for non-commercial educational use and not covered by the license of these notes.

22.3 In-class worksheet
Fast radio bursts are thought to be millisecond-long broad-band radio flares, produced during particularly violent magnetar flares, and possibly other astrophysical events. As the radio waves propagates from the source to Earth through the interstellar medium, the signal is dispersed, as shown in Figure 22.6:






Figure 22.6: Time-frequency signal for FRB 010724. Adapted from Lorimer (2018) (figure by E. Keane); © Springer Nature, reproduced for non-commercial educational use and not covered by the license of these notes.



The time of arrival of the peak of the burst at angular frequency \(\omega\), \(t_p (\omega)\) is given by \[
t_p = \int_0^d \frac{\mathrm{d} s}{v_g (\omega)},
\tag{22.50}\] where \(d\) is the (luminosity) distance to the source and \(v_g (\omega)\) is the group velocity at frequency \(\omega\). The approximate arrival times for  FRB 010724 are tabulated below

Assume that the interstellar medium is a cold plasma, with plasma frequency \[

Show that \[

Compute the DM for FRB 010724. In the direction of this source, the DM due to free electrons within the Milky Way is estimated to be \(\operatorname{DM} = 25 \mathrm{cm}^{- 3} \operatorname{pc}\). Is this source extragalactic?

title: 23  The MHD Equations
text:
23.1 Lorentz Force
These notes present a concise derivation of the equations of magnetohydrodynamics (MHD) and a discussion of the underlying assumptions. We consider a quasi-neutral gas of ions and electrons immersed in an external magnetic field. Let \(\mathbf{w}_e\) and \(\mathbf{w}_i\) be the drift velocities of electrons and ions, respectively. The Lorentz force experienced by each electron is \[
\mathbf{F}_e = - \frac{e}{c} \mathbf{w}_e \times \mathbf{B}.
\tag{23.1}\] The force experienced by the ions is \[
\mathbf{F}_i = \frac{Ze}{c} \mathbf{w}_i \times \mathbf{B}.
\tag{23.2}\] So the total force per unit volume is \[
\mathbf{f}= n_e \mathbf{F}_e + n_i \mathbf{F}_i = \frac{e}{c}  (n_i
Z\mathbf{w}_i - n_e \mathbf{w}_e) \times \mathbf{B} =: \mathbf{j}
\times \mathbf{B}.
\tag{23.3}\] Note that we have absorbed the \(1 / c\) factor in the definition of \(\mathbf{j}\), following a standard convention in magnetohydrodynamics.
The equations of MHD are just the “usual” hydrodynamics equations with the addition of the Lorentz force on the RHS: \[
\begin{aligned}
\frac{\mathrm{d} \rho}{\mathrm{d} t} &= - \rho \nabla \cdot \mathbf{v}, \\
\rho \frac{\mathrm{d} \mathbf{v}}{\mathrm{d} t} &= \boxed{\mathbf{j} \times \mathbf{B}} - \nabla p, \\
\rho \frac{\mathrm{d} \varepsilon}{\mathrm{d} t} &= - p \nabla \cdot \mathbf{v}.
\end{aligned}
\tag{23.4}\] These equations look deceivably simple. The real complication is that \(\mathbf{j}\) and \(\mathbf{B}\) are not prescribed, but are self-consistently produced by the fluid. We have also implicitly made the following assumption
This assumption is satisfied in most situations encountered in terrestrial and astrophysical applications, because the currents are sufficiently weak and the charge densities sufficiently large that we can treat the plasma as being a single fluid. This can be violated in very tenuous plasmas, for example in the magnetosphere of dying pulsars, in which the field and spin have decayed to the point that pair production is no longer efficient. In this case, one needs to go beyond magnetohydrodynamics and use the multi-fluid magnetohydrodynamics equations, or employ a fully kinetic treatment. Another situation in which this assumption can fail is if the degree of ionization of the plasma is small, so there is drift between the charged component of the gas and the neutrals, ambipolar diffusion. As we will see later, ambipolar diffusion plays an important role, for example, in stellar formation.

title: 23  The MHD Equations
text: Assumption 23.1 (Negligible drift momentum) The drift motion of the charged particles in the plasma that gives rise to the current is sufficiently small that we can neglect its contribution to the macroscopic momentum \(\rho \mathbf{v}\). In other words, in a frame in which \(\mathbf{v}= 0\), we have \(m_i n_i \mathbf{w}_i + m_e n_e \mathbf{w}_e \approx 0\).

title: 23  The MHD Equations
text:
23.2 Ohm’s Law
We need two more equations, in addition to the equation of state, to close Equation 23.4. A first equation is the equation prescribing how currents \(\mathbf{j}\) arise in the plasma. The simplest model for the current is to assume that it is proportional to the electric field.

Assumption 23.2 (Ohm’s law) The electric current in the plasma \(\mathbf{j}\) is proportional to the electric field \(\mathbf{E}'\) in the frame of the plasma (in which \(\mathbf{v}= 0\)): \(\mathbf{j}= \sigma \mathbf{E}'\).

The quantity \(\sigma\) is called the electrical conductivity, it is the inverse of the electrical resistivity \(\eta = 1 / \sigma\), which you might be familiar from electromagnetism. In CGS units1 \[
[\mathbf{E}] = \mathrm{cm}^{- 1 / 2} \mathrm{g}^{1 / 2} \mathrm{s}^{- 1},
\qquad [\mathbf{j}] = \mathrm{cm}^{- 3 / 2} \mathrm{g}^{1 / 2} \mathrm{s},
\tag{23.5}\] so the units of electrical conductivity is \[
[\sigma] = \mathrm{cm}^{- 1} \mathrm{s}^2 .
\tag{23.6}\] Again, note that in CGS units all electromagnetic quantities have units that can be expressed in terms of fundamental length, time, and mass. Charge and current are not independent quantities. This means that the Maxwell and MHD equations do not have new fundamental constants. Be very careful not to mix CGS and SI units, because the equations are different in the two cases.
One subtlety with the new assumption is what we mean for the “electric field in the frame of the plasma”. The hydrodynamics equations are invariant with respect to Galilean transformations, that if \(\mathbf{u}\) is a velocity in the Eulerian frame, then in the fluid frame we have \[
\mathbf{u}' =\mathbf{u}-\mathbf{v}.
\tag{23.7}\] On the other hand, Maxwell equations are invariant with respect to Lorentz transformations. As such, Maxwell equations and the equations of non-relativistic hydrodynamics are fundamentally incompatible. To be able to put them together in a consistent way, we need to assume that \(\mathbf{E}\) and \(\mathbf{B}\) transform according to Lorentz transformations in the nonrelativistic limit.

Assumption 23.3 (Nonrelativistic limit) We assume \(v \ll c\), \(| \mathbf{E} | \ll | \mathbf{B} |\), and \(\left| \frac{1}{c} \frac{\partial \mathbf{E}}{\partial t} \right| \ll | \mathbf{j} |\). The second two assumptions are needed to ensure that charges are not relativistic and the plasma quasi-neutral.

Under these assumptions, it is possible to show that \[
\mathbf{B}' =\mathbf{B}, \qquad \mathbf{E}' =\mathbf{E}+ \frac{\mathbf{v}
\times \mathbf{B}}{c}, \qquad \mathbf{j}' =\mathbf{j}.
\tag{23.8}\] Accordingly, Ohm’s law becomes \[
\mathbf{j}' = \sigma \mathbf{E}' \Longrightarrow \mathbf{j}= \sigma \left(
\mathbf{E}+ \frac{\mathbf{v} \times \mathbf{B}}{c} \right) .
\tag{23.9}\] In Ampere’s law2, \[
\nabla \times \mathbf{B}= 4 \pi \mathbf{j}+ \frac{1}{c}  \frac{\partial
\mathbf{E}}{\partial t},
\tag{23.10}\] we can drop the displacement current to obtain \[
\nabla \times \mathbf{B}= 4 \pi \mathbf{j}.
\tag{23.11}\] Then the Lorentz force becomes \[
\boxed{\mathbf{f}=\mathbf{j} \times \mathbf{B}= \frac{1}{4 \pi}  (\nabla
\times \mathbf{B}) \times \mathbf{B}.}
\tag{23.12}\] With this, we have completely eliminated the current from the MHD equations: \[
\boxed{\rho \frac{\mathrm{d} \mathbf{v}}{\mathrm{d} t} = \frac{1}{4 \pi}
(\nabla \times \mathbf{B}) \times \mathbf{B}- \nabla p.}
\tag{23.13}\] We still need another equation for \(\mathbf{B}\) to completely close the MHD equations.

title: 23  The MHD Equations
text:
23.3 Faraday’s Law
The missing equation is given by Faraday’s law, also known as the induction equation: \[
\frac{\partial \mathbf{B}}{\partial t} = - c \nabla \times \mathbf{E}.
\tag{23.14}\] Here, we use again Ohm’s law to eliminate \(\mathbf{E}\): \[
\frac{1}{\sigma} \mathbf{j} =: \eta \mathbf{j}=\mathbf{E}+
\frac{\mathbf{v} \times \mathbf{B}}{c} \Longrightarrow \mathbf{E}= \eta
\mathbf{j}- \frac{\mathbf{v} \times \mathbf{B}}{c} .
\tag{23.15}\] We use again Ampere’s law to remove \(\mathbf{j}= \frac{1}{4 \pi} \nabla \times \mathbf{B}\): \[
\mathbf{E}= \frac{\eta}{4 \pi} \nabla \times \mathbf{B}- \frac{\mathbf{v}
\times \mathbf{B}}{c} .
\tag{23.16}\] Inserting this back into the induction equation yields: \[
\begin{aligned}
\frac{\partial \mathbf{B}}{\partial t} &= - c \nabla \times \mathbf{E} \\
&= \nabla \times (\mathbf{v} \times \mathbf{B}) - \frac{c}{4 \pi} \nabla \times
(\eta \nabla \times \mathbf{B}) .
\end{aligned}
\tag{23.17}\] If \(\eta\) is constant, then \[
\nabla \times (\nabla \times \mathbf{B}) = \nabla (\nabla \cdot \mathbf{B})
- \nabla^2 \mathbf{B},
\tag{23.18}\] so we find \[
\boxed{\frac{\partial \mathbf{B}}{\partial t} = \nabla \times
(\mathbf{v} \times \mathbf{B}) + \frac{c \eta}{4 \pi} \nabla^2 \mathbf{B}.}
\tag{23.19}\] This is the last equation. The full set of MHD equation is \[
\begin{aligned}
\frac{\mathrm{d} \rho}{\mathrm{d} t} &= - \rho \nabla \cdot \mathbf{v}, \\
\rho \frac{\mathrm{d} \mathbf{v}}{\mathrm{d} t} &= \frac{1}{4 \pi}  (\nabla
\times \mathbf{B}) \times \mathbf{B}- \nabla p - \rho \nabla \Psi, \\
\rho \frac{\mathrm{d} \varepsilon}{\mathrm{d} t} &= - p \nabla \cdot \mathbf{v}, \\
\frac{\partial \mathbf{B}}{\partial t} &= \nabla \times (\mathbf{v} \times
\mathbf{B}) + \frac{c \eta}{4 \pi} \nabla^2 \mathbf{B}.
\end{aligned}
\tag{23.20}\] They can be converted to the Eulerian frame with the usual substitution \[
\frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d} t} \longrightarrow \frac{\partial}{\partial t} +
(\mathbf{v} \cdot \nabla) .
\tag{23.21}\] If \(\eta = 0\), these are known as the ideal-MHD equations. If \(\eta > 0\), these are called the resistive-MHD equations.

title: 23  The MHD Equations
text:
23.4 Conservation Laws
It is possible to rearrange the terms of the momentum equation to obtain an equation that shows the conservation of the linear momentum: \[
\boxed{
\begin{aligned}
& \frac{\partial (\rho \mathbf{v})}{\partial t} \\
& \quad + \nabla \cdot \biggl[ \rho \mathbf{v} \otimes \mathbf{v}+ \Bigl( p + \frac{B^2}{8 \pi}
\Bigr) \mathbf{I} \\
& \qquad\qquad - \frac{\mathbf{B} \otimes \mathbf{B}}{4 \pi} \biggr]
=\mathbf{f},
\end{aligned}}
\tag{23.22}\] where \(\mathbf{f}\) is some external force, e.g., gravity. The derivation of this equation is tedious, but straight forward. Here, we limit ourselves to discuss a couple of the consequences of this equation. The first is that the magnetic field does not contribute to the momentum \(\rho \mathbf{v}\), consistently with Assumption 23.1. This is not the case in relativistic MHD, in which the inertia of the electromagnetic field is also taken into account. Second, we see that the Lorentz force splits into two components: one that resembles an additional pressure term \(B^2 / 8 \pi\), plus a term proportional to \(\mathbf{B} \otimes \mathbf{B}\). We will discuss these terms in more detail in the next set of notes.
The energy conservation equation now takes into account both the gas energy and the energy in the electromagnetic field and can be obtained by combining the gas-dynamics energy equation with the Poynting theorem. Specifically, the equation describing the energy conservation for the gas is \[
\begin{aligned}
& \frac{\partial e}{\partial t} + \nabla \cdot [(e + p) \mathbf{v}]
=\mathbf{f} \cdot \mathbf{v}+ (\mathbf{j} \times \mathbf{B}) \cdot
\mathbf{v}, \\
& e = \rho \varepsilon + \tfrac{1}{2} \rho v^2 .
\end{aligned}
\tag{23.23}\] This is just the usual energy equation, with the inclusion of a new term representing the work done by the Lorentz force. The latter can be rewritten using Equation 23.16 as \[
(\mathbf{j} \times \mathbf{B}) \cdot \mathbf{v}= - (\mathbf{v} \times
\mathbf{B}) \cdot \mathbf{j}= c\mathbf{E} \cdot \mathbf{j}.
\tag{23.24}\] You might recognize this as being the energy sink term in the Poynting equation: \[
\frac{\partial u_{\mathrm{EM}}}{\partial t} + \nabla \cdot \mathbf{S}= -
c\mathbf{j} \cdot \mathbf{E},
\tag{23.25}\] where \(u_{\mathrm{EM}}\) is the electromagnetic field energy, which in our case is: \[
u_{\mathrm{EM}} = \frac{B^2 + E^2}{8 \pi} \approx \frac{B^2}{8 \pi} =
u_{\mathrm{B}},
\tag{23.26}\] consistently with our assumption that the dynamics is nonrelativistic. The Poynting vector is, using again Equation 23.16: \[
\mathbf{S}= \frac{c}{4 \pi}  (\mathbf{E} \times \mathbf{B}) =
\frac{\mathbf{B} \times (\mathbf{v} \times \mathbf{B})}{4 \pi} .
\tag{23.27}\] Combining Equation 23.23 and Equation 23.25, we obtain \[
\frac{\partial (e + u_{\mathrm{B}})}{\partial t} + \nabla \cdot [(e + p)
\mathbf{v}+\mathbf{S}] =\mathbf{f} \cdot \mathbf{v}.
\tag{23.28}\] In full form: \[
\boxed{
\begin{aligned}
& \partial_t  \left[ \rho \left( \varepsilon + \tfrac{1}{2} v^2
\right) + \frac{B^2}{8 \pi} \right] \\
& \quad + \nabla \cdot \left[ (e + p)
\mathbf{v}+ \frac{\mathbf{B} \times (\mathbf{v} \times \mathbf{B})}{4 \pi}
\right] =\mathbf{f} \cdot \mathbf{v}.
\end{aligned}}
\tag{23.29}\] This equation highlights the fact that magnetic and fluid energies are not separately conserved, but their sum is. In other words, it is possible to convert gas kinetic energy into magnetic energy (dynamo effect) or magnetic energy into kinetic and internal energy (magnetic reconnection).

title: 23  The MHD Equations
text:
23.6 Exercises

Exercise 23.1 (Angular momentum of the solar wind)  

Starting from the equations of ideal-MHD, show that the angular momentum of plasma, \[
J = \int_V \mathbf{r} \times \rho \mathbf{v} \mathrm{d} V,
\tag{23.31}\] subject to an external force per unit mass \(\mathbf{f}\), satisfies \[
\frac{\mathrm{d} J}{\mathrm{d} t} = \int_V \mathbf{r} \times \mathbf{f} \mathrm{d} V
- \oint_S \left[ (\mathbf{v} \cdot \mathrm{d} \mathbf{S})  (\mathbf{r} \times
\rho \mathbf{v}) + \left( p + \tfrac{B^2}{8 \pi} \right) \mathbf{r}
\times \mathrm{d} \mathbf{S}- \tfrac{1}{4 \pi}  (\mathbf{r} \times
\mathbf{B})  (\mathbf{B} \cdot \mathrm{d} \mathbf{S}) \right] .
\tag{23.32}\] [Hint. Follow the steps of Exercise 6.1.]
Assume that the magnetic field is stationary in a frame rotating with the angular velocity of the Sun. Show that if the solar wind is infinitely conducting, then (in cylindrical coordinates \(r, \phi, z\)) \[
B_{\phi} v_R = (v_{\phi} - \Omega R) B_R,
\tag{23.33}\] where \(\Omega\) is the angular velocity of the Sun.
Assuming that the angular torque \(\dot{J}\) across a cylinder of height \(2 R\) is constant with \(R\). Show that it can be written as \[
- \dot{J} = 2 \pi \int_{- R}^R \left( R \rho v_R v_{\phi} - R
\frac{B_{\phi} B_R}{4 \pi} \right) R \mathrm{d} z.
\tag{23.34}\] Assume that the expression in parenthesis is independent of \(z\), and that \(4 \pi \rho R^2 v_R\), the Solar wind flux through the cylinder, is a constant. Show that \[
- \frac{\dot{J}}{4 \pi \rho R^2 v_R} = Rv_{\phi}  \left( 1 - \frac{B_R^2}{4 \pi
\rho v_R^2} \right) + \frac{B_R^2}{4 \pi \rho v_R^2} \Omega R^2 .
\tag{23.35}\]
There is a radius, \(R_A\), called the Alfvén radius where the radial Alfvén speed \(v_A = B_R / \sqrt{4 \pi \rho}\) is equal to \(v_R\). Evaluate the angular momentum loss per unit mass at this radius and show that it is equal to \(\Omega R_A^2\).
If \(R_A\) is 10 \(R_{\odot}\), approximately what fraction of its mass must the Sun lose to slow its rotation down? Take the moment of inertia of the Sun to be \(0.06 M_{\odot} R_{\odot}^2\). What fraction of its mass has the Sun lost in 5 billion years if the solar wind was steady and the number density at the Earth is \(10 \, \mathrm{cm}^{- 3}\) and the velocity is \(300 \, \mathrm{km} / \mathrm{s}\)?
