title: 24  Flux Freezing
text:
24.1 The Ideal-MHD Limit
Flux-freezing is an important phenomenon in highly conducting plasmas. In these notes, we derive flux-freezing in ideal magnetohydrodynamics (MHD), however it is important to remark that flux-freezing also applies beyond ideal MHD, at least in an approximate way. We also discuss the role of flux freezing in the context of some important astrophysical systems. The key equation we will consider is the induction equation (or Faraday’s Law), which reads (when \(\eta = \operatorname{const}\), see Equation 23.19): \[
\frac{\partial \mathbf{B}}{\partial t} = \nabla \times (\mathbf{v} \times
\mathbf{B}) + \frac{c \eta}{4 \pi} \nabla^2 \mathbf{B}.
\tag{24.1}\]
Let \(L\) and \(V\) be characteristic length and velocity scales for the plasma. We can introduce the dimensionless time and space coordinates and velocity \[
\hat{t} = t \frac{V}{L}, \qquad \hat{x} = \frac{x}{L}, \qquad
\hat{\mathbf{v}} = \frac{\mathbf{v}}{V} .
\tag{24.2}\] Faraday’s law can be written as \[
\frac{V}{L}  \frac{\partial \mathbf{B}}{\partial \hat{t}} = \frac{V}{L}
\hat{\nabla} \times (\hat{\mathbf{v}} \times \mathbf{B}) + \frac{c \eta}{4
\pi L^2}  \hat{\nabla}^2 \mathbf{B}.
\tag{24.3}\] That is \[
\frac{\partial \mathbf{B}}{\partial \hat{t}} = \hat{\nabla} \times
(\hat{\mathbf{v}} \times \mathbf{B}) + \left( \frac{c \eta}{4 \pi LV}
\right)  \hat{\nabla}^2 \mathbf{B}= \hat{\nabla} \times (\hat{\mathbf{v}}
\times \mathbf{B}) + \frac{1}{\mathrm{R}_M}  \hat{\nabla}^2 \mathbf{B}.
\tag{24.4}\] We have introduced the magnetic Reynolds number \[
\mathrm{R}_M = \frac{LV}{c \eta / 4 \pi} .
\tag{24.5}\] The magnetic Reynolds number measures the relative importance of advection and resistivity in the evolution of the magnetic field. It is analogous to the “usual” Reynolds number, which measures the ratio of inertial to viscous forces in a fluid. When \(\mathrm{R}_M \gg 1\), we say that we are in the ideal-MHD limit.
In the ideal-MHD limit, the Faraday law simplifies to \[
\frac{\partial \mathbf{B}}{\partial t} = \nabla \times (\mathbf{v} \times
\mathbf{B}) \Longrightarrow \frac{\partial \mathbf{B}}{\partial t} + \nabla
\times (\mathbf{B} \times \mathbf{v}) = 0.
\tag{24.6}\] Remarkably this is identical to the vorticity equation for a barotropic fluid: \[
\frac{\partial \boldsymbol{\omega}}{\partial t} + \nabla \times (\boldsymbol{\omega}
\times \mathbf{v}) = 0.
\tag{24.7}\] The analogy between vorticity and magnetic field plays an important role in our understanding of MHD phenomena such as dynamos and is sometimes known as the Batchelor’s analogy.
We remember that the vorticity satisfies Kelvin’s circulation theorem, which states that the circulation of the flux of the vorticity across a material surface bounded by a curve \(C (t)\) (moving with the fluid) is conserved: \[
\frac{\mathrm{d} \Gamma (t)}{\mathrm{d} t} = \oint_{C (t)} \boldsymbol{\omega} \cdot
\mathrm{d} \mathbf{A}= 0.
\tag{24.8}\] By analogy, we find that the magnetic flux across any surface co-moving with the flow is constant in ideal-MHD: \[
\boxed{\frac{\mathrm{d} \Phi (t)}{\mathrm{d} t} = \oint_{C (t)} \mathbf{B} \cdot
\mathrm{d} \mathbf{A}= 0.}
\tag{24.9}\] This fact is called flux freezing and is one of the most important properties of MHD. To understand this consider a magnetic flux tube. As the name suggests, a flux tube is an imaginary bundle of magnetic field lines dragged by the plasma. This is illustrated in Figure 24.1.
Consider the surface bounding the flux tube on the sides. This surface is such that the magnetic flux across it is zero, since there is no component of the field perpendicular to it. If we let this surface move with the plasma velocity, the flux freezing condition requires the magnetic field to deform to stay always parallel to it, as illustrated in Figure 24.1. In other words, the magnetic field is dragged by the plasma as if it was painted on the fluid elements. As we will see shortly, flux freezing has other important consequences.
At the microscopic level, the reason why flux freezing occurs in strongly-magnetized plasmas is that the charged particles are “stuck” to the magnetic field lines1. Another way to think about flux freezing is in terms of induced currents. In order for the magnetic field lines to drift with respect to the plasma with velocity \(\mathbf{v}_d\), one would need to induce an electric field (in the plasma frame) \[
\mathbf{E}' = \frac{\mathbf{v}_d \times \mathbf{B}}{c}
\tag{24.10}\] which corresponds to a current \(\mathbf{j}' =\mathbf{E}' / \eta\). However, \(\eta \rightarrow 0\) in the ideal-MHD limit, meaning that an infinite current is required to cause the field lines to slip.

title: 24  Flux Freezing
text:
Figure 24.1: Effect of flux freezing.






24.1.1 Magnetic Field Amplification
Flux freezing also implies that, if a flux tube is compressed by the flow, then its magnetic field intensity is amplified. To see this, consider the situation illustrated in Figure 24.2.






Figure 24.2: Field amplification from the compression of a magnetic flux tube: a wide tube of cross-section \(A_1\) and field \(\mathbf{B}_1\) is squeezed from the sides by a velocity \(\mathbf{v}\) into a thinner tube of cross-section \(A_2\) and field \(\mathbf{B}_2\). Redrawn after 1.



When a flux tube is compressed and its area changes from \(A_1\) to \(A_2\), the B-field strength needs to change in such a way so that the magnetic flux remains unchanged: \[
A_1 B_1 = A_2 B_2 .
\tag{24.11}\] So the magnetic field strength must be amplified: \[
B_2 = \frac{A_1}{A_2} B_1 .
\tag{24.12}\] It is instructive to compare this with the rate at which the plasma density is changed during the same process. In this case, the quantity that is conserved is the mass of the plasma in the flux tube, so \[
\rho A \ell = \operatorname{const} \Longrightarrow \rho_1 A_1 \ell = \rho_2 A_2 \ell
\Longrightarrow \rho_2 = \frac{A_1}{A_2} \rho_1 .
\tag{24.13}\] In this situation, we find that the ratio of magnetic field strength to density in the plasma stays constant: \[
\frac{B}{\rho} = \operatorname{const} .
\tag{24.14}\] Things are very different if the magnetic flux tube is compressed in the direction parallel to the magnetic field, as illustrated in Figure 24.3.






Figure 24.3: Compression along a flux tube.



In this case, the density of the plasma changes according to \[
\rho A \ell = \operatorname{const} \Longrightarrow \frac{\rho_2}{\rho_1} =
\frac{\ell_1}{\ell_2} .
\tag{24.15}\] However, \(B\) remains constant, because the cross-section of the flux tube, \(A\), is unchanged.






TipExample: Stellar collapse



The core of a massive star \(r_1 \sim 10^{11} \mathrm{cm}\) collapses to form a neutron star \(r_2 \sim 10^6 \mathrm{cm}\).

By what factor does the magnetic field increase?
By what factor does the density increase?
If the initial field is \(B_1 \sim 100\mathrm{G}\), what will be the field of the neutron star?

Answer. The density evolves according to \(\rho r^3 = \operatorname{const}\), while the magnetic field evolves according to \(Br^2 = \operatorname{const}\) (assuming the field to be approximately radial), this means that \[
B_2 = \left( \frac{r_1}{r_2} \right)^2 B_1, \qquad \rho_2 = \left(
\frac{r_1}{r_2} \right)^3 \rho_1, \qquad B \sim \rho^{2 / 3} .
\tag{24.16}\] For example, an initial field of \(100\mathrm{G}\) is amplified to \(10^{12} \mathrm{G}\) as result of the collapse of the star. The strong amplification of the magnetic field during the collapse of a star is the reason why neutron stars have extremely strong magnetic fields, up to \(10^{15} \mathrm{G}\).




24.1.2 Resistive Evolution
If the resistivity is finite, \(\eta > 0\), then the magnetic field lines are not stuck to the plasma, but can drift. To understand how this process operates, we consider the evolution of a magnetic field under the sole influence of Ohmic diffusion: \[
\frac{\partial \mathbf{B}}{\partial t} = \frac{\eta c}{4 \pi} \nabla^2
\mathbf{B}.
\tag{24.17}\] If the typical curvature radius of the field lines is \(L\), then we can approximate the previous equation as \[
\frac{\partial B}{\partial t} \sim \frac{\eta c}{4 \pi L^2} B =
\frac{1}{T_{\operatorname{decay}}} B, \qquad T_{\operatorname{decay}} = \frac{4 \pi
L^2}{\eta c} .
\tag{24.18}\] For many astrophysical applications \(L\) is very large, so \(T_{\operatorname{decay}}\) is very long. We will put actual numbers for \(\eta\) and \(L\) when we discuss the problem of star formation below. If the magnetic field has more than one characteristic scale, then the smaller scales will be dissipated more rapidly by the resistivity. This has the effect of “smoothing” the field lines. To quantify this,  we can use the Fourier transform. Accordingly, we represent the magnetic field as a superposition of plane waves \[
\mathbf{B} (t, \mathbf{x}) = \int \mathrm{d}^3 \mathbf{k}
\hat{\mathbf{B}}_{\mathbf{k}} (t) e^{\mathrm{i} \mathbf{k} \cdot \mathbf{x}},
\qquad \hat{\mathbf{B}}_{\mathbf{k}} = \frac{1}{2 \pi} \int \mathrm{d}^3
\mathbf{x}\mathbf{B} (t, \mathbf{x}) e^{- \mathrm{i} \mathbf{k} \cdot
\mathbf{x}} .
\tag{24.19}\] Note that the \(\mathbf{k}= 0\) mode of the B-field corresponds to the average value of the field: \[
\hat{\mathbf{B}}_0 = \frac{1}{2 \pi} \int \mathrm{d}^3 \mathbf{x}\mathbf{B} (t,
\mathbf{x}) = \frac{1}{2 \pi} \langle \mathbf{B} \rangle .
\tag{24.20}\] Inserting Equation 24.19 into Equation 24.17, we obtain: \[
\int \mathrm{d}^3 \mathbf{k}e^{\mathrm{i} \mathbf{k} \cdot \mathbf{x}}  \left[
\frac{\mathrm{d} \hat{\mathbf{B}}_{\mathbf{k}}}{\mathrm{d} t} + \frac{\eta ck^2}{4
\pi}  \hat{\mathbf{B}}_{\mathbf{k}} \right] = 0
\tag{24.21}\] The integral can be zero only if all the infinite quantities in the square parenthesis are zero: \[
\frac{\mathrm{d} \hat{\mathbf{B}}_{\mathbf{k}}}{\mathrm{d} t} = - \frac{\eta ck^2}{4
\pi}  \hat{\mathbf{B}}_{\mathbf{k}} .
\tag{24.22}\] So we have transformed Equation 24.17 into a simple system having an infinite number of decoupled equations, with solutions \[
\hat{\mathbf{B}}_{\mathbf{k}} (t) = \hat{\mathbf{B}}_{\mathbf{k}} (0) \exp
\left( - \frac{\eta ck^2}{4 \pi} t \right) .
\tag{24.23}\] We can see that different modes of the B-field decay exponentially and that large \(k\) modes are damped exponentially more quickly than smaller \(k\) modes. On the other hand, the \(k = 0\) mode is not affected at all and stays constant for all times. This means that the action of the resistivity is not really to make the field decay, but rather to straighten out all field lines, as illustrated in Figure 24.4.






Figure 24.4: Evolution of the magnetic field under the effect of resistivity.

title: 24  Flux Freezing
text:
24.2 Star Formation
One situation in which flux freezing must be violated is star formation. Consider the collapse of a region of a molecular cloud to form a star. If flux freezing were to hold, using the same approach as for the stellar collapse example, we would find \[
\begin{array}{clcc}
\rho : & 10^{- 24} \mathrm{g} \mathrm{cm}^{- 3} & \longrightarrow &
1\mathrm{g} \cdot \mathrm{cm}^{- 3}\\
B : & 10^{- 6} \mathrm{G} & \longrightarrow & 10^{10} \mathrm{G}
\end{array}
\tag{24.24}\] That is, the protostar would be embedded with a pulsar-like magnetic field. This is actually impossible. Indeed, the gravitational binding energy of the protostar would be \[
\Omega \sim - \frac{3 GM^2}{5 R} \sim 2 \cdot 10^{48} M_1^2 \mathrm{erg},
\tag{24.25}\] where \(M_1\) is the protostar mass in solar masses. The energy density in the magnetic field would be \[
U_B \sim \frac{4}{3} \pi R^3 \cdot \frac{1}{8 \pi} B^2 \sim 5 \cdot 10^{51}
\mathrm{erg} \gg \Omega !
\tag{24.26}\] The protostar would be unbound, meaning that the magnetic stresses would tear it apart. In reality, the magnetic field tension halts the collapse of an ideal-MHD cloud well before these levels of magnetic field strength can be achieved. Obviously, Nature has a way to form stars from magnetized clouds, so how does it defeat flux freezing?
It turns out that resistivity is not sufficient to do the trick. The resistivity of ionized hydrogen plasma depends weakly on density and can be approximated as (Kulsrud 2005) \[
\frac{\eta c}{4 \pi} \approx \frac{0.42 \cdot 10^7}{T_{\operatorname{eV}}^{3 / 2}}
\mathrm{cm}^2 /\mathrm{s}.
\tag{24.27}\] For a star \(T_{\operatorname{eV}} \approx 10^2\) and \(L \sim R_{\odot} \sim 10^{11} \mathrm{cm}\) so the decay time is \[
T_{\operatorname{decay}} = \frac{L^2}{\eta c / 4 \pi} \sim 10^{18} \mathrm{s} \sim
30 \mathrm{Gyr} .
\tag{24.28}\] This is longer than the age of the Universe, so resistivity is clearly not sufficient to release the magnetic tension and allow stars to form.
The mechanism currently thought to be responsible for the drift between magnetic fields and the plasma is ambipolar diffusion. The details go beyond the scope of this course, but the key observation is that molecular clouds are only weakly ionized. The neutral component of the gas is not affected by the Lorentz force, so it can flow perpendicular to field lines. The Lorentz force on the ions, on the other hand, is orders of magnitude larger than gravity, so the ions are stuck on the field lines. The mutual friction between ions and neutrals has the effect of regulating the rate of collapse and determines the time for the formation of protostars. This physics is illustrated in Figure 24.5.






Figure 24.5: Ambipolar diffusion.



Magnetic fields do not just regulate the collapse of clouds into protostars. They also play a key role enabling it. Indeed, magnetic fields allow the protostar to lose angular momentum and prevent the gas from getting stuck at the centrifugal barrier. This happens because the collapsing cloud forces a large column of gas, parallel to the mean magnetic field, to corotate with it. This allows the forming protostar to dissipate angular momentum. We explore this in a more quantitative way in the homework.

title: 24  Flux Freezing
text:
24.3 Io and Jupiter
The unipolar-inductor model for the interaction between Jupiter and its moon Io is one of the early successes of plasma astrophysics. This model has also been adopted to explain a variety of other astrophysical systems, including the launching of electromagnetic waves by black holes moving through plasma. The main idea of this model is that the motion of a conductor, in this case Io, in an external magnetic field, in this case Jupiter’s field, generates an electric current.
The original motivation for this model was the discovery in the 60’s of radio flares from Jupiter in phase with the rise and setting of Io. More precisely, Jupiter has a rotation period of about 10 hours, while Io has an orbital period of about 43 hours. Radio flares are preferentially detected when Io has a longitude of \(90^{\circ}\) or \(240^{\circ}\) with respect to Jupiter, as shown in Figure 24.6, taken from Duncan (1965).






Figure 24.6: Number of radio bursts detected from Jupiter as a function of the phase of Io. From Duncan (1965); © Elsevier, reproduced for non-commercial educational use and not covered by the license of these notes.



In 1969, Goldreich and Lynden-Bell (Goldreich and Lynden-Bell 1969) proposed a model to explain:

the mechanism generating the radiation;
the reason for the phase difference between the rising and setting of Io and the radiation bursts.

We explain this model in a qualitative way and then build a semi-quantitative simplified model below.
Io is primarily composed of silicates and iron, so it has a good electrical conductivity. This means that there is no electric field inside Io, in Io’s frame of reference, and the magnetic field lines of Jupiter are stuck to it (flux freezing). However, because in Jupiter’s frame of reference Io completes a revolution every 13 hours, the field lines cannot be frozen everywhere, otherwise the magnetic energy in the magnetosphere would grow without bound2. This means that the field lines must slip somewhere. It turns out that this happens in Jupiter’s atmosphere, where the gas resistivity is the highest, due to the presence of a neutral gas. The geometry of the magnetic flux tube connecting Jupiter and Io is illustrated in Figure 24.7.






Figure 24.7: Magnetic flux tube connecting Io and Jupiter. Redrawn after Goldreich and Lynden-Bell (1969).



The slippage of the field lines on Jupiter’s surface drives a current along the flux tube connecting the planet to the moon. Electrons gyrate in the field lines producing cyclotron radiation, which is beamed primarily in the direction perpendicular to the field lines, explaining the offset between Io’s rises and settings and the radio bursts. This is illustrated in more detail in Figure 24.8.






Figure 24.8: Left panel: footprint of the magnetic-flux tube connecting Io and Jupiter on Jupiter’s atmosphere. Right panel: cross-section of the magnetic-flux tube connecting Jupiter and Io and direction in which the current \(I\) flows between the planet and the moon. Redrawn after Goldreich and Lynden-Bell (1969).



A strong electric field is created in the direction perpendicular to the \(B\)-field, in the \(Y\)-direction shown in the figure. The potential difference across the flux tube is \(\Delta \Phi \sim 10^8 \mathrm{V}\)3. However, the motion of electrons perpendicular to the field lines is suppressed by the Lorentz force, so a current is driven along the field lines, through the moon, and back to the planet, as shown in the right panel of Figure 24.8. The current intensity is \(I \sim 10^6 \mathrm{amp}\), which is sufficient to produce cyclotron and synchrotron radiation.
Here, we consider a toy model in which we see how the electric field is created by the slippage of the field lines. We consider a conductor moving in an external B-field anchored in a wall with infinite conductivity, as shown in Figure 24.9.






Figure 24.9: Toy model for the Io and Jupiter problem.



In our analogy, the conductor is Jupiter’s atmosphere, while the wall represents Io. We imagine that initially the field is vertical and the conductor is at rest. At \(t = 0\), we start moving the conductor with velocity \(\mathbf{v}\) in the \(x\)-direction. The field is dragged up to a distance \(L\) and then starts to slip, realizing the configuration shown in Figure 24.9.
There is no external electric field, so the electric field in the frame of the conductor is \[
\mathbf{E}' =\mathbf{E}+ \frac{\mathbf{v} \times \mathbf{B}}{c} =
\frac{\mathbf{v} \times \mathbf{B}}{c} = \frac{v_x B_y}{c}
\hat{\mathbf{z}},
\tag{24.29}\] and the associated current is \(\mathbf{j}= \sigma \left( \frac{\mathbf{v} \times \mathbf{B}}{c} \right) = \sigma \frac{v_x B_y}{c} \hat{\mathbf{z}}\). The current is responsible for the creation of the \(x\)-component of the \(B\)-field (setting \(\eta = 1 / \sigma\)): \[
\nabla \times \mathbf{B}= 4 \pi \mathbf{j} \Longrightarrow - \partial_y B_x
= 4 \pi j_z \Longrightarrow B_x = - 4 \pi j_z y = - \frac{4 \pi}{\eta c} v_x
B_y y.
\tag{24.30}\] On the other hand, from the geometry of the system, we have: \[
B_x = \left. \frac{B_y L}{D} \right|_{y = d} \Longrightarrow L = \frac{v_x
Dd}{\eta c / 4 \pi} = v_x T_{\operatorname{decay}} .
\tag{24.31}\]
This shows the two key features of the system. The relative motion of the conductor and the walls generates an electric field (a consequence of Faraday’s Law). The electric field drives a current in the system. The current, in turn, causes the field lines to bend and slip (from Ampere’s Law).






NoteGoing further: Pulsars



Pulsars were discovered by Jocelyn Bell in 1967. It was later realized that pulsars are rotating neutron stars endowed with strong magnetic fields. In 1969, Goldreich and Julian (Goldreich and Julian 1969) developed the first model of a pulsar. Like the unipolar induction model, Goldreich and Julian’s model applies to a variety of astrophysical systems and shows another key physical effect associated with flux freezing. Namely, the fact that rotating neutron stars fill their surroundings with a dense plasma, creating the so called magnetosphere.






Figure 24.10: Schematic illustration of a pulsar magnetosphere. Redrawn after Goldreich and Julian (1969).



In this model, shown in Figure 24.10, we neglect the misalignment between magnetic North pole and rotational axis, which would be needed to produce the pulsated emission. However, this model contains all required physical ingredients. We assume at first that the pulsar is a neutron star with a dipole magnetic field in vacuum. The magnetic field is then given by \[
\mathbf{B}= B_0  \left( \tfrac{R}{r} \right)^3  (2 \cos \theta
\hat{\mathbf{r}} + \sin \theta \hat{\boldsymbol{\theta}}) .
\tag{24.32}\] The angular velocity of the star is given by \[
\boldsymbol{\Omega}= \Omega \hat{\mathbf{z}}, \qquad \hat{\mathbf{z}} = \cos
\theta \hat{\mathbf{r}} - \sin \theta \hat{\boldsymbol{\theta}} .
\tag{24.33}\] In the previous equation \(\hat{\mathbf{z}}\) is the unit vector in the \(z\)-direction. Since neutron stars are essentially perfect conductors, there should be no electric field in their frame \(\mathbf{E}' = 0\). This means that in the inertial frame there is an electric field inside the star given by \[
\mathbf{E}= - \frac{\mathbf{v} \times \mathbf{B}}{c} = - \frac{1}{c}
(\boldsymbol{\Omega} \times \mathbf{r}) \times \mathbf{B}= \frac{B_0 \Omega
r}{c}  \left( \frac{R}{r} \right)^3 (\sin^2 \theta \hat{\mathbf{r}} - 2 \cos
\theta \sin \theta \hat{\boldsymbol{\theta}}) .
\tag{24.34}\] In the previous equation we have used the fact that \[
\boldsymbol{\Omega} \times \mathbf{r}= \Omega r \sin \theta
\hat{\boldsymbol{\varphi}}
\tag{24.35}\] and \[
\hat{\boldsymbol{\varphi}} \times (2 \cos \theta \hat{\mathbf{r}} + \sin \theta
\hat{\boldsymbol{\theta}}) = 2 \cos \theta \hat{\boldsymbol{\theta}} - \sin \theta
\hat{\mathbf{r}} .
\tag{24.36}\] If there is vacuum in the exterior (and assuming axisymmetry), then the external electric potential is \[
\Phi (r, \theta) = \sum_{\ell = 0}^{\infty} \frac{\phi_{\ell}}{r^{\ell + 1}}
P_{\ell} (\cos \theta), \qquad r > R
\tag{24.37}\] where \(\phi_{\ell}\) are fixed by the fact that the perpendicular component of the electric field should be continuous on the surface of the star4 \[
[\![ \mathbf{E}_{\perp} ]\!] = 0 \Longrightarrow E_{\theta} (r =
R) = \frac{1}{R} \partial_{\theta} \Phi (r = R) .
\tag{24.38}\] If the external field is quadrupolar, meaning that \[
\Phi (r, \theta) = \frac{\phi_2}{r^3} P_2 (\cos \theta),
\tag{24.39}\] then Equation 24.38 implies \[
\boxed{\Phi = - \frac{2 B_0 \Omega R^5}{3 cr^3} P_2 (\cos \theta) .}
\tag{24.40}\] So we find that there is an enormous electrostatic potential at the surface of the star: \[
\Phi \approx 2 \times 10^{13}  (B_{12} R^2_6 / P) \mathrm{statV} \approx 5
\times 10^{15}  (B_{12} R^2_6 / P) \mathrm{V}.
\tag{24.41}\] For example, the ratio of electrostatic to gravitational force is \[
\frac{| \mathbf{F}_{\operatorname{EM}} |}{| \mathbf{F}_{\mathrm{G}} |} \sim
\frac{\Phi e}{\frac{GM}{R} m} = \left\{\begin{array}{ll}
5 \times 10^7, & \text{protons},\\
8 \times 10^{10}, & \text{electrons} .
\end{array}\right. \gg 1.
\tag{24.42}\] The electromagnetic forces are strong enough to pull charges out of the surface of the neutron star and fill all the region around it with plasma. The field is so strong that electron-positron cascade production is triggered once the first particles are extracted. This is the so-called magnetosphere. The magnetosphere creates currents that to leading order short out the electric potential to infinity.
In the extreme conditions found in pulsar or black-hole magnetospheres, the electromagnetic energy density is so large compared to the plasma inertia that the plasma is forced to move in such a way as to cancel the Lorentz force. In other words, electrons, positrons, and ions can only flow along \(B\)-field lines and the induced currents are such that the electric field is shorted out. This is the so-called force-free electrodynamics approximation: \[
\mathbf{E} \cdot \mathbf{B}= 0,  \mathbf{E}+ \frac{1}{c} \mathbf{v}
\times \mathbf{B}= 0.
\tag{24.43}\] From the first condition, if the system is axisymmetric, we have that \[
\mathbf{E}= E_0  \hat{\boldsymbol{\phi}} \times \mathbf{B} \Longrightarrow
\mathbf{E}= - \frac{\Omega r \sin \theta}{c}  \hat{\boldsymbol{\phi}} \times
\mathbf{B}.
\tag{24.44}\] From the last two equations, we find \[
0 = \frac{1}{c}  (\mathbf{v}- \Omega r \sin \theta) \times \mathbf{B}
\Longrightarrow \mathbf{v}= \Omega r \sin \theta \hat{\boldsymbol{\phi}}
+\mathbf{v}_d  \hat{\mathbf{B}} .
\tag{24.45}\] So the plasma velocity has two components. The plasma is forced to co-rotate with the pulsar (first term in the first equation). However, when \(\Omega r \sin \theta \geq c\), the drift velocity \(\mathbf{v}_d\) of plasma along the field lines must be non-zero so that \(| \mathbf{v} | < c\). The region at which \(\Omega r \sin \theta = c\) is called the light cylinder. It is the boundary of the region in which magnetic field lines can be closed. Outside the light cylinder, the \(B\)-field lines bend and reach infinity so that plasma can flow away from/to the pulsar (depending on its charge) creating a current.
The plasma charge density is given by Gauss’ law of electrodynamics: \[
q = \frac{\nabla \cdot \mathbf{E}}{4 \pi} .
\tag{24.46}\] Note that \[
4 \pi q = \nabla \cdot \mathbf{E}= \nabla \cdot \left[ - \frac{1}{c}
\mathbf{v} \times \mathbf{B} \right] = - \frac{1}{c} \mathbf{B} \cdot
(\nabla \times \mathbf{v}) + \frac{1}{c} \mathbf{v} \cdot (\nabla \times
\mathbf{B}) .
\tag{24.47}\] This can be computed using \[
\nabla \times \mathbf{v}= \nabla \times (\boldsymbol{\Omega} \times
\mathbf{r}) =\boldsymbol{\Omega} (\nabla \cdot \mathbf{r}) -
(\boldsymbol{\Omega} \cdot \nabla) \mathbf{r}= 2\boldsymbol{\Omega}
\tag{24.48}\] and \[
\nabla \times \mathbf{B}= 4 \pi \mathbf{j}= 4 \pi q \frac{\mathbf{v}}{c}
\tag{24.49}\] So the charge density is \[
4 \pi q = - \frac{2}{c} \mathbf{B} \cdot \boldsymbol{\Omega}+ 4 \pi q
\frac{v^2}{c^2} \Longrightarrow q_{\operatorname{GJ}} = - \frac{\boldsymbol{\Omega}
\cdot \mathbf{B}}{2 \pi c}  \frac{1}{1 - v^2 / c^2} .
\tag{24.50}\] Note that \(\boldsymbol{\Omega} \cdot \mathbf{B}\) changes sign across a critical line in the magnetosphere. This means that there is charge separation in the magnetosphere.
The minimum electron number density is the so-called Goldreich-Julian density \[
n_{\operatorname{GJ}} = \frac{q_{\operatorname{GJ}}}{e} = 10^{10}  (B_{12} / P) \mathrm{cm}^{-
3} .
\tag{24.51}\] This is \(\sim 10\) orders of magnitude larger than the typical density of electrons in the ISM. More recent theoretical models show that the plasma number density can be several orders of magnitude larger than the Goldreich-Julian density. This is because the plasma is rich of electron-positron pairs and \(n_{\operatorname{GJ}}\) only measures the net density of charges. For example, see Figure 24.11.






Figure 24.11: \(\log (n / n_{\operatorname{GJ}})\) in a particle-in-cell simulation with approximate treatment of pair creation. Coherent plasma waves are thought to be responsible for the production of the radio pulses. From Philippov et al. (2015); © The American Astronomical Society, reproduced for non-commercial educational use and not covered by the license of these notes.

Figure 24.12: Dipolar magnetic field of a sphere.

In the process of forming a neutron star, an object with mass \(M \sim 10^{34} \mathrm{g}\) contracts from an initial radius \(R_0 \sim 10^{11} \mathrm{cm}\) to \(R_1 \sim 10^6 \mathrm{cm}\). By what factor is the magnetic field amplified? If the typical magnetic field strength for a star is \(B \sim 100\mathrm{G}\), what is the field strength expected for a neutron star?
Gas in a molecular cloud with density \(\rho \sim 10^{- 24} \mathrm{g}/ \mathrm{cm}^3\) and typical magnetic field \(B \sim 1 \mu \mathrm{G}\) contracts to form a star with \(\rho \sim 1\mathrm{g}/ \mathrm{cm}^3\). What is the strength of the resulting field if flux freezing holds?

title: 24  Flux Freezing
text:
24.5 Exercises

Exercise 24.1 (Flux freezing in an Alfvén wave) Consider a small-amplitude disturbance in a homogeneous plasma in a uniform magnetic field \(\mathbf{B}\) in the \(z\)-direction. Set \(\rho = \mathrm{const}\) and \(p = \mathrm{const}\), and \[
\mathbf{v}= \epsilon v_A \sin (kz - \omega t)  \hat{\mathbf{x}}, \qquad
\mathbf{B}= B_0  \hat{\mathbf{z}} - \epsilon B_0 \sin (kz - \omega t)
\hat{\mathbf{x}} .
\tag{24.52}\]

Show that, if \(\omega = kv_A\) and \(v_A = B_0 / \sqrt{4 \pi \rho}\), then these equations satisfy the ideal-MHD equations to first order in \(\epsilon\) (neglecting all terms of order \(\epsilon^2\) and higher).
Calculate the displacement current and show that it is small compared to \(4 \pi j\), if \(v_A \ll c\).
Calculate the resistive correction to \(\mathbf{B}\) and show that it is small if \(\omega T_{\operatorname{decay}} \gg 1\), where \(T_{\operatorname{decay}} = 4 \pi / (k^2 \eta c)\).
Find the equation for the magnetic field lines to order \(\epsilon\) by integrating \[
\frac{\mathrm{d} x}{\mathrm{d} z} = \frac{B_x}{B_0}
\tag{24.53}\] and show that we get the same equation from the displacement of the fluid \[
x (z, t) = \int v_x \mathrm{d} t
\tag{24.54}\] assuming flux freezing of the lines in the plasma.

title: 25  Magnetic Tension and Hydromagnetic Equilibria
text:
25.1 Magnetic Tension Force
Up to now we have been primarily concerned with the consequences of the induction equation (Faraday’s law). We have seen that, in the ideal-MHD limit, the magnetic field lines are frozen in the flow and explored some of the consequences of this fact. Now, we consider the feedback of the magnetic field on the plasma, that is the impact of the \(\mathbf{j} \times \mathbf{B}\) term in the momentum equation.
A first somewhat obvious, but important remark is that the magnetic force \(\mathbf{j} \times \mathbf{B}\) is always perpendicular to the magnetic field. In other words, there is no impediment to the plasma flow along field lines. On the other hand, the field might resist or drive plasma motion perpendicular to the field lines. The latter, in turn, causes the field lines to move, in accordance with the induction equation. It is important to keep this in mind, because we are now going to rewrite the Lorentz force in a form in which this constraint is not manifest. Using the vector identity \[
\nabla (\mathbf{A} \cdot \mathbf{B}) =\mathbf{A} \times (\nabla \times
\mathbf{B}) +\mathbf{B} \times (\nabla \times \mathbf{A}) + (\mathbf{A}
\cdot \nabla) \mathbf{B}+ (\mathbf{B} \cdot \nabla) \mathbf{A}
\tag{25.1}\] and Ampere’s law (\(4 \pi \mathbf{j}= \nabla \times \mathbf{B}\)), we can rewrite the Lorentz force as \[
\mathbf{j} \times \mathbf{B}= \frac{(\nabla \times \mathbf{B}) \times
\mathbf{B}}{4 \pi} = \frac{(\mathbf{B} \cdot \nabla) \mathbf{B}}{4 \pi} -
\nabla \frac{B^2}{8 \pi} .
\tag{25.2}\] The second term is often improperly referred to as the magnetic pressure, because it is reminiscent of the \(- \nabla p\) term in the momentum equation, while the first term is improperly referred to as magnetic tension. However, remember that magnetic pressure is only effective perpendicular to the field lines, as we have already remarked. To better understand the nature of the Lorentz force in MHD, we factor \[
\mathbf{B}= B \hat{\mathbf{b}},
\tag{25.3}\] where \(\hat{\mathbf{b}}\) is a unit vector. Accordingly, we can write \[
\begin{aligned}
(\mathbf{B} \cdot \nabla) \mathbf{B} &= B (\hat{\mathbf{b}} \cdot \nabla)
(B \hat{\mathbf{b}}) \\
&= B^2  (\hat{\mathbf{b}} \cdot \nabla) \hat{\mathbf{b}}
+ B \hat{\mathbf{b}}  (\hat{\mathbf{b}} \cdot \nabla) B \\
&= B^2  (\hat{\mathbf{b}} \cdot \nabla)  \hat{\mathbf{b}} + \frac{1}{2}
\hat{\mathbf{b}}  (\hat{\mathbf{b}} \cdot \nabla) B^2 .
\end{aligned}
\tag{25.4}\] The last term on the RHS is, apart from a factor 2, the projection of \(\nabla B^2\) parallel to \(\mathbf{B}\): \[
[\hat{\mathbf{b}}  (\hat{\mathbf{b}} \cdot \nabla) B^2]_i = \sum_{j = 1}^3
\hat{b}_i  \hat{b}_j \partial_j  (B^2) = [(\hat{\mathbf{b}} \otimes
\hat{\mathbf{b}}) \nabla (B^2)]_i = : \nabla_{\parallel} B^2 .
\tag{25.5}\] Plugging this back into Equation 25.2 yields \[
\mathbf{j} \times \mathbf{B}= \frac{B^2}{4 \pi}  (\hat{\mathbf{b}} \cdot
\nabla)  \hat{\mathbf{b}} - [\mathbf{I}- \hat{\mathbf{b}} \otimes
\hat{\mathbf{b}}]  \frac{\nabla B^2}{8 \pi} = \frac{B^2}{4 \pi}
(\hat{\mathbf{b}} \cdot \nabla)  \hat{\mathbf{b}} - \nabla_{\perp}
\frac{B^2}{8 \pi} .
\tag{25.6}\] The last term is the component of \(\nabla (B^2 / 8 \pi)\) perpendicular to the field lines. This is the correct form of the magnetic pressure, while the first term on the RHS is the proper form of the magnetic tension.
We remark that \(u_B = B^2 / 8 \pi\) is the energy in the magnetic field, so the magnetic pressure force is \[
p_B = (\Gamma_B - 1) u_B,
\tag{25.7}\] with an effective adiabatic index \(\Gamma_B = 2\). For ionized hydrogen \(\Gamma = 5 / 3\), so magnetic energy is more effective at resisting compression than gas internal energy. Of course, magnetic pressure can only resist compression perpendicular to the field lines.
To understand the meaning of the first term on the RHS of Equation 25.6, note that \[
(\hat{\mathbf{b}} \cdot \nabla)  \hat{\mathbf{b}} =\boldsymbol{\kappa},
\tag{25.8}\] where \(1 / | \boldsymbol{\kappa} |\) is the curvature radius of the field lines. That is \(\boldsymbol{\kappa}= 0\) for straight field lines. For a circular field line, \(1 / | \boldsymbol{\kappa} |\) is the radius of the circle spanned by the line. This means that the magnetic field lines back-react on the plasma as if they were elastic springs with spring constant \(B^2 / 4 \pi\).
Summarizing, we find that there are two components of the Lorentz force. The first is the magnetic pressure, according to which the magnetic field lines resist being bundled together. The second is the magnetic tension, according to which the magnetic field lines resist bending. This situation is illustrated in Figure 25.1.
As we have already anticipated (see Equation 23.22), the Lorentz force can be rewritten as the divergence of the magnetic stresses: \[
\frac{(\mathbf{B} \cdot \nabla) \mathbf{B}}{4 \pi} - \nabla \frac{B^2}{8
\pi} = \nabla \cdot \left[ \frac{\mathbf{B} \otimes \mathbf{B}}{4 \pi} -
\frac{B^2}{8 \pi} \mathbf{I} \right] =: \nabla \cdot
\mathbf{T}_{\operatorname{EM}} .
\tag{25.9}\] The derivation is conceptually simple, although it requires some tedious vector calculus calculations. Including both fluid \(\mathbf{T}\) and magnetic stresses, the Euler equation reads: \[
\rho \frac{\mathrm{d} \mathbf{v}}{\mathrm{d} t} = \nabla \cdot
[\mathbf{T}+\mathbf{T}_{\operatorname{EM}}] .
\tag{25.10}\] For an ideal fluid \(\mathbf{T}= - p\mathbf{I}\), however shear and bulk viscosity can also be included in \(\mathbf{T}\) to obtain the viscous MHD equations. In conservation form, the momentum equation reads \[
\frac{\partial (\rho \mathbf{v})}{\partial t} + \nabla \cdot [\rho
\mathbf{v} \otimes \mathbf{v}-\mathbf{T}-\mathbf{T}_{\operatorname{EM}}] = 0,
\tag{25.11}\] where \(\mathbf{R}= - \rho \mathbf{v} \otimes \mathbf{v}\) are the Reynolds stresses or inertial forces1.

title: 25  Magnetic Tension and Hydromagnetic Equilibria
text:
Figure 25.1: Left panel: effect of the magnetic pressure force. Right panel: effect of the magnetic tension force.










TipExample: Solar prominence



Solar prominences are plasma arches which rise above the Solar photo-sphere and are supported by the magnetic tension, as illustrated by Figure 25.2 and Figure 25.3.






Figure 25.2: Solar prominence in UV. Credit: NASA (What is a solar prominence?); not covered by the license of these notes.









Figure 25.3: Force diagram for a Solar prominence.



To understand how prominences are supported against gravity, let us consider the balance of forces on the region in the volume \(V\) with boundary surface \(S\): \[
\begin{aligned}
0 &= \frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d} t} \int_V \rho \mathbf{v} \mathrm{d} V \\
&= \int_V \nabla \cdot [\rho \mathbf{v} \otimes
\mathbf{v}-\mathbf{T}-\mathbf{T}_{\operatorname{EM}}] \mathrm{d} V + \int_V \rho
\mathbf{g} \mathrm{d} V \\
&= \int_S \rho \mathbf{v}\mathbf{v} \cdot \mathrm{d} \mathbf{S}- \int_S
\left( p + \frac{B^2}{8 \pi} \right) \mathrm{d} \mathbf{S} \\
& \quad + \int_S \frac{\mathbf{B}}{4 \pi} \mathbf{B} \cdot \mathrm{d} \mathbf{S}+ \int_V \rho
\mathbf{g} \mathrm{d} V.
\end{aligned}
\tag{25.12}\] The main force balancing gravity is the magnetic tension, arising from the \(\mathbf{B}\mathbf{B} \cdot \mathrm{d} \mathbf{S}\) term. Notice that, \(\mathbf{B} \cdot \mathrm{d} \mathbf{S}\) is negative on the left, where \(\mathbf{B}\) points down, giving a net force in the vertical direction. Similarly, \(\mathbf{B} \cdot \mathrm{d} \mathbf{S}\) is positive on the right giving a force along \(\mathbf{B}\), which points up. Magnetic pressure force, arising from the squeezing of the field lines below the prominence also contribute, but is subdominant.
The attentive reader might have noticed the \(\mathbf{B}\mathbf{B} \cdot \mathrm{d} \mathbf{S}\) term always contribute a force in the direction of \(\mathbf{B}\) with magnitude \(B^2 \hat{\mathbf{b}} \cdot \mathrm{d} \mathbf{S}\). How can this be possible? We have previously commented on the fact that magnetic forces are always perpendicular to \(\mathbf{B}\). The issue here is that this terms represents the net force from magnetic tension over \(V\) and not the force in a specific point and the net force over an extended region average can be parallel to the net magnetic field. In other words, we should not confuse the force on individual fluid elements, which is always perpendicular to \(\mathbf{B}\), to the net force experienced over a control volume, which does not have to be in any particular direction a priori.

title: 25  Magnetic Tension and Hydromagnetic Equilibria
text:
25.2 Hydromagnetic Equilibria
Consider the hydrostatic equilibrium of a plane-parallel, magnetized atmosphere in a vertical gravitational potential \(\Psi\), as illustrated in Figure 25.4. This equilibrium configuration could be representative of the disk in a spiral galaxy, or of the photo-sphere of the Sun.






Figure 25.4: Force diagram for a plane-parallel magnetized atmosphere.



The force-balance equation for hydromagnetic equilibrium is \[
- \nabla p - \rho \nabla \Psi + \frac{1}{4 \pi} (\nabla \times \mathbf{B})
\times \mathbf{B}= 0.
\tag{25.13}\] We will make two simplifying assumptions.

The gas is isothermal, so \(p = a^2 \rho\). This means that, in absence of magnetic fields, \[
\rho (z) = \tilde{\rho} \exp (- \Psi / a^2) .
\tag{25.14}\]
We assume that the magnetic field is planar and does not depend on \(x\), meaning that \[
\mathbf{B}= B_y (y, z)  \hat{\mathbf{y}} + B_z (y, z)  \hat{\mathbf{z}} .
\tag{25.15}\] This means that there exist a vector potential \(\mathbf{A}= A (y, z) \hat{\mathbf{x}}\) such that \(\nabla \times \mathbf{A}=\mathbf{B}\). In particular, \[
B_y = \partial_z A, \quad B_z = - \partial_y A \qquad \Longleftrightarrow
\qquad \mathbf{B}= \nabla A \times \hat{\mathbf{x}} .
\tag{25.16}\] Note that \(\mathbf{A} \perp \mathbf{B}\) and \(\mathbf{A}= \operatorname{const}\) on the magnetic field lines, so the isocontours of \(A (y, z)\) are the field lines.

To compute the Lorentz force we use \[
\nabla \times \mathbf{B}= \nabla \times (\nabla \times \mathbf{A}) = -
\nabla^2 \mathbf{A}+ \nabla (\nabla \cdot \mathbf{A}) = - \hat{\mathbf{x}}
\nabla^2 A.
\tag{25.17}\] and \[
(\nabla \times \mathbf{B}) \times \mathbf{B}= - (\nabla^2 A)
\hat{\mathbf{x}} \times (- \hat{\mathbf{x}} \times \nabla A) = - (\nabla^2
A) \nabla A.
\tag{25.18}\] For reasons that will be more clear later, we rewrite \[
\nabla p + \rho \nabla \Psi = e^{- \Psi / a^2} \nabla q, \qquad q = pe^{\Psi
/ a^2} .
\tag{25.19}\] The force equation finally reduces to \[
\boxed{- \frac{1}{4 \pi} (\nabla^2 A) \nabla A = e^{- \Psi / a^2} \nabla
q.}
\tag{25.20}\] The last equation shows that \(\nabla q \parallel \nabla A\), which means that \(q = q (A)\). One can then find equilibrium configuration by specifying \(q = q (A)\), which encodes the amount of matter enclosed by the field lines \(A\) and \(A + \mathrm{d} A\), and solving the resulting equation for \(A\). We shall not follow this line of reasoning here, instead we will make two more simplifying assumption, following Parker (1966).

We assume that the magnetic field lines are parallel, \(\mathbf{B}= B (z) \hat{\mathbf{y}}\).
We assume that the ratio of gas to magnetic pressure is constant \[
\frac{B^2}{8 \pi p} = \alpha_0 .
\tag{25.21}\]

With these simplifications, the equation for equilibrium becomes \[
(1 + \alpha_0)  \frac{\mathrm{d} p}{\mathrm{d} z} = - \frac{p}{a^2}  \frac{\mathrm{d}
\Psi}{\mathrm{d} z} .
\tag{25.22}\] Apart from the additional factor \(\alpha_0\), this is the usual equation for hydrostatic equilibrium of a plane-parallel isothermal atmosphere. The solution is \[
p (z) = p_0 \exp \left( - \frac{\Psi (z)}{(1 + \alpha_0) a^2} \right),
\qquad B (z) = B_0 \exp \left( - \frac{\Psi (z)}{2 (1 + \alpha_0) a^2}
\right) .
\tag{25.23}\] Remarkably, this solution turns out to be unstable for any \(\alpha_0 > 0\) to long-wavelength perturbations, the so-called Parker instability (Parker 1966). This is demonstrated in the MHD simulations shown in Figure 25.5.






Figure 25.5: Development of the Parker instability in 3D MHD simulations, at three times. From Matsumoto and Shibata (1992); © Astronomical Society of Japan, reproduced for non-commercial educational use and not covered by the license of these notes.



Imagine starting from a plane parallel field, like in the left-most panel in the figure, and adding a small bend to the field lines. The fluid elements in the region with inclined field lines (solid lines in the figure) are still supported by the thermal pressure, but the magnetic pressure they experience is diminished, since the magnetic pressure can only act perpendicular to the field lines. As a result, they slide along the field lines and gain gravitational potential energy in the process. This is shown in the middle panel (the arrows denote the fluid velocity). As the mass loading on the field line decreases, its central part, which is still parallel to the \(y\)-axis, finds itself with higher pressure than the surrounding and starts to raise. This instability is responsible, for example, for the emergence of flux tubes from the Solar photo-sphere, giving rise to the type of prominence we have discussed previously.
In the case of the Solar corona, the field lines at the foot of the prominences are anchored in the outer convection layers of the Sun. The motion of plasma in this region moves the field lines in random ways and builds enormous tension in the field. When field lines of opposite polarities find themselves sufficiently close they can annihilate in a so-called reconnection event. This suddenly releases the magnetic tension and generates Solar flares and coronal mass ejections. Solar eruptions can significantly impact satellites and space communication and can be hazardous for astronauts. The prediction of Solar eruptions using ground- and space-based observations, in conjunction with MHD simulations, is a field of its own: space weather modeling.

25.3 In-class worksheet
Explosive Reconnection. Plasma is contained in a region bounded by two perfectly conducting plates. Two magnetic flux tubes are anchored on the plates and stretched by the application of an external force \(\mathbf{f}\) as shown in panel (a) of Figure 25.6.






Figure 25.6: Explosive reconnection of two magnetic flux tubes anchored on conducting plates: (a) before and (b) after reconnection.



When \(\ell \approx D\), the field lines reconnect and snap to a new configuration shown in panel (b). This process releases energy stored in the magnetic tension of the field to accelerate the plasma to a velocity \(\mathbf{v}\), which reaches a maximum when the field lines are perfectly straight. Assume that the ideal-MHD approximation holds at all times, except when reconnection takes place.

Show that, apart from geometric factors of order unity, the force per unit volume necessary to hold the field lines in place with \(\ell \approx D\) is \[
| \mathbf{f} | \approx \frac{B^2}{4 \pi}  \frac{\ell}{D^2} .
\tag{25.24}\]
Show that the maximum velocity of the plasma after the reconnection event is \[
v \approx v_A,
\tag{25.25}\] where \(v_A\) is the Alfvén velocity \[
v_A = \frac{B}{\sqrt{4 \pi \rho}} .
\tag{25.26}\]

title: 26  MHD Waves
text:
26.1 Waves in a Homogeneous Plasma
Waves play a very important role in the dynamics of magnetized plasmas. Particle-wave interaction with the interstellar medium regulates the propagation of cosmic rays in the galaxy. In strong MHD turbulence, the non-linear interaction between Alfvén waves acts as the main driver of the turbulence cascade. Torsional Alfvén waves extract angular momentum from proto-stellar cores allowing them to collapse and form stars. These are just a few examples. In these notes, we discuss the phenomenology of waves in compressible MHD.
We consider a homogeneous plasma described by the ideal-MHD equations with \[
\rho_0 = \operatorname{const}, \qquad \mathbf{v}_0 = 0, \qquad \mathbf{B}_0 = B_0
\hat{\mathbf{z}} .
\tag{26.1}\] We proceed in the same way as when we derived the dispersion relation for sound waves in unmagnetized media (Chapter 9). However, as we will see shortly, the phenomenology of MHD waves is significantly more complex than that of sound waves. As before, we introduce a perturbation with a Lagrangian displacement \(\boldsymbol{\xi}\), shown in Figure 26.1.
The pressure and density perturbations in the Lagrangian frame are \[
\delta \rho = - \rho_0 \nabla \cdot \boldsymbol{\xi}, \qquad \delta p =
\frac{\Gamma p_0}{\rho_0} \delta \rho = - \Gamma p_0 \nabla \cdot
\boldsymbol{\xi}.
\tag{26.2}\] The magnetic field perturbations can be computed from the linearized induction equation: \[
\frac{\partial \delta \mathbf{B}}{\partial t} = \nabla \times \left(
\frac{\partial \boldsymbol{\xi}}{\partial t} \times \mathbf{B}_0 \right)
\Longrightarrow \delta \mathbf{B}= \nabla \times (\boldsymbol{\xi} \times
\mathbf{B}_0) .
\tag{26.3}\] The linearized momentum equation becomes (note that the unperturbed current vanishes \(\mathbf{j}_0 = 0\)): \[
\rho \frac{\mathrm{d} \mathbf{v}}{\mathrm{d} t} = - \nabla p +\mathbf{j} \times
\mathbf{B} \Longrightarrow \rho_0  \frac{\partial^2 \boldsymbol{\xi}}{\partial
t^2} = - \nabla \delta p + \delta \mathbf{j} \times \mathbf{B}_0 .
\tag{26.4}\] The perturbed current is \[
\delta \mathbf{j}= \frac{1}{4 \pi} \nabla \times \delta \mathbf{B}=
\frac{1}{4 \pi} \nabla \times [\nabla \times (\boldsymbol{\xi} \times
\mathbf{B}_0)],
\tag{26.5}\] so putting everything together we get the oscillation equation \[
\boxed{
\begin{aligned}
\rho_0  \frac{\partial^2 \boldsymbol{\xi}}{\partial t^2} = {} & \Gamma p_0
\nabla (\nabla \cdot \boldsymbol{\xi}) \\
& + \frac{1}{4 \pi} \{ \nabla \times
[\nabla \times (\boldsymbol{\xi} \times \mathbf{B}_0)] \} \times \mathbf{B}_0 .
\end{aligned}}
\tag{26.6}\] Of course, if \(\mathbf{B}_0\)=0, this equation reduces to the equation for sound waves. All the new physics is in the last term on the RHS. To derive a dispersion relation, we take the usual ansatz \[
\boldsymbol{\xi} (t, \mathbf{x}) =\boldsymbol{\xi}_1 e^{\mathrm{i} (\mathbf{k} \cdot
\mathbf{x}- \omega t)},
\tag{26.7}\] which we plug into the oscillation equation. This yields \[
\begin{aligned}
- \rho_0 \omega^2 \boldsymbol{\xi}_1 = {} & - \Gamma p_0 \mathbf{k} (\mathbf{k} \cdot
\boldsymbol{\xi}_1) \\
& - \frac{1}{4 \pi}  \{ \mathbf{k} \times [\mathbf{k} \times
(\boldsymbol{\xi}_1 \times \mathbf{B}_0)] \} \times \mathbf{B}_0 .
\end{aligned}
\tag{26.8}\] As expected from the general perturbation theory, the oscillation equation give rise to an eigenvalue problem in the form \[
- \rho_0 \omega^2 \boldsymbol{\xi}_1 =\mathbf{F} (\mathbf{k}) \boldsymbol{\xi}_1,
\tag{26.9}\] where \(\mathbf{F} (\mathbf{k})\) is a matrix. This equation has solutions with \(\boldsymbol{\xi}_1 \neq 0\) if and only if \[
\det [\mathbf{F} (\mathbf{k}) + \rho_0 \omega^2 \mathbf{I}] = 0.
\tag{26.10}\] The last equation is defines the dispersion relation \(\omega = \omega (\mathbf{k})\). The eigenvectors of \(\mathbf{F} (\mathbf{k})\) define the polarization vector \(\boldsymbol{\xi}_1\) of the wave.

title: 26  MHD Waves
text: Figure 26.1: Lagrangian displacement of a fluid element from position \(\mathbf{x}\) to position \(\mathbf{x}+\boldsymbol{\xi}\).

title: 26  MHD Waves
text:
26.2 Families of MHD Waves
In general, there are three solutions to the eigenvalue problem Equation 26.9, corresponding to three different modes. In the unmagnetized case, the three modes are degenerate (in a uniform medium), so we find only sound waves. In the magnetized case, there are always three types of waves: Alfvén waves, slow-, and fast-magnetosonic waves. We consider these separately below.

26.2.1 Alfvén Waves
We consider at first the situation depicted in Figure 26.2:

\(\mathbf{B}_0\) is along \(z\)
\(\mathbf{k}\) is in the \(x z\)-plane
\(\boldsymbol{\xi}\) is along \(y\)

Note that \(\mathbf{k} \cdot \boldsymbol{\xi}= 0\), meaning that \(\delta \rho = \delta p = 0\).






Figure 26.2: Geometry of the Alfvén wave: \(\mathbf{B}_0\) along \(z\), \(\mathbf{k}\) in the \(xz\)-plane at an angle \(\theta\) from \(\mathbf{B}_0\), and displacement \(\boldsymbol{\xi}\) along \(y\).



To compute the Lorentz force we proceed as follows. First we note that \[
\boldsymbol{\xi} \times \mathbf{B}_0 {= \xi_y}  B_0  \hat{\mathbf{x}} .
\tag{26.11}\] Next, we compute the magnetic field perturbation as \[
\mathbf{k} \times (\boldsymbol{\xi} \times \mathbf{B}_0) = k \xi_y B_0 \cos
\theta \hat{\mathbf{y}} = \delta \mathbf{B}.
\tag{26.12}\] The current is given by \[
\mathbf{k} \times [\mathbf{k} \times (\boldsymbol{\xi} \times \mathbf{B}_0)] = -
k^2 \xi_y B_0 \cos \theta \hat{\mathbf{k}}_{\perp} = 4 \pi \delta
\mathbf{j}.
\tag{26.13}\] Finally, the Lorentz force is \[
4 \pi \delta \mathbf{j} \times \mathbf{B}_0 = k^2 B_0^2 \cos^2 \theta \xi_y
\hat{\mathbf{y}} = (\mathbf{k} \cdot \mathbf{B}_0)^2 \boldsymbol{\xi}.
\tag{26.14}\] So \(\boldsymbol{\xi}\) evolves as a mass attached to an elastic spring with spring constant \((\mathbf{k} \cdot \mathbf{B}_0)^2\). In formulas, \[
\begin{aligned}
- \rho_0 \omega^2 \xi_y &= \tfrac{1}{4 \pi} k^2 B_0^2 \cos^2 \theta \xi_y \\
\Longrightarrow \quad & \boxed{\omega = \pm \frac{B_0}{\sqrt{4 \pi \rho_0}} k
\cos \theta = kv_A \cos \theta .}
\end{aligned}
\tag{26.15}\] This type of waves are called Alfvén waves from Alfvén (1942) (Physics Nobel Prize in 1970). Some comments are in order.

If  \(\theta = 0\), these waves propagate along the field lines with velocity (Alfvén velocity): \[
v_A = \frac{B_0}{\sqrt{4 \pi \rho_0}} .
\tag{26.16}\] If \(\theta > 0\), the waves can still propagate (as long as \(\theta \neq 90^{\circ}\) or \(270^{\circ}\)), but at a reduced speed.
The displacement \(\boldsymbol{\xi}\) is perpendicular to the background field \(\mathbf{B}_0\), so these waves are transverse. More precisely, Alfvén waves behave as transverse waves in an elastic string (the magnetic field). Indeed, the restoring force for these waves is magnetic tension.
As already mentioned \(\delta \rho = \delta p = 0\) for these waves. As such, Alfvén waves are incompressible and exist also in incompressible flows.

Although we have derived Alfvén waves as small perturbations, it turns out that Alfvén waves are an exact solution to the full non-linear equations. This means that MHD flows can support arbitrarily strong waves.


26.2.2 Magnetosonic Waves
We consider at first the situation depicted in Figure 26.3:

\(\mathbf{B}_0\) is along \(z\)
\(\mathbf{k}\) is in the \(x z\)-plane
\(\boldsymbol{\xi}\) is also in the \(x z\)-plane

Note that \(\delta p, \delta \rho\) are no longer necessarily zero.






Figure 26.3: Geometry of the magnetosonic wave: \(\mathbf{B}_0\) along \(z\), \(\mathbf{k}\) in the \(xz\)-plane at an angle \(\theta\) from \(\mathbf{B}_0\), and displacement \(\boldsymbol{\xi}\) also in the \(xz\)-plane.



We can compute the current using the following vector identity \[
\mathbf{a} \times (\mathbf{b} \times \mathbf{c}) =\mathbf{b} (\mathbf{a}
\cdot \mathbf{c}) -\mathbf{c} (\mathbf{a} \cdot \mathbf{b})
\tag{26.17}\] and the fact that \(\mathbf{k} \perp \boldsymbol{\xi} \times \mathbf{B}_0\), since the latter is in the \(y\)-direction, we can write \[
\mathbf{k} \times [\mathbf{k} \times (\boldsymbol{\xi} \times \mathbf{B}_0)]
=\mathbf{k} [\mathbf{k} \cdot (\boldsymbol{\xi} \times \mathbf{B}_0)] - k^2
(\boldsymbol{\xi} \times \mathbf{B}_0) = - k^2 (\boldsymbol{\xi} \times
\mathbf{B}_0) .
\tag{26.18}\] Plugging this into the expression for the Lorentz force gives \[
\delta \mathbf{j} \times \mathbf{B}_0 = \frac{1}{4 \pi}  \{ \mathbf{k}
\times [\mathbf{k} \times (\boldsymbol{\xi} \times \mathbf{B}_0)] \} \times
\mathbf{B}_0 = - \frac{k^2}{4 \pi}  (\boldsymbol{\xi} \times \mathbf{B}_0)
\times \mathbf{B}_0 = - \frac{k^2 B_0^2 \xi_x}{4 \pi}  \hat{\mathbf{x}} .
\tag{26.19}\] The pressure force is \[
- \Gamma p_0 \mathbf{k} (\mathbf{k} \cdot \boldsymbol{\xi}) = - k^2 \Gamma p_0
(\xi_x \sin \theta + \xi_z \cos \theta)  (\sin \theta \hat{\mathbf{x}} +
\cos \theta \hat{\mathbf{z}}) .
\tag{26.20}\] Using \(c_s^2 = \Gamma p_0 / \rho_0\) and \(v_A = B_0 / \sqrt{4 \pi \rho_0}\), we find \[
\omega^2  \left(\begin{array}{c}
\xi_x\\
\xi_z
\end{array}\right) = k^2 \left(\begin{array}{cc}
c_s^2 \sin^2 \theta + v_A^2 & c_s^2 \sin \theta \cos \theta\\
c_s^2 \sin \theta \cos \theta & c_s^2 \cos^2 \theta
\end{array}\right) \left(\begin{array}{c}
\xi_x\\
\xi_z
\end{array}\right) .
\tag{26.21}\] The dispersion relation is (after a long calculation): \[
\boxed{
\begin{aligned}
\left( \frac{\omega}{k} \right)^2 = {} & \frac{v_A^2 + c_s^2}{2} \\
& \pm \frac{1}{2} \sqrt{(v_A^2 - c_s^2)^2 + 4 c_s^2 v_A^2 \sin^2 \theta} .
\end{aligned}}
\tag{26.22}\] So there are two solutions and two corresponding polarization vectors \(\boldsymbol{\xi}_s\) and \(\boldsymbol{\xi}_f\). Note that \(\boldsymbol{\xi}_s \perp \boldsymbol{\xi}_f\), since the matrix \(\mathbf{F} (\mathbf{k})\) in Equation 26.21 is self-adjoint. Conventionally, \(\boldsymbol{\xi}_s\) is taken to be the polarization corresponding to the smaller group velocity. This is the so-called slow magnetosonic wave. Conversely, \(\boldsymbol{\xi}_f\) is called the fast magnetosonic wave. As we will see shortly, these have a mixed character of sound and magnetic waves.

title: 26  MHD Waves
text:
26.3 Effect of Propagation Direction
We can get additional insight into the nature of the three modes by considering the properties of waves propagating along the magnetic field lines, or perpendicular to them. The general case will turn out to be intermediate between these two limits.

26.3.1 Parallel Propagating Waves (\(\theta = 0\))
Let us consider the case of waves propagating along the background magnetic field lines, that is \(\theta = 0\). In this case, the dispersion relation for Alfvén, slow, and fast modes are \[
\left( \frac{\omega}{k} \right)^2 = v_A^2, \qquad \left( \frac{\omega}{k}
\right)^2 = \frac{1}{2}  [v_A^2 + c_s^2 \pm |v_A^2 - c_s^2 |] .
\tag{26.23}\] There are two different cases, depending on whether \(v_A > c_s\) or \(v_A < c_s\), shown in Figure 26.4.






Figure 26.4: Polarization diagram for MHD waves propagating along the background magnetic field.




If \(v_A > c_s\), then

The slow mode polarization is along the magnetic field, the mode propagate at speed \(c_s\) and its restoring force is pressure.
Fast and Alfvén modes are orthogonal to the magnetic field and to each other and both have the character of Alfvén waves propagating with speed \(v_A\). Magnetic tension is their restoring force.

If \(v_A < c_s\), then the situation is similar as before, but slow and fast mode exchange character: the fast mode is now a sound wave, while the slow mode is an Alfvén wave.



26.3.2 Perpendicularly Propagating Waves (\(\theta = 90^{\circ}\))
Let us consider the case of waves propagating perpendicular to the field lines. In this case, Alfvén and slow modes cannot propagate (they have \(\omega_{A, s} = 0\)). The fast-magnetosonic wave satisfies the dispersion relation \[
\left( \frac{\omega}{k} \right)^2 = v_A^2 + c_s^2 .
\tag{26.24}\] In this case \(\boldsymbol{\xi}_f\) is parallel to \(\mathbf{k}\). The restoring force for the mode is the sum of both magnetic tension and pressure, which explains why this mode is called the “magnetosonic” mode.


26.3.3 Friedrichs Diagrams
Friedrichs diagrams show the propagation velocity of the different MHD modes as a function of a generic propagation angle \(\theta\). The special cases of \(\theta = 0, 90^{\circ}\) discussed above correspond to the \(x\)- and \(y\)-axis in Figure 26.5. In general, slow and fast modes have a mixed character between sound waves and Alfvén waves.






Figure 26.5: Friedrichs Diagrams for ideal-MHD.

title: 26  MHD Waves
text:
26.4 Weak and Strong Field Limits
Finally, it is also instructive to compare slow- and fast-magnetosonic waves in the limits of weak magnetic field (\(c_s \gg v_A\)) and strong magnetic field \((v_A \gg c_s)\), as illustrated in Figure 26.6. Note that when \(v_A\) becomes a sizable fraction of the speed of light, we can no longer use Newtonian MHD, because the displacement current becomes important. In this limit, one needs to use the (significantly more complex) equations of relativistic magnetohydrodynamics.






Figure 26.6: Slow and fast magnetosonic waves in the limits of weak (left panel) and strong (right panel) magnetic fields.




Left panel: the fast mode is \(\sim\) a sound wave and the slow mode is nearly perpendicular to \(\mathbf{k}\).
Right panel: the fast mode is \(\sim\) an Alfvén wave and the slow mode is nearly parallel to \(\mathbf{B}_0\).

title: 26  MHD Waves
text:
26.5 Shock Waves
As for non-magnetized gasses, MHD waves can steepen into shock waves. Alfvén waves can steepen into rotational discontinuities, in which the magnetic field direction suddenly changes across an interface. Slow- and fast-magnetosonic waves can give rise to (slow and fast) shocks and rarefaction waves. The theory of MHD shocks is very complex and beyond the scope of this course. A good overview is given in Bazer and Ericson (1959). It is important to be aware of that, even in the case of shocks propagating along magnetic field lines, MHD effects can be important. For example, hydrodynamics shocks can split into a slow and a fast shock, separated by a region in which a perpendicular component of the \(B\)-field is created. These are sometimes called switch on and switch off discontinuities.
We treat in detail only one case that is relevant for the interstellar medium: a shock propagating in an isothermal flow with perpendicular magnetic field, as illustrated in Figure 26.7.






Figure 26.7: Isothermal shock propagating in a medium with perpendicular magnetic field.



The shock conditions for the shock shown in Figure 26.7 are: \[
[\![ \rho u ]\!] = 0, \quad [\![ Bu ]\!] = 0,
\quad \left[\!\left[ p + \rho u^2 + \frac{B^2}{8 \pi} \right]\!\right]
= 0,
\tag{26.25}\] where \([\![ \cdot ]\!]\) denotes the jump across the shock.
We remind that, in the absence of a magnetic field, the compression factor of an isothermal shock is \[
\frac{\rho_2}{\rho_1} = \left( \frac{u_1}{a} \right)^2,
\tag{26.26}\] which can become arbitrarily large for large upstream Mach numbers. This is dramatically different when a magnetic field is present, as long as it is sufficiently strong: \[
u_1 \gg v_A = \frac{B_1}{\sqrt{4 \pi \rho_1}} \gg a.
\tag{26.27}\] In this case, from \([\![ \rho u ]\!] = [\![ Bu ]\!] = 0\), we conclude that \[
\frac{B_1}{\rho_1} = \frac{B_2}{\rho_2} .
\tag{26.28}\] From the conservation of momentum, we have (using \(u_1 \gg v_{A, 1} \gg a\)) \[
\begin{aligned}
\frac{\rho_2}{\rho_1} &= \frac{a^2 + u_1^2 + \frac{1}{2} v_A^2}{a^2 + u_2^2 +
\frac{B_2^2}{8 \pi \rho_2}} \\
&\approx \frac{u_1^2}{a^2 + u_2^2 +
\frac{B_2^2}{8 \pi \rho_2^2} \rho_2} \\
&= \frac{u_1^2}{a^2 + u_2^2 +
\frac{B_1^2}{8 \pi \rho_1}  \frac{\rho_2}{\rho_1}} \\
&\approx \frac{u_1^2}{\frac{v_A^2}{2}  \frac{\rho_2}{\rho_1}} .
\end{aligned}
\tag{26.29}\] Solving for \(\rho_2 / \rho_1\), we obtain \[
\boxed{\frac{\rho_2}{\rho_1} = \sqrt{2}  \frac{u_1}{v_A} .}
\tag{26.30}\] This shows that the compression ratio now scales with the Alfvénic Mach number, instead of the Mach number squared, of the upstream gas. This is another example showing that magnetic fields play an important role in the dynamics of the interstellar medium and in star formation.

title: 26  MHD Waves
text:
26.6 In-class worksheet
Fast Magnetosonic Waves. Consider a homogeneous plasma described by the ideal-MHD equations with \[
\rho_0 = \mathrm{const}, \qquad \mathbf{v}_0 = 0, \qquad \mathbf{B}_0 =
B_0  \hat{\mathbf{z}} .
\tag{26.31}\]

Introduce a small perturbation in the form of a displacement \(\boldsymbol{\xi} (t, \mathbf{x})\) of the fluid elements and show that the oscillation equation is \[
\begin{aligned}
& \rho_0  \frac{\partial^2 \boldsymbol{\xi}}{\partial t^2} = \Gamma p_0 \nabla
(\nabla \cdot \boldsymbol{\xi}) \\
& \quad + \frac{1}{4 \pi} \{ \nabla \times [\nabla
\times (\boldsymbol{\xi} \times \mathbf{B}_0)] \} \times \mathbf{B}_0 .
\end{aligned}
\tag{26.32}\]
Introduce the ansatz \(\boldsymbol{\xi} (t, \mathbf{x}) = e^{\mathrm{i} (\mathbf{k} \cdot \mathbf{x}- \omega t)}\) and show that Equation 26.32 reduces to \[
\begin{aligned}
& - \rho_0 \omega^2 \boldsymbol{\xi}_1 = - \Gamma p_0 \mathbf{k} (\mathbf{k}
\cdot \boldsymbol{\xi}_1) \\
& \quad - \frac{1}{4 \pi}  \{ \mathbf{k} \times
[\mathbf{k} \times (\boldsymbol{\xi}_1 \times \mathbf{B}_0)] \} \times
\mathbf{B}_0 .
\end{aligned}
\tag{26.33}\] [Hint. Use \(\partial_t \rightarrow \mathrm{i} \omega\) and \(\nabla \rightarrow \mathrm{i} \mathbf{k}\).]
Consider waves with \(\mathbf{k} \parallel \hat{\mathbf{x}}\) and \(\boldsymbol{\xi} \parallel \mathbf{k}\). Find the dispersion relation \(\omega = \omega (\mathbf{k})\) and compute group and phase velocities for these waves.

title: 26  MHD Waves
text:
26.7 Exercises

Exercise 26.1 (Torsional Alfvén waves)  

Show that in cylindrical coordinates the toroidal Alfvén wave \[
\begin{aligned}
\mathbf{v} &= \epsilon v_A g (R) f (z - v_A t)  \hat{\boldsymbol{\phi}}, \\
\mathbf{B} &= B_0  \hat{\mathbf{z}} - \epsilon B_0 g (R) f (z - v_A t)
\hat{\boldsymbol{\phi}},
\end{aligned}
\tag{26.34}\] satisfies the ideal-MHD equations to order \(\epsilon\), where \(f\) and \(g\) are arbitrary functions.
Consider a region filled with uniform plasma at rest and introduce an infinitely conducting, thin disk of radius \(a\) at the origin in the \(x y\)-plane. Suddenly the disk starts rotating with the small constant angular velocity \(\omega\). Use the above solution and the condition that the tangential velocity at the disk is continuous to show that at any later time \(t\) all the plasma with \(R < a\), \(| z | < v_A t\) is rotating with angular velocity \(\omega\) and that the rest of the plasma is still at rest.
If the disk has surface density \(\Sigma\), how long will it be before it “starts” to slow down?

title: 27  The Magnetorotational Instability
text:
27.1 Qualitative Picture
The magnetorotational instability (MRI) was first discovered in the context of plasma fusion reactors by Velikhov (1959) and Chandrasekhar (1961) and then rediscovered in the context of accretion disks by Balbus and Hawley (1991). This is the instability thought to be responsible for the \(\alpha\)-viscosity in many astrophysical systems: from X-ray binaries to AGN disks. It is one of the most important, among the many instabilities operating in plasmas, so we will cover it in detail in these notes.
It was long known that a way to transport angular momentum in the disk is through magnetic stresses, that is the \(B_r B_{\theta} / 4 \pi\) term in the momentum equation. However, to explain the observed luminosities from accretion disks, the magnetic stresses must be similar in magnitude to the pressure in the disk \(p\) (the proportionality constant being the \(\alpha\)-viscosity coefficient). Given a small component of the field in the radial direction, flux freezing can grow \(B_{\theta}\) linearly in time. However, since \(B_r\) is small, this mechanism can transport angular momentum efficiently only if \(B_{\theta}^2 \gg p\). Such a strong toroidal field cannot be contained in the disk. The requirement for the magnetic stresses to do the job of transporting angular momentum is that \(B_r^2 \approx B_{\theta}^2 \approx 4 \pi \rho c_s^2\). Detailed simulations have shown that MRI is a mechanism that naturally produces the required field strengths over a short timescale.
Consider an accretion disk with Keplerian angular velocity profile \[
\Omega (R) = \Omega_0  \left( \frac{R_0}{R} \right)^{3 / 2},
\tag{27.1}\] initially threaded by a vertical magnetic field \(B_0 \hat{\mathbf{z}}\). Let \(A\) and \(B\) be two fluid elements connected by a magnetic field line (initially vertical) and displace their positions according to \(\xi_r = \epsilon \cos k z\), as shown in Figure 27.1. The fluid elements \(A\) and \(B\) immediately accelerate to match the local angular velocity. However, as a result of the change in angular velocity, a toroidal component of the field, \(B_{\theta}\) is generated by the stretching of the original field line.
The magnetic tension then creates an attractive force between \(A\) and \(B\), which has the effect of transporting angular momentum from \(A\) to \(B\). This causes \(A\) to lose angular momentum and sink further inwards, while \(B\) gains angular momentum and starts moving outwards. In turn, because the angular velocity decreases with radius, \(A\) increases its angular velocity, while \(B\) slows down, further separating the two points. This in turn enhances the magnetic tension force. The cycle we have just described is unstable, so the initial perturbation grows exponentially in time, until the system becomes nonlinear.
The mechanism we have just described involves the magnetic tension force, so it is natural to expect a characteristic growth rate of \[
\gamma \approx kv_A, \qquad v_A = \frac{B_z}{\sqrt{4 \pi \rho}} .
\tag{27.2}\] In our derivation, we have assumed the field to be sufficiently weak, so that the displaced fluid elements can acquire the angular velocity of their surroundings. This should be valid as long as \[
\omega_A = kv_A \lesssim \Omega .
\tag{27.3}\] We will find that the exact condition for instability is \(kv_A < \sqrt{3} \Omega\), so the maximum growth rate is achieved by taking \(k\) sufficiently large, so that \(\gamma \approx kv_A \approx \Omega\). This is a very short timescale: the MRI grows over the orbital time scale! Moreover, the growth rate is independent of the field strength, as long as \(v_A\) is not so large that the required \(k\) to satisfy \(kv_A < \sqrt{3} \Omega\) corresponds to perturbation with characteristic size larger than the vertical size of the disk.

title: 27  The Magnetorotational Instability
text: Figure 27.1: Qualitative description of the magnetorotational instability transporting angular momentum between fluid elements \(A\) and \(B\). Left panel: meridional view. Right panel: orbital plane.

title: 27  The Magnetorotational Instability
text:
27.2 Detailed Calculation
The starting point is the Euler equation, which we write in the usual form in cylindrical coordinates \((R, \theta, z)\): \[
\rho \left[ \frac{\partial \mathbf{v}}{\partial t} + (\mathbf{v} \cdot
\nabla) \mathbf{v} \right] = - \nabla \left( p + \frac{B^2}{8 \pi} \right) +
\frac{(\mathbf{B} \cdot \nabla) \mathbf{B}}{4 \pi} +\mathbf{g} \rho .
\tag{27.4}\] We consider a disk that is Keplerian and threaded by a vertical magnetic field: \[
\mathbf{v}= R \Omega \hat{\boldsymbol{\theta}} +\mathbf{u}, \qquad \mathbf{B}=
B_0  \hat{\mathbf{z}} +\mathbf{b}, \qquad p + \frac{B^2}{8 \pi} = P_0 + P.
\tag{27.5}\] We will treat \(\mathbf{u}\) and \(\mathbf{b}\) as (small) Eulerian perturbations. We will only consider modes that are axisymmetric (no \(\theta\) dependence) and incompressible \[
\nabla \cdot \mathbf{u}= \frac{1}{R}  \frac{\partial (Ru_r)}{\partial R} +
\frac{\partial u_z}{\partial z} = 0.
\tag{27.6}\] To leading order in \(\mathbf{u}\) (using Kepler’s law) \[
\begin{alignedat}{2}
(\mathbf{v} \cdot \nabla) \mathbf{v} &{}\rightarrow{} && (R \Omega)
\hat{\boldsymbol{\theta}} \cdot \nabla \mathbf{u}+\mathbf{u} \cdot \nabla (R
\Omega \hat{\boldsymbol{\theta}}) =  \\
& && - 2 \Omega u_{\theta}  \hat{\mathbf{R}} + \left( R \frac{\mathrm{d}
\Omega}{\mathrm{d} R} + 2 \Omega \right) u_R \hat{\boldsymbol{\theta}} = \\
& && \frac{1}{2} \Omega u_R  \hat{\boldsymbol{\theta}} - 2 \Omega u_{\theta}
\hat{\mathbf{R}} .
\end{alignedat}
\tag{27.7}\] Similarly, \[
\begin{alignedat}{2}
(\mathbf{B} \cdot \nabla) \mathbf{B} &{}\rightarrow{} && B_0  \hat{\mathbf{z}}
\cdot \nabla \mathbf{b}+\mathbf{b} \cdot \nabla (B_0  \hat{\mathbf{z}}) =
\\
& && B_0  \dfrac{\partial b_R}{\partial z}  \hat{\mathbf{R}} + B_0
\frac{\partial b_{\theta}}{\partial z}  \hat{\boldsymbol{\theta}} + B_0
\frac{\partial b_z}{\partial z}  \hat{\mathbf{z}} .
\end{alignedat}
\tag{27.8}\] So the linearized momentum equation reads \[
\frac{\partial \mathbf{u}}{\partial t} + \frac{1}{2} \Omega u_R
\hat{\boldsymbol{\theta}} - 2 \Omega u_{\theta}  \hat{\mathbf{R}} = -
\frac{1}{\rho} \nabla P + B_0  \dfrac{\partial b_R}{\partial z}
\hat{\mathbf{R}} + B_0  \frac{\partial b_{\theta}}{\partial z}
\hat{\boldsymbol{\theta}} + B_0  \frac{\partial b_z}{\partial z}
\hat{\mathbf{z}} .
\tag{27.9}\] The induction equation can be linearized in a similar way: \[
\begin{aligned}
& \nabla \times (\mathbf{v} \times \mathbf{B}) \\
& \quad \rightarrow \nabla \times \bigl[(R \Omega \hat{\boldsymbol{\theta}}) \times (b_R \hat{\mathbf{R}} + b_{\theta} \hat{\boldsymbol{\theta}} + b_z \hat{\mathbf{z}}) \\
& \qquad\qquad + (u_R \hat{\mathbf{R}} + u_{\theta} \hat{\boldsymbol{\theta}} + u_z \hat{\mathbf{z}}) \times (B_0 \hat{\mathbf{z}})\bigr] \\
& \quad = \nabla \times [- R \Omega b_R \hat{\mathbf{z}} + R \Omega b_z \hat{\mathbf{R}} \\
& \qquad\qquad - u_R B_0 \hat{\boldsymbol{\theta}} + u_{\theta} B_0 \hat{\mathbf{R}}] \\
& \quad = \nabla \times [ (R \Omega b_z + u_{\theta} B_0) \hat{\mathbf{R}} \\
& \qquad\qquad - u_R B_0 \hat{\boldsymbol{\theta}} - R \Omega b_R \hat{\mathbf{z}}] \\
& \quad = \left( \frac{\partial u_R}{\partial z} B_0 \right) \hat{\mathbf{R}} + \biggl( R \Omega \frac{\partial b_z}{\partial z} + \frac{\partial u_{\theta}}{\partial z} B_0 \\
& \qquad\qquad - \frac{3}{2} \Omega b_R + \Omega \frac{\partial (Rb_R)}{\partial R} \biggr) \hat{\boldsymbol{\theta}} \\
& \qquad\qquad - \frac{1}{R} \left[ \frac{\partial (Ru_R B_0)}{\partial R} \right] \hat{\mathbf{z}} \\
& \quad = \left( \frac{\partial u_R}{\partial z} B_0 \right) \hat{\mathbf{R}} + \left( \frac{\partial u_{\theta}}{\partial z} B_0 - \frac{3}{2} \Omega b_R \right) \hat{\boldsymbol{\theta}} \\
& \qquad\qquad - \frac{1}{R} \left[ \frac{\partial (Ru_R B_0)}{\partial R} \right] \hat{\mathbf{z}} .
\end{aligned}
\tag{27.10}\] In the last equation we have also used the condition that \(\nabla \cdot \mathbf{b}= 0\).
We will consider a small patch of the disk, so that we can use the Fourier (WKB) ansatz: \[
\mathbf{u}=\mathbf{u}_0 e^{\lambda t + \mathrm{i} (k_R R + k_z z)}, \qquad
\mathbf{b}=\mathbf{b}_0 e^{\lambda t + \mathrm{i} (k_R R + k_z z)}
\tag{27.11}\] with the additional assumption that \(k_z \gg k_R\). Substituting this into the linearized equations of motions yields \[
\begin{alignedat}{2}
\lambda u_r - 2 \Omega u_{\theta} &{}={} && - \mathrm{i} k_R  \frac{P}{\rho} +
\frac{\mathrm{i} k_z B_0 b_r}{4 \pi \rho},  \\
\lambda u_{\theta} + \frac{\Omega}{2} u_r &{}={} && \frac{\mathrm{i} k_z B_0
b_{\theta}}{4 \pi \rho}, \\
\lambda u_z &{}={} && - \mathrm{i} k_z  \frac{P}{\rho} + \frac{\mathrm{i} k_z B_0 b_z}{4
\pi \rho} .
\end{alignedat}
\tag{27.12}\] We can eliminate \(P / \rho\) from the last equation and insert it into the first to obtain (in the limit \(k_z \gg k_R\)): \[
\lambda u_r - 2 \Omega u_{\theta} = \mathrm{i} k_z  \frac{B_0 b_r}{4 \pi \rho} .
\tag{27.13}\] The linearized induction equation yields \[
\begin{alignedat}{2}
\lambda b_R &{}={} && \mathrm{i} k_z B_0 u_R  \\
\lambda b_{\theta} &{}={} && - \frac{3}{2} \Omega b_R + \mathrm{i} k_z B_0
u_{\theta} .
\end{alignedat}
\tag{27.14}\] Eliminating \(b_R\) in the second equation yields \[
\lambda b_{\theta} = - \frac{3}{2}  \frac{\mathrm{i} k_z B_0 \Omega}{\lambda}
u_R + \mathrm{i} k_z B_0 u_{\theta} .
\tag{27.15}\] Eliminating \(b_{\theta}\) and \(b_R\) in the momentum equations above and introducing \(\omega_A^2 = k_z^2 B_0^2 / 4 \pi \rho\) yields \[
\begin{alignedat}{2}
(\lambda^2 + \omega_A^2) u_R &{}={} && 2 \lambda \Omega u_{\theta},  \\
(\lambda^2 + \omega_A^2) u_{\theta} &{}={} && \left( - \frac{\lambda}{2} \Omega
+ \frac{3}{2}  \frac{\omega_A^2 \Omega}{\lambda} \right) u_R .
\end{alignedat}
\tag{27.16}\] Introducing \[
\mu^2 = \lambda^2 + \omega_A^2,
\tag{27.17}\] the dispersion relation becomes \[
f (\mu^2) = \mu^4 + \Omega^2 \mu^2 - 4 \Omega^2 \omega_A^2 = 0.
\tag{27.18}\] The instability is present when the second root of \(f (\mu^2)\) occurs for \(\mu^2 > \omega_A^2\). This occurs if \[
f (\omega_A^2) = \omega_A^4 - 3 \Omega^2 \omega_A^2 < 0 \Longrightarrow
\boxed{\frac{k_z B_0}{\sqrt{4 \pi \rho}} = \omega_A < \sqrt{3} \Omega .}
\tag{27.19}\] We find that if \(k_z\) is sufficiently small (sufficiently large wavelength of the perturbation), then the mode is unstable. However, if the background field is too large, then the condition in Equation 27.19 might only be satisfied for \(k_z\) that corresponds to modes larger than the disk size, so the system is stable.
The growth rate of the instability is found by solving the dispersion relation to find \[
\lambda^2 = \frac{\Omega}{2}  \left( - \Omega + \sqrt{\Omega^2 + 16
\omega_A^2} \right) - \omega_A^2,
\tag{27.20}\] which is maximized when \[
\omega_A = \frac{\sqrt{15}}{4} \Omega \approx \Omega,
\tag{27.21}\] which corresponds to \[
k_{\max} \approx \frac{\sqrt{4 \pi \rho}}{B_0} \Omega .
\tag{27.22}\] The growth rate of the most unstable mode is \[
\boxed{\lambda_{\max} = \frac{3}{4} \Omega .}
\tag{27.23}\] It is instructive to check the limit of our analysis when \(B_0 \rightarrow 0\), which corresponds to \(\omega_A \rightarrow 0\). If \(\omega_A \equiv 0\), then Equation 27.16 reduces to \[
\lambda^2 u_R = - \Omega^2 u_R, \qquad \lambda^2 u_{\theta} = - \Omega^2
u_{\theta} .
\tag{27.24}\] That is the perturbations oscillate with the epicyclic frequency \(\Omega\).
In the limit of \(0 < \omega_A \ll \Omega\) (long wavelength perturbations, or weak magnetic field), we can drop all the \(\omega_A\) terms in Equation 27.16, with the exception of the term multiplied by \(\Omega\) to obtain \[
\begin{alignedat}{2}
\lambda^2 u_R &{}={} && 2 \lambda \Omega u_{\theta},  \\
\lambda^2 u_{\theta} &{}={} && \left( - \frac{\lambda}{2} \Omega + \frac{3}{2}
\frac{\omega_A^2 \Omega}{\lambda} \right) u_R .
\end{alignedat}
\tag{27.25}\] Eliminating \(u_{\theta}\), we obtain: \[
\lambda^2 u_R = \left( \frac{3 \omega_A^2 \Omega^2}{\lambda^2} - \Omega^2
\right) u_R,
\tag{27.26}\] which has unstable solutions with \(\lambda^2 > 0\) as long as \(\omega_A > 0\).

title: 27  The Magnetorotational Instability
text:
27.3 In-class worksheet
There is a simple mechanical equivalent of the magnetorotational instability (MRI) in a disk with vertical magnetic field. This model is concerned with two particles of mass \(m\) orbiting a central object with angular velocity \(\Omega = \Omega (R)\) (not necessarily Keplerian). The particles are connected by a spring with spring constant \(mK\), as shown in Figure 27.2.






Figure 27.2: Mechanical analogue of the magnetorotational instability: two masses connected by a spring, orbiting a central object.



The coordinates \(x\) and \(y\) denote the displacement of one of the two masses from the common center of mass.

Assuming \(0 \leq x, y \ll R\), show that the displacement satisfies the differential equations \[
\begin{alignedat}{2}
\ddot{x} - 2 \Omega \dot{y} &{}={} && - \left( K + \frac{\mathrm{d}
\Omega^2}{\mathrm{d} \log R} \right) x, \\
\ddot{y} + 2 \Omega \dot{x} &{}={} && - Ky.
\end{alignedat}
\tag{27.27}\] Note that these are the same equations as those obtained for the MRI in a disk threaded by a vertical magnetic field, \(k_R = 0\), and \(K = (v_A k_z)^2 = \omega_A^2\).
Look for solutions in the form \(x (t) = x_0 e^{\lambda t},\) \(y (t) = y_0 e^{\lambda t}\). Find \(\lambda\).
Under what conditions is the system unstable?

title: Appendix A — Vector Calculus
text: A.1 In-class worksheet

title: Appendix A — Vector Calculus
text:
Compute the gradient of the function \[
f (x, y, z) = \frac{x}{\sqrt{x^2 + y^2 + z^2}} .
\tag{A.1}\]
Consider the vector field \[
\mathbf{E}= \hat{\mathbf{r}} = \left(\begin{array}{c}
\frac{x}{\sqrt{x^2 + y^2 + z^2}}\\
\frac{y}{\sqrt{x^2 + y^2 + z^2}}\\
\frac{z}{\sqrt{x^2 + y^2 + z^2}}
\end{array}\right) .
\tag{A.2}\] Compute

the gradient \[
\nabla \mathbf{E}= \left(\begin{array}{ccc}
\partial_x E_x & \partial_x E_y & \partial_x E_z\\
\partial_y E_x & \partial_y E_y & \partial_y E_z\\
\partial_z E_x & \partial_z E_y & \partial_z E_z
\end{array}\right) ;
\tag{A.3}\]
\(\nabla \cdot \mathbf{E}\);
\(\nabla \times \mathbf{E}\).

Prove that \[
\nabla \cdot \nabla f = \nabla^2 f = \frac{\partial^2 f}{\partial x^2} +
\frac{\partial^2 f}{\partial y^2} + \frac{\partial^2 f}{\partial z^2} .
\tag{A.4}\]
The divergence of a tensor field \[
\mathbf{T}= \left(\begin{array}{ccc}
T_{x x} & T_{x y} & T_{x z}\\
T_{y x} & T_{y y} & T_{y z}\\
T_{z x} & T_{z y} & T_{z z}
\end{array}\right)
\tag{A.5}\] is defined as \[
\nabla \cdot \mathbf{T}= \left(\begin{array}{c}
\partial_x T_{x x} + \partial_y T_{x y} + \partial_z T_{x z}\\
\partial_x T_{y x} + \partial_y T_{y y} + \partial_z T_{y z}\\
\partial_x T_{z x} + \partial_y T_{z y} + \partial_z T_{z z}
\end{array}\right) .
\tag{A.6}\] Prove that \[
\nabla \cdot (p\mathbf{I}) = \nabla \cdot \left(\begin{array}{ccc}
p &  & \\
& p & \\
&  & p
\end{array}\right) = \nabla p.
\tag{A.7}\]
